Chapter 4 Energy principles and virtual work

4.2 Mathematics: integrals over a body and the divergence theorem

So far we have integrated only over intervals. In section 3.5 we wrote the work of a force that changes along a straight path as an integral along the path, and in section 4.1 the work and the energy of a bar as an integral along the bar. We cut the bar into short pieces along its axis. Since we assumed that the energy density is the same over each cross section, each piece was described by a single number, its position \(x\). In a body that is not a bar, stresses and strains change in all three directions. We get the energy of such a body by cutting it into small pieces in all three directions and adding up the energies of the pieces. We get the force with which the surroundings act on the body across its surface by cutting the surface into small patches and adding up the forces on them. For such sums we need an integral over the body and an integral over its surface.

We have met both kinds of sums before, but without an integral. In section 2.8.4 we computed the moment of a force distributed over a face of a small cube as a sum of the moments of small forces on equal rectangles, and announced an exact form with an integral. In section 2.7.6 we put off the question whether the equilibrium equations at every point imply the equilibrium of every finite part of the body, precisely because it needs the exact sum of the forces over the surface of that part.

The goal of the section is twofold. First we will define the integral of a function over a body and over its surface. Then we will prove a theorem that turns an integral of derivatives over a body into an integral over its surface. For an interval we already know such a theorem. By the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.40, the integral of a derivative \(G'\) over the interval \([a, b]\) equals \(G(b) - G(a)\), so it depends only on the values at the end points that bound the interval. The theorem we will prove is the same idea for a body in space. With it we will show that every part of a body is in equilibrium, and we will also need it in section 4.5.

The route is this. Over a rectangle and over a box we will integrate in one variable at a time, for which we need uniform continuity in space, and we will show that it does not matter in which variable we integrate first. Then we will extend the integral to bodies made up of boxes and to their surface, and for such bodies we will also prove the theorem. Throughout we integrate only continuous functions, as all functions in our examples are. Then we will prove it also for bodies bounded above and below by the graph of a function, and for bodies that can be cut into such pieces, such as the round hanging bar. For bodies that we get by bending a box continuously, such as the pieces of a ball, we will prove it in section 4.3, and this will cover all the bodies of our examples. At the end we will test it on the hanging bar.

4.2.1 The force of water on a wall

Let us start with a face on which a force does not act evenly. A tank in the shape of a box is filled with still water to the height \(H = 1\) m. One of its vertical walls is a rectangle \(b = 2\) m wide (figure 4.12). How large is the force with which the water pushes on this wall?

We set up the coordinate system much as in section 2.7.6. The origin \(O\) is at the upper corner of the wall, at the water surface. The axis \(x\) points vertically down, the axis \(y\) horizontally along the wall, and the axis \(z\) perpendicular to the wall, out of the water. When we look at the wall from outside, the axis \(x\) points down, the axis \(y\) to the right and the axis \(z\) toward us. The quarter turn of the positive axis \(x\) into the positive axis \(y\) is then seen counterclockwise, so the system is right-handed (definition 2.29). The wall is a rectangle in the plane \(z = 0\). It consists of the points \((x, y, 0)\) with \(0 \le x \le H\) and \(0 \le y \le b\), and the coordinate \(x\) of a point is its depth below the surface.

In section 2.7.6 we obtained the law of hydrostatics from the equilibrium equations. The pressure in still water at the depth \(x\) is \(p = p_0 + \rho g\,x\), where \(p_0\) is the pressure of the air above the surface and \(\rho = 1000\) kg/m³ the density of water (VK appendix A.4, PDF p. 637). The water pushes on every bit of the wall perpendicular to it, with the force \(p\) per unit area (section 2.6.6). We assume that on the other side of the wall there is air at the same pressure \(p_0\), which pushes the wall the opposite way. The two shares \(p_0\) cancel, so in the direction of the axis \(z\) the wall is loaded by the force

\[\rho g\,x\]

per unit area. At the surface it is zero, at the bottom \(\rho g H = 1000 \cdot 9{,}81 \cdot 1\) Pa \(= 9810\) Pa. We take the wall to be flat and rigid, so that it does not bend under the pressure. This is a simplification that does not change the distribution of the pressure in the water.

How do we add up a force that changes over the wall? As the work in section 3.5.1, by cutting into small pieces. We cut the wall with horizontal lines at the depths \(0 = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_{\mathrm{l}} = H\) and with vertical lines at \(0 = y_0 < y_1 < \dots < y_{\mathrm{m}} = b\) into small rectangles (figure 4.12, right). The rectangle between the depths \(x_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\) and between the positions \(y_{\mathrm{j}-1}\) and \(y_{\mathrm{j}}\) has the area \(\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\), where \(\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}} = x_{\mathrm{i}} - x_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) and \(\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}} = y_{\mathrm{j}} - y_{\mathrm{j}-1}\). On it the pressure changes only a little, so the force on it is approximately \(\rho g\,\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\), where \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the depth of a chosen point of the rectangle, \(x_{\mathrm{i}-1} \le \xi_{\mathrm{i}} \le x_{\mathrm{i}}\). All these forces point in the direction of the axis \(z\), so their sum is also a force in this direction, with the magnitude equal to the sum of the magnitudes:

\[F \approx \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{l} \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{m} \rho g\,\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}} . \tag{4.6}\]

The double summation sign means that we add over all pairs \(i\) and \(j\), that is, over all \(l \cdot m\) rectangles.

Figure 4.13 shows what the sum measures. We draw the wall as if it lay on the floor and put up over each rectangle a column of height \(\rho g\,\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\). The volume of a column is one term of the sum (4.6), the sum is the volume of all columns. The tops of the columns fit a slanted surface whose height over the point at depth \(x\) is \(\rho g\,x\). As the rectangles get smaller, the sum approaches the volume of the wedge under this surface, if we measure the height in pascals and the base in square metres. The force on the wall is the volume of the wedge.

On this wall the pressure depends only on the depth, so horizontal strips would be enough. In general, however, the force per unit area changes over a face in both directions, as on the faces of the small cube in section 2.8.4, and we need rectangles.

We can add up the sum (4.6) in two steps (figure 4.14). First we add the rectangles in one horizontal row, at a fixed \(i\). They all have the same depth \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\) and the same height \(\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\), and their widths \(\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\) add up to \(b\). The row therefore contributes \(\rho g\,\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\,b\,\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\), the force on a horizontal strip of the wall. Then we add the strips:

\[F \approx \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{l} \rho g\,b\,\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}} .\]

This is a Riemann sum of the function \(x \mapsto \rho g\,b\,x\) on the interval \([0, H]\) (definition 3.32). The function is continuous, so by theorem 3.38, item 3, such a sum approaches the integral as the pieces get shorter,

\[\int_0^H \rho g\,b\,x\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{\rho g\,b\,H^2}{2} = \frac{1000 \cdot 9{,}81 \cdot 2 \cdot 1^2}{2}\ \text{N} = 9810\ \text{N} .\]

We computed the integral with the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.40, item 1, with the function \(G(x) = \rho g\,b\,x^2/2\), whose derivative is \(\rho g\,b\,x\) by the rules of differentiation (lemma 1.81).

We can also add up the sum in the other order, first along a vertical column of rectangles, at a fixed \(j\). This column is a vertical strip of the wall of width \(\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\). The sum over \(i\) is \(\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\) times a Riemann sum of the function \(x \mapsto \rho g\,x\) on \([0, H]\). It approaches the number \(\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}} \int_0^H \rho g\,x\,\mathrm{d}x = \Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\,\rho g H^2/2\), which is \(4905\ \text{N/m} \cdot \Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\), the force on a vertical strip. The vertical strips are all alike, because the pressure does not change along the axis \(y\), and their widths add up to \(b\). Altogether we get \(4905\ \text{N/m} \cdot 2\ \text{m} = 9810\) N, the same number.

This computation showed the idea, but not yet a proof. We used two things that we still have to justify. First, that the double sum (4.6) approaches one single number as the rectangles get smaller. Second, that this number equals the number we get by integrating in two steps, first in one variable with the other held fixed and then the result in the other, no matter in which variable we integrate first. We will prove both claims for continuous functions, on a rectangle and on a box.

4.2.2 The integral over a rectangle and over a box

The function we will integrate takes as input a point of a rectangle or a box, given by three coordinates, and gives as output a number. The pressure is such a function: its input is a point of the wall, its output the force per unit area. A box with edges along the axes is the set of points \(K = [a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\), that is, of all points \((x, y, z)\) with \(a_1 \le x \le b_1\), \(a_2 \le y \le b_2\) and \(a_3 \le z \le b_3\), where \(a_1 < b_1\), \(a_2 < b_2\) and \(a_3 < b_3\) are numbers (section 1.13.4). Its volume is \(V_{\mathrm{K}} = (b_1 - a_1)(b_2 - a_2)(b_3 - a_3)\). A rectangle with edges along the axes lies in a plane perpendicular to one of the axes. The wall of the tank lies in the plane \(z = 0\). Every face of a box is such a rectangle.

We will define the integral of a function over a box the way we computed the force on the wall in the second step. First we integrate in \(z\) with \(x\) and \(y\) fixed, then the result in \(y\) with \(x\) fixed, and finally that in \(x\). For this to make sense, every intermediate result must be integrable, for example continuous. Is the inner integral

\[g(x, y) = \int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} f(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\]

continuous in \(x\) and \(y\) when \(f\) is continuous? By linearity the difference \(g(x', y') - g(x, y)\) is the integral of the difference \(f(x', y', z) - f(x, y, z)\) over \(z\). This integral is small if the difference of the values of \(f\) at the points \((x, y, z)\) and \((x', y', z)\) is small, and that for all \(z\) at once. Continuity at each point separately does not ensure this, because the band \(\delta\) may be different at each point (section 3.5.4). We need one band for all points of the box, that is, uniform continuity. In section 3.5.4 we showed that a continuous function on a closed interval is uniformly continuous. The same proof works on every closed and bounded set of points.

Theorem 4.6 A continuous function on a closed bounded set is uniformly continuous (zvezna funkcija na zaprti omejeni množici je enakomerno zvezna)

Let \(K\) be a closed and bounded set of points of space (definition 1.74) and \(f\) a function that is defined and continuous on \(K\) (definition 1.67). Then for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that

\[|f(P) - f(Q)| < \eta \quad \text{for all points } P, Q \in K \text{ with } |PQ| < \delta .\]
Proof

We must show that for every error there is one band for all pairs of points. The proof is the proof of theorem 3.37, with points in place of numbers. We argue by contradiction.

  1. Suppose the claim does not hold. Then there is an error \(\eta > 0\) for which no band works: for every \(\delta > 0\) there are points \(P, Q \in K\) with \(|PQ| < \delta\) and \(|f(P) - f(Q)| \ge \eta\).
  2. We use this with the band \(\delta = 1/n\) for every natural number \(n\) and choose such points \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(Q_{\mathrm{n}}\). For them \(|P_{\mathrm{n}} Q_{\mathrm{n}}| < 1/n\) and \(|f(P_{\mathrm{n}}) - f(Q_{\mathrm{n}})| \ge \eta\).
  3. The set \(K\) is bounded, so the sequence \((P_{\mathrm{n}})\) is bounded. By lemma 1.77, the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem in space, it has a subsequence \((P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) that converges to some point \(C\).
  4. The set \(K\) is closed, so \(C\) lies in \(K\).
  5. Let us show that \((Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) converges to \(C\) too. We write the coordinates as \(P_{\mathrm{n}} = (x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}}, z_{\mathrm{n}})\), \(Q_{\mathrm{n}} = (x_{\mathrm{n}}', y_{\mathrm{n}}', z_{\mathrm{n}}')\) and \(C = (x_{\mathrm{C}}, y_{\mathrm{C}}, z_{\mathrm{C}})\). By the triangle inequality for numbers (lemma 1.6, item 1), and since no difference of coordinates is larger than the distance (step 2 of the proof of lemma 1.66),
    \[|x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}' - x_{\mathrm{C}}| \le |x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}' - x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}| + |x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}} - x_{\mathrm{C}}| \le |P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}} Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}| + |x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}} - x_{\mathrm{C}}| < \frac1k + |x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}} - x_{\mathrm{C}}| .\]
    In the last inequality we used step 2 and \(1/n_{\mathrm{k}} \le 1/k\), which follows from \(n_{\mathrm{k}} \ge k\) (lemma 1.53 on the indices of a subsequence).
  6. By lemma 1.66 on convergence coordinate by coordinate, \(x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}\) converges to \(x_{\mathrm{C}}\), so \(|x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}} - x_{\mathrm{C}}|\) goes to \(0\). Also \(1/k\) goes to \(0\) (lemma 1.39). By lemma 1.60 on limit laws for sequences, item 1, the right side of the inequality in step 5 therefore goes to \(0\). By the squeeze lemma 1.46 with the lower sequence \(0, 0, \dots\), also \(|x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}' - x_{\mathrm{C}}|\) goes to \(0\), and \(x_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}'\) converges to \(x_{\mathrm{C}}\). In the same way \(y_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}'\) converges to \(y_{\mathrm{C}}\) and \(z_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}'\) to \(z_{\mathrm{C}}\). By lemma 1.66, \((Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) therefore converges to \(C\).
  7. The function \(f\) is continuous at \(C\). By lemma 1.68 on continuity through sequences of points, \(f(P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) converges to \(f(C)\) and \(f(Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) converges to \(f(C)\).
  8. By lemma 1.60, items 1 and 2, the difference \(f(P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}) - f(Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) converges to \(f(C) - f(C) = 0\). For the error \(\eta\) of step 1 there is therefore an index \(N\) such that \(|f(P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}) - f(Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})| < \eta\) for every \(k \ge N\).
  9. This contradicts step 2, by which \(|f(P_{\mathrm{n}}) - f(Q_{\mathrm{n}})| \ge \eta\) for every \(n\), also for \(n = n_{\mathrm{N}}\). The assumption of step 1 is false.

Source: LEBL1 Def. 7.5.10 and Thm. 7.5.11 (PDF p. 291), for continuous functions on compact sets, where the proof uses covers. By Thm. 7.4.14 (PDF p. 284), closed and bounded sets in space are compact. The proof with sequences follows the proof of Thm. 3.4.4 (PDF p. 139) and is not from the source.

The proof repeated the proof for an interval. Boundedness gave a convergent subsequence, and closedness made sure that its limit lies in \(K\), where \(f\) is continuous. A box is closed and bounded (section 1.13.4). The same holds for a rectangle with edges along the axes, for example in the plane \(z = c\). It is given by the equation \(z = c\) and by four non-strict inequalities for \(x\) and \(y\), so it is closed by lemma 1.75, and it is bounded by the same computation as the box. A continuous function on a box or on a rectangle is therefore uniformly continuous.

Let us now show that an integral over one variable keeps the continuity in the others.

Lemma 4.7 Continuity of an integral over one variable (zveznost integrala po eni spremenljivki)
  1. Let \(f\) be a continuous function on the box \(K = [a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\). Then for all \(x \in [a_1, b_1]\) and \(y \in [a_2, b_2]\) the integral
    \[g(x, y) = \int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} f(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\]
    exists, and for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|g(x', y') - g(x, y)| < \eta\) for all \(x, x' \in [a_1, b_1]\) and \(y, y' \in [a_2, b_2]\) with \((x' - x)^2 + (y' - y)^2 < \delta^2\).
  2. Let a function \(g\), defined for \(x \in [a_1, b_1]\) and \(y \in [a_2, b_2]\), have the property of item 1: for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|g(x', y') - g(x, y)| < \eta\) whenever \((x' - x)^2 + (y' - y)^2 < \delta^2\). Then for every \(x \in [a_1, b_1]\) the function \(y \mapsto g(x, y)\) is continuous on \([a_2, b_2]\), and the function
    \[G(x) = \int_{\mathrm{a}_2}^{b_2} g(x, y)\,\mathrm{d}y\]
    is continuous on \([a_1, b_1]\).

The same holds if we exchange the roles of the coordinates, for example if we integrate first in \(x\) and then in \(z\).

Proof

We must show that the inner integral exists and that it changes little when the other variables change little.

1. The integral in \(z\).

  1. Let \(x\) and \(y\) be fixed. The function \(z \mapsto f(x, y, z)\) is continuous on \([a_3, b_3]\). For a number \(z_0\) and an error \(\eta\), the band \(\delta\) that definition 1.67 gives the function \(f\) at the point \((x, y, z_0)\) works, since the distance between the points \((x, y, z)\) and \((x, y, z_0)\) is \(|z - z_0|\). By theorem 3.38 the function is integrable, and \(g(x, y)\) exists.
  2. We choose \(\eta > 0\). The box is closed and bounded, so by theorem 4.6 there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|f(P) - f(Q)| < \eta/(2(b_3 - a_3))\) for all points \(P, Q \in K\) with \(|PQ| < \delta\).
  3. Let \((x' - x)^2 + (y' - y)^2 < \delta^2\). For every \(z \in [a_3, b_3]\) the distance between the points \((x, y, z)\) and \((x', y', z)\) is by (1.10) \(\sqrt{(x' - x)^2 + (y' - y)^2}\), which by lemma 1.28 is less than \(\delta\). By step 2 therefore
    \[-\frac{\eta}{2(b_3 - a_3)} < f(x', y', z) - f(x, y, z) < \frac{\eta}{2(b_3 - a_3)} .\]
  4. By linearity (lemma 3.39, item 1), \(g(x', y') - g(x, y) = \int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} \big(f(x', y', z) - f(x, y, z)\big)\,\mathrm{d}z\). The integrand is a difference of two continuous functions of \(z\) and is continuous by corollary 1.64. By the bound (same lemma, item 3) with the bounds of step 3,
    \[|g(x', y') - g(x, y)| \le \frac{\eta}{2(b_3 - a_3)}\,(b_3 - a_3) = \frac{\eta}{2} < \eta .\]

2. The integral in \(y\).

  1. Let \(x\) be fixed, \(\eta > 0\) and \(\delta\) the band that the assumption gives for this error. For \(|y' - y| < \delta\) we have \((x - x)^2 + (y' - y)^2 = (y' - y)^2 < \delta^2\), so \(|g(x, y') - g(x, y)| < \eta\). The function \(y \mapsto g(x, y)\) is therefore continuous on \([a_2, b_2]\) (definition 1.58) and integrable by theorem 3.38, so \(G(x)\) exists.
  2. We choose \(\eta > 0\) and take the band \(\delta\) that the assumption gives for the error \(\eta/(2(b_2 - a_2))\). For \(|x' - x| < \delta\) we have \((x' - x)^2 + (y - y)^2 < \delta^2\), so \(|g(x', y) - g(x, y)| < \eta/(2(b_2 - a_2))\) for every \(y \in [a_2, b_2]\).
  3. As in step 4 of the first part, \(|G(x') - G(x)| \le \eta/2 < \eta\). The function \(G\) is therefore continuous at every point of the interval \([a_1, b_1]\).

Source: LEBL1 Prop. 7.5.12 (PDF p. 292), for a continuous function of two variables on a rectangle. The proof follows the source.

The key was uniform continuity. One bound \(\eta/(2(b_3 - a_3))\) held for all \(z\) at once, so in the integration it was only multiplied by the length of the interval. Now we can define the integral.

Definition 4.8 Integral over a box (integral po kvadru)

Let \(f\) be a continuous function on the box \(K = [a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\). The integral of \(f\) over the box \(K\) is the number

\[\int_{\mathrm{K}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{a}_1}^{b_1} \bigg( \int_{\mathrm{a}_2}^{b_2} \bigg( \int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} f(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z \bigg) \mathrm{d}y \bigg) \mathrm{d}x . \tag{4.7}\]

Let \(R\) be a rectangle in the plane \(z = c\), made of the points \((x, y, c)\) with \(a_1 \le x \le b_1\) and \(a_2 \le y \le b_2\), and \(f\) a continuous function on \(R\). The integral of \(f\) over the rectangle \(R\) is the number

\[\int_{\mathrm{R}} f\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{a}_1}^{b_1} \bigg( \int_{\mathrm{a}_2}^{b_2} f(x, y, c)\,\mathrm{d}y \bigg) \mathrm{d}x .\]

For a rectangle in the plane \(x = c\) or \(y = c\), the coordinates that vary over the rectangle, \(y\) and \(z\) or \(x\) and \(z\), take the place of \(x\) and \(y\) in this formula, in this order. The integrals on the right are called iterated integrals (zaporedni integrali).

Source: LEBL2 Def. 10.1.7 (PDF p. 95) defines the integral over a rectangle with any number of coordinates by lower and upper sums. Thm. 10.1.15 (PDF p. 98) shows that every continuous function is integrable, and Fubini's theorem 10.2.2 with the corollary on PDF p. 106 that for continuous functions this integral equals the iterated integral as we define it.

The integral over a box is thus a number obtained by three integrals in one variable. The inner integral exists and has the property of item 1 by lemma 4.7, item 1. By item 2 the middle integral therefore exists and is a continuous function of \(x\), and the outer integral exists by theorem 3.38. For a rectangle in the plane \(z = c\), the function \((x, y) \mapsto f(x, y, c)\) has the property of item 1 of the lemma, because by theorem 4.6 \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \(R\), and the distance between the points \((x, y, c)\) and \((x', y', c)\) is \(\sqrt{(x' - x)^2 + (y' - y)^2}\). So by item 2 the integral over the rectangle exists too. The symbols \(\mathrm{d}V\) and \(\mathrm{d}A\) are not numbers. They only recall the volume and the area of small pieces, as \(\mathrm{d}x\) in section 3.5.3. We will shorten the notation with brackets to \(\int_{\mathrm{a}_1}^{b_1}\int_{\mathrm{a}_2}^{b_2}\int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} f\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x\). The sign \(\int\) that stands furthest to the right belongs to the symbol \(\mathrm{d}z\) that stands furthest to the left, and this integral is computed first.

Let us test the definition on the wall of the tank, in the plane \(z = 0\), with the function \(f(x, y, 0) = \rho g\,x\). The inner integral in \(y\) has a constant integrand (figure 4.14, left), so by lemma 3.39, item 3, it equals \(\int_0^b \rho g\,x\,\mathrm{d}y = \rho g\,x\,b\). The outer integral is \(\int_0^H \rho g\,b\,x\,\mathrm{d}x = \rho g\,b\,H^2/2 = 9810\) N, as in section 4.2.1.

The definition chooses the order \(z\), \(y\), \(x\). Would another order give another number? For the wall both orders gave 9810 N. That this is so for every continuous function is the content of the next section.

4.2.3 The order of integration

We can cut a box into slices in six ways, because three coordinates can be ordered in six ways. For each order we get an iterated integral, which exists by lemma 4.7 used with the roles of the coordinates exchanged. We will show that they are all equal, and more: they are all close to the same sum, like the sum (4.6), when we cut the box into small enough boxes. The idea is the same as in theorem 3.38. On a small box a continuous function hardly changes, so the iterated integral over it, in any order, is almost the value of the function times the volume of the box.

We compute a double integral as an iterated integral: first with respect to one variable, then with respect to the other, and the question is whether it matters which we take first.

From history

Euler and Laplace declared that for double integrals it does not matter (CAJORI, PDF p. 436). Cauchy, in a memoir on definite integrals read in 1814 and printed in 1825, showed that this holds only when the expression being integrated nowhere becomes indeterminate in the region of integration, that is, without a determined value (CAJORI, PDF p. 436).

Back to the iterated integral of a function on a cuboid. That the order can affect even whether the iterated integral exists at all is shown by an example from LEBL2, which we give after the theorem. For a continuous function on a closed cuboid there is no such difficulty, since the function is defined everywhere. This is why the theorem below demands continuity.

The theorem is named after Guido Fubini (1879-1943), an Italian mathematician (LEBL2, PDF p. 104). Why this is not self-evident is said at the start of the chapter in LEBL2: for an integrable function it is not immediately clear that the expressions with different orders are equal, or even that they are all defined (LEBL2, PDF p. 103).

First let us name the cutting. The partitions \(D_1 = \{x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{\mathrm{l}}\}\), \(D_2 = \{y_0, y_1, \dots, y_{\mathrm{m}}\}\) and \(D_3 = \{z_0, z_1, \dots, z_{\mathrm{n}}\}\) of the edges \([a_1, b_1]\), \([a_2, b_2]\) and \([a_3, b_3]\) (definition 3.31) cut the box with the planes \(x = x_{\mathrm{i}}\), \(y = y_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(z = z_{\mathrm{k}}\) into small boxes

\[K_{\mathrm{ijk}} = [x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}] \times [y_{\mathrm{j}-1}, y_{\mathrm{j}}] \times [z_{\mathrm{k}-1}, z_{\mathrm{k}}]\]

with the volumes \(\Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}} = \Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\,\Delta z_{\mathrm{k}}\). Such a cutting is called a grid (mreža), and the small boxes are the cells (celice) of the grid. The wall in figure 4.12 was cut by a grid in a plane, whose cells are rectangles. If we choose a point \(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) in each cell, the number

\[\sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{l} \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{m} \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{n} f(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}})\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}}\]

is a Riemann sum of the function \(f\) for this grid, following definition 3.32. We will write the triple sum more briefly as \(\sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j},\mathrm{k}}\). It means the sum over all cells of the grid.

Theorem 4.9 Order of integration, Fubini's theorem for continuous functions (vrstni red integriranja)

Let \(f\) be a continuous function on the box \(K = [a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\) with the volume \(V_{\mathrm{K}}\).

  1. For every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that for every grid in which all pieces of the partitions \(D_1\), \(D_2\) and \(D_3\) are shorter than \(\delta\), and for every choice of points \(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}} \in K_{\mathrm{ijk}}\),
    \[\Big| \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j},\mathrm{k}} f(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}})\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}} - I \Big| \le \eta\,V_{\mathrm{K}} ,\]
    where \(I\) is the iterated integral of \(f\) over \(K\) in any of the six orders of integration.
  2. All six iterated integrals equal the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\). For example
    \[\int_{\mathrm{a}_1}^{b_1}\int_{\mathrm{a}_2}^{b_2}\int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} f\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3}\int_{\mathrm{a}_2}^{b_2}\int_{\mathrm{a}_1}^{b_1} f\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}z .\]

The same holds for a continuous function on a rectangle, with two orders and with the area in place of the volume.

Proof

We must show that every iterated integral is close to every Riemann sum for a fine enough grid, and derive from this that they are all equal. We write the proof for the order of definition 4.8. For the other orders the steps are the same, only the integrals follow each other in a different order.

1. The iterated integral is close to a Riemann sum.

  1. We choose \(\eta > 0\). By theorem 4.6 there is a \(\delta' > 0\) such that \(|f(P) - f(Q)| < \eta\) for all points \(P, Q \in K\) with \(|PQ| < \delta'\). We take \(\delta = \delta'/2\).
  2. Let all pieces of the partitions be shorter than \(\delta\), and let \(P\) and \(Q\) be points of the same cell \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}}\). Each difference of their coordinates is smaller than \(\delta'/2\) in absolute value, so by lemma 1.28 its square is smaller than \(\delta'^2/4\), and by (1.10)
    \[|PQ|^2 < 3 \cdot \frac{\delta'^2}{4} < \delta'^2 .\]
    By the same lemma \(|PQ| < \delta'\), and by step 1 \(|f(P) - f(Q)| < \eta\).
  3. Let \(c_{\mathrm{ijk}} = f(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}})\). By step 2, \(c_{\mathrm{ijk}} - \eta < f(x, y, z) < c_{\mathrm{ijk}} + \eta\) for every point \((x, y, z)\) of the cell \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}}\). Let \(I_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) be the iterated integral of \(f\) over the cell \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}}\). For fixed \(x\) and \(y\) of the cell, by the bound (lemma 3.39, item 3),
    \[(c_{\mathrm{ijk}} - \eta)\,\Delta z_{\mathrm{k}} \le \int_{\mathrm{z}_{\mathrm{k}-1}}^{z_{\mathrm{k}}} f(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z \le (c_{\mathrm{ijk}} + \eta)\,\Delta z_{\mathrm{k}} .\]
    The inner integral is a continuous function of \(y\) by lemma 4.7, lying between these two constants, so by the same bound on \([y_{\mathrm{j}-1}, y_{\mathrm{j}}]\) the middle integral lies between \((c_{\mathrm{ijk}} - \eta)\,\Delta z_{\mathrm{k}}\,\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \((c_{\mathrm{ijk}} + \eta)\,\Delta z_{\mathrm{k}}\,\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\). The middle integral is a continuous function of \(x\) by the same lemma, and by the bound on \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\) we finally get
    \[(c_{\mathrm{ijk}} - \eta)\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}} \le I_{\mathrm{ijk}} \le (c_{\mathrm{ijk}} + \eta)\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}} , \qquad \text{so} \qquad |I_{\mathrm{ijk}} - c_{\mathrm{ijk}}\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}}| \le \eta\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}} .\]
  4. The iterated integral \(I\) over the whole box is the sum of the integrals over the cells. By additivity (lemma 3.39, item 2), used \(n - 1\) times, the inner integral splits into a sum of integrals over the pieces \([z_{\mathrm{k}-1}, z_{\mathrm{k}}]\), and each of them is a continuous function of \(y\) by lemma 4.7. The middle integral of the sum is by linearity (same lemma, item 1) the sum of the middle integrals, and each we split by additivity into the pieces \([y_{\mathrm{j}-1}, y_{\mathrm{j}}]\). In the same way we split the outer integral into the pieces \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\). We get
    \[I = \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j},\mathrm{k}} I_{\mathrm{ijk}} .\]
  5. By step 4, by the triangle inequality for numbers (lemma 1.6, item 1) used on a sum of \(l\,m\,n\) terms, and by step 3,
    \[\Big| I - \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j},\mathrm{k}} c_{\mathrm{ijk}}\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}} \Big| = \Big| \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j},\mathrm{k}} \big(I_{\mathrm{ijk}} - c_{\mathrm{ijk}}\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}}\big) \Big| \le \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j},\mathrm{k}} \eta\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}} .\]
  6. The volumes of the cells add up to the volume of the box. By distributivity \(\sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j},\mathrm{k}} \Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\,\Delta z_{\mathrm{k}} = \big(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\big)\big(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\big)\big(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \Delta z_{\mathrm{k}}\big)\), and each sum of the lengths of the pieces is a telescoping sum equal to the length of the edge (section 3.5.2). The right side of the inequality in step 5 is therefore \(\eta\,V_{\mathrm{K}}\).

2. All orders give the same number.

  1. Let \(I\) and \(I'\) be iterated integrals of \(f\) in two orders. We choose \(\eta > 0\) and take the band \(\delta\) that the first part gives for the error \(\eta/(2V_{\mathrm{K}})\). The band depends only on the uniform continuity of \(f\), not on the order, so it works for both integrals.
  2. A grid with pieces shorter than \(\delta\) exists. By the Archimedean property 1.35 there is a natural number \(N\) such that \(N\delta\) is larger than the length of each of the three edges, and we divide each edge into \(N\) equal pieces. We choose points \(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) in the cells, and let \(S\) be the Riemann sum.
  3. By the first part \(|I - S| \le \eta/2\) and \(|I' - S| \le \eta/2\). By the triangle inequality for numbers \(|I - I'| \le |I - S| + |S - I'| \le \eta\).
  4. We chose the error \(\eta\) arbitrarily, so by lemma 1.34 on an inequality tested with all positive numbers \(|I - I'| = 0\).

3. A rectangle.

  1. The steps are the same, with two partitions and two integrals in place of three. The cells are rectangles with the areas \(\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\), and in step 2 of the first part \(|PQ|^2 < 2 \cdot \delta'^2/4 < \delta'^2\).

Source: LEBL2 Thms. 10.2.2 and 10.2.3 (PDF pp. 104-106) for integrable functions, the corollary for continuous functions with any number of coordinates and in any order on PDF p. 106. The source uses lower and upper sums. The proof with Riemann sums is not from the source.

The theorem says two things. The first is that the integral over a box is the limit of the sums of values of the function times the volumes of small pieces, like the sum of the forces on the rectangles of the wall. This is how we computed forces and moments on the faces of a small cube in section 2.8.4, with equal rectangles and points at their centres. Item 1 says that such sums approach the integral for a continuous force per unit area as the rectangles get smaller. The second is that we may choose the order of integration as it suits us. We saw this on the wall: horizontal and vertical strips gave the same force of 9810 N.

How fast the sums approach the integral is shown by the wall of figure 4.12. Let us cut it into \(l\) equal horizontal strips and into any number of vertical ones, and choose in each rectangle a point on its upper edge, at the depth \(x_{\mathrm{i}-1} = (i - 1)\,H/l\). The sum over the vertical strips gives the factor \(b\) as in section 4.2.1. We compute the sum over \(i\) with the formula \(0 + 1 + \dots + (l - 1) = (l - 1)\,l/2\), which we derived for the work of a force in section 3.5.1:

\[\sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{l} \rho g\,b\,\frac{(i - 1)\,H}{l}\,\frac{H}{l} = \frac{\rho g\,b\,H^2}{l^2}\,\frac{(l - 1)\,l}{2} = 9810\ \text{N} \cdot \Big(1 - \frac1l\Big) .\]

For \(l = 4\) this is 7357,5 N, for \(l = 16\) it is 9196,9 N. The error is \(9810\ \text{N}/l\). Item 1 of the theorem bounds it from above. On a strip of height \(H/l\) the force per unit area changes by at most \(\rho g H/l = 9810\ \text{Pa}/l\). Steps 3 and 5 of the proof, with this number in place of \(\eta\), therefore give the bound \(9810\ \text{Pa}/l \cdot 2\ \text{m}^2 = 19\,620\ \text{N}/l\), where \(2\ \text{m}^2\) is the area of the wall. This is twice the true error. The bound is rough, but it is enough to make the error go to zero.

Why does the theorem require continuity? For a function that is not continuous, the inner integral may not exist at all. In example 10.2.1 (PDF pp. 103-104) LEBL2 takes the function on the square \([0, 1] \times [0, 1]\) that equals \(1\) when \(x = \tfrac12\) and \(y\) is a fraction, and \(0\) elsewhere. The iterated integral in which we integrate first in \(x\) is zero. At \(x = \tfrac12\), however, the function \(y \mapsto f(\tfrac12, y)\) is the function of section 3.5.3 that is \(1\) at fractions and \(0\) elsewhere and is not integrable, so the iterated integral in the other order makes no sense. Such functions do not occur in mechanics, but they show that the claim is not self-evident.

For computing we need a few more rules, which we get for the integral over a box from the properties of the integral over an interval.

Lemma 4.10 Properties of the integral over a box (lastnosti integrala po kvadru)

Let \(f\) and \(g\) be continuous functions on the box \(K = [a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\) with the volume \(V_{\mathrm{K}}\), and \(\alpha\) a number.

  1. Linearity: \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} (f + g)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{K}} f\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{K}} g\,\mathrm{d}V\) and \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} \alpha f\,\mathrm{d}V = \alpha \int_{\mathrm{K}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  2. Constant function: \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} \alpha\,\mathrm{d}V = \alpha\,V_{\mathrm{K}}\).
  3. Additivity: if the plane \(x = c\) with \(a_1 < c < b_1\) divides \(K\) into the boxes \(K' = [a_1, c] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\) and \(K'' = [c, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\), then \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{K}'} f\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{K}''} f\,\mathrm{d}V\). The same holds for the planes \(y = c\) and \(z = c\).
  4. Monotonicity: if \(f(P) \le g(P)\) for every point \(P \in K\), then \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} f\,\mathrm{d}V \le \int_{\mathrm{K}} g\,\mathrm{d}V\). In particular, the integral of a non-negative function is non-negative.

The same holds for the integral over a rectangle, with the area in place of the volume.

Proof

We must show four items. All follow from the properties of the integral over an interval (lemma 3.39), used on each of the three iterated integrals.

1. Linearity.

  1. The function \(f + g\) is continuous on \(K\) by corollary 1.69, item 1, so its integral exists.
  2. For fixed \(x\) and \(y\), by linearity of the integral over an interval, \(\int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} (f + g)\,\mathrm{d}z = \int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} f\,\mathrm{d}z + \int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} g\,\mathrm{d}z\).
  3. Both functions on the right are continuous in \(y\) by lemma 4.7, so by the same linearity the middle integral of the sum splits into the sum of the middle integrals. These are continuous functions of \(x\), and the outer integral splits in the same way.
  4. For \(\alpha f\) the computation is the same, with the rule \(\int \alpha\,h = \alpha \int h\) at each of the three steps.

2. Constant function.

  1. By item 3 of lemma 3.39, \(\int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} \alpha\,\mathrm{d}z = \alpha\,(b_3 - a_3)\), which is again a constant number. By the same item the middle integral equals \(\alpha\,(b_3 - a_3)(b_2 - a_2)\), and the outer one \(\alpha\,(b_3 - a_3)(b_2 - a_2)(b_1 - a_1) = \alpha\,V_{\mathrm{K}}\).

3. Additivity.

  1. For the plane \(x = c\) we use the additivity of the integral over an interval (item 2 of lemma 3.39) on the outer integral in \(x\), whose integrand is continuous on \([a_1, b_1]\) by lemma 4.7. The two inner integrals are the same for \(K\), \(K'\) and \(K''\) at every \(x\).
  2. For the plane \(y = c\), by theorem 4.9 on the order of integration, we write all three integrals as iterated integrals in which the outer integral is in \(y\), and repeat step 1. We proceed in the same way for the plane \(z = c\).

4. Monotonicity.

  1. For fixed \(x\) and \(y\), \(f(x, y, z) \le g(x, y, z)\) for every \(z\), so by monotonicity of the integral over an interval (item 4 of lemma 3.39) \(\int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} f\,\mathrm{d}z \le \int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} g\,\mathrm{d}z\).
  2. Both sides are continuous functions of \(y\) by lemma 4.7, so by the same item the inequality survives the middle integral, and in the same way the outer one.
  3. For a non-negative function \(g\) we take \(f = 0\), whose integral is zero by item 2.

Source: LEBL2 Props. 10.1.10 and 10.1.11 (PDF p. 96) for linearity and monotonicity, and example 10.1.9 (PDF p. 95) for the constant function, for integrable functions. Item 3 and the proofs with iterated integrals are not from the source.

Let us use the rules on the weight of a part of the hanging bar. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m with a round cross section of diameter 10 mm hangs under its own weight. It is held in the idealized way: only the centre \(O\) of the top face is fixed, and a force that carries the weight pulls the top face up evenly (section 1.7.1). The axis \(x\) points vertically down from \(O\), the axes \(y\) and \(z\) are horizontal. In our minds we cut out of the bar the box \(K = [3, 6] \times [-c, c] \times [-c, c]\), with coordinates in metres and with \(c = 0{,}003\) m. It lies inside the bar, because each of its points is at most \(\sqrt{c^2 + c^2} = 4{,}243\) mm from the axis, less than the radius of 5 mm. The body force on the material is the weight, \(\vek b = \rho g\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) with \(\rho g = 7800 \cdot 9{,}81\ \text{N/m}^3 = 76\,518\ \text{N/m}^3\) (definition 2.26). A small piece of volume \(\Delta V\) has a weight of approximately \(\rho g\,\Delta V\). The sum of the weights of the cells of a grid is a Riemann sum of the function \(\rho g\), which approaches the integral by theorem 4.9, item 1. The weight of the box is therefore

\[\int_{\mathrm{K}} \rho g\,\mathrm{d}V = \rho g\,V_{\mathrm{K}} = 76\,518\ \text{N/m}^3 \cdot 3\ \text{m} \cdot (0{,}006\ \text{m})^2 = 8{,}264\ \text{N} ,\]

by item 2 of lemma 4.10. So we write the total body force on a part of a body as the integral of the body force, as SADD (3.7.1) (PDF p. 77) does. Since \(\vek b\) is a vector, we agree that the integral of a vector function is the vector of the integrals of its components:

\[\int_{\mathrm{K}} \vek b\,\mathrm{d}V = \Big( \int_{\mathrm{K}} b_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}V,\ \int_{\mathrm{K}} b_{\mathrm{y}}\,\mathrm{d}V,\ \int_{\mathrm{K}} b_{\mathrm{z}}\,\mathrm{d}V \Big) .\]

For our box this is \(8{,}264\ \text{N} \cdot \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), a force of \(8{,}264\) N vertically down. The same agreement holds for the integral of a vector function over a rectangle.

4.2.4 Bodies made of boxes and the integral over the surface

A box is a simple body. Many machine parts, beams with a rectangular cross section, plates and brackets, are made up of several boxes, just as the letter L is made up of two rectangles (figure 4.15). The integral over such a body is the sum of the integrals over the boxes it is made of. That this sum does not depend on how we cut the body is easiest to show when all boxes are cells of a single grid.

Definition 4.11 Body made of boxes (telo iz kvadrov)

Let \(K\) be a box and a grid that cuts it into cells \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) (section 4.2.3). A set of points \(V\) is a body made of boxes (telo iz kvadrov) if it is the union of some cells of this grid, at least one. These cells are the cells of the body \(V\).

  1. The integral of a continuous function \(f\) over the body \(V\) is the sum of the integrals over its cells, \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \sum_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ijk}} \subseteq \mathrm{V}} \int_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ijk}}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  2. A face of a cell of the body \(V\) is an outer face if the cell on the other side of the face is not a cell of the body \(V\) or if the face lies on the surface of the box \(K\). The surface (površina) \(S\) of the body \(V\) is the union of its outer faces. The outward normal \(\vek n\) on an outer face is the outward normal of the cell the face belongs to, so one of the vectors \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\).
  3. Let \(f\) be a function that is continuous on every outer face. The surface integral (ploskovni integral) of \(f\) over the surface \(S\) is the sum of the integrals over the outer faces, \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,\mathrm{d}A\).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7 (PDF p. 478) defines the integral over a body in space as the limit of sums over the boxes of a grid that lie in the body. The definition for bodies made of boxes is not from the source.

A body made of boxes is thus a set of points made up of finitely many cells of one grid. The integral over it and the surface integral are sums of integrals over cells and over rectangles, so linearity and monotonicity of lemma 4.10, items 1 and 4, hold for them. Figure 4.15 shows a section of an L-shaped body made of four cells. The faces on which two cells of the body touch are not outer faces and do not belong to the surface, which agrees with the picture: from outside we do not see them. The function under a surface integral may have two values on an edge where two outer faces meet, one for each face. This is so for the normal, which on one face is, for example, \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and on the other \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). The surface integral allows this, because each face is integrated separately. The simplest body made of boxes is a box itself, with a grid of one single cell. Its surface is its six faces.

Lemma 4.12 The integral does not depend on the grid (integral ni odvisen od mreže)

Let \(V\) be a body made of boxes. The integral of a continuous function over \(V\), the surface \(S\), the outward normals and the surface integral over \(S\) do not depend on the grid with which we cut \(V\) into cells. For the surface integral we assume that the function is continuous on every outer face of both grids that we compare. This holds for instance for the function \(g\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\) with \(g\) continuous on \(V\).

Proof

We must show that two grids that both cut \(V\) into cells give the same. First we compare a grid with a grid that has one more plane, then any two grids.

  1. Let the second grid have one more plane, for example \(x = c\) with \(x_{\mathrm{i}-1} < c < x_{\mathrm{i}}\) (figure 4.15, right). The plane cuts each cell between the planes \(x = x_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) and \(x = x_{\mathrm{i}}\) into two, and the other cells remain. The body \(V\) is the union of the halves of its cut cells and of its uncut cells, so these are the cells of the body \(V\) in the new grid. Half of a cell that is not a cell of the body \(V\) is not in \(V\) either. Its points that lie on no plane of the grid lie in no other cell of the old grid, and so not in \(V\).
  2. By lemma 4.10, item 3, the integral over a cut cell is the sum of the integrals over its halves. The integral over \(V\) is therefore the same in both grids.
  3. The faces of cells that are perpendicular to the axis \(y\) or \(z\) and lie between the planes \(x = x_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) and \(x = x_{\mathrm{i}}\) are cut in two by the plane \(x = c\). A half is an outer face exactly when the whole face was, because the cell on the other side is cut in the same way and is a cell of the body exactly when it was before. The new faces in the plane \(x = c\) separate the two halves of the same old cell, which are both in \(V\) or both outside, so no new face is an outer face. The faces perpendicular to the axis \(x\) remain. The surface \(S\) and the normals are therefore the same, and by lemma 4.10, item 3, for a rectangle, so is the surface integral.
  4. Let two arbitrary grids for \(V\) be given. First we extend both to a common box that contains both original boxes, by adding new end points to the partitions. The new cells lie outside \(V\), so nothing changes. The grid that has all the planes of both grids is obtained from each of them by adding planes one after another. By steps 1 to 3, each of the two grids gives the same integrals, surface and normals as this common grid.

Source: The lemma is not from the source. LEBL2 Prop. 10.1.5 (PDF p. 93) uses the same idea of a common refinement for sums on a rectangle.

The lemma lets us cut a body made of boxes into cells as it suits us. Whenever we need a finer grid, for example so that some face or some smaller cube is made of whole cells, we may take it without changing the integrals.

4.2.5 The divergence theorem

Let us return to the fundamental theorem of calculus. For a function \(G\) with a continuous derivative on \([a, b]\), one-sided at the endpoints (definition 1.9),

\[\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b G'(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = G(b) - G(a) .\]

We can read the right side as a sum over the boundary of the interval. The boundary of the interval is the two end points \(a\) and \(b\). At the end point \(b\) the direction out of the interval points toward larger numbers, which we write as the number \(+1\), at the end point \(a\) toward smaller ones, which we write as \(-1\). The right side is \(G(b) \cdot (+1) + G(a) \cdot (-1)\), the value times the outward direction, summed over the boundary. For a box we expect the same. The role of the function \(G\) is taken by a function of three variables \(f\), the role of the derivative by the partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial x\), and the role of the end points by the faces of the box (figure 4.16). The two faces perpendicular to the axis \(x\) have the outward normals \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), whose component \(x\) is \(\pm 1\). On the other four faces the component \(x\) of the normal is zero.

From history

Theorems that turn an integral of derivatives over a body into an integral over its surface arose in the theory of attractive and electric forces, not in the mechanics of solids. In 1828 the self-taught Englishman Green, who began as a baker, published by subscription an essay on the application of mathematical analysis to the theory of electricity and magnetism, printed in about a hundred copies (CAJORI, PDF p. 488, KREYSZIG, PDF p. 459). It contained the theorem now called Green's theorem, for the treatment of attractive forces (CAJORI, PDF p. 488). The essay stayed unnoticed, even by English mathematicians. Gauss independently established similar results in 1839 and saw to it that they became known among mathematicians (BALL, PDF p. 520). In the meantime all of Green's general theorems had been rediscovered by Thomson, Michel Chasles, Jacques Charles François Sturm and Gauss (CAJORI, PDF p. 488). In 1846 Thomson had Green's essay reprinted in Crelle's Journal (CAJORI, PDF p. 488). In the same year Cauchy also wrote down a similar theorem for the plane: for functions continuous in a closed region, the integral of the expression \(X\,\mathrm{d}x + Y\,\mathrm{d}y\) along the boundary equals an integral over the interior (CAJORI, PDF p. 436).

Back to the cuboid and to the expectation that the integral of a partial derivative of a function of three variables over a cuboid is a sum over the faces, multiplied by a component of the outer normal. For a vector field we add up three such terms, one for each component. The sum of the three partial derivatives has its own name.

Definition 4.13 Divergence of a field (divergenca polja)

Let \(\vek v = (v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\) be a vector field, that is, a rule that assigns a vector to every point of some set, and let its components have partial derivatives at the point \(P\) (definition 1.25). The divergence (divergenca) of the field \(\vek v\) at the point \(P\) is the number

\[\frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}(P) + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}(P) + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z}(P) .\]

Source: KREYSZIG §9.8 (1) (PDF p. 428), where it is written \(\operatorname{div}\vek v\), CM (2.4.34) (PDF p. 76), where it is written \(\nabla\cdot\vek A\).

What the divergence measures we will see after the theorem. Let us state it.

Theorem 4.14 Divergence theorem (izrek o divergenci)

Let \(V\) be a body made of boxes with the surface \(S\) and the outward normal \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\) (definition 4.11), \(D\) an open set of points that contains \(V\), and \(f\), \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) functions that are continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 1.90).

  1. We have
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}A , \tag{4.8}\]
    and the same with \(y\) and \(n_{\mathrm{y}}\) and with \(z\) and \(n_{\mathrm{z}}\) in place of \(x\) and \(n_{\mathrm{x}}\).
  2. For the field \(\vek v = (v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\),
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \Big( \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \big( v_{\mathrm{x}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + v_{\mathrm{y}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + v_{\mathrm{z}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} \big)\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{4.9}\]
Proof

We must show both items. We prove item 1 first for one box, with the fundamental theorem of calculus and the theorem on the order of integration, then for a body made of boxes, where the contributions of the inner faces cancel. Item 2 is the sum of three cases of item 1.

1. One box.

  1. Let \(V = K = [a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\) be a box with a grid of one cell. The function \(f\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\), so it is also continuous on \(D\) (lemma 1.91), and all integrals over the faces of the box exist. On the face \(x = b_1\) we have \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 1\), on the face \(x = a_1\) we have \(\vek n = -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = -1\), and on the other four faces \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) (figure 4.16). The integral of the zero function is zero (lemma 4.10, item 2, for a rectangle), so by definition 4.11, item 3, and by linearity
    \[\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{a}_2}^{b_2}\int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} f(b_1, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y - \int_{\mathrm{a}_2}^{b_2}\int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} f(a_1, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y .\]
  2. The function \(\partial f/\partial x\) is continuous on \(D\), hence also on \(K\). By theorem 4.9 on the order of integration we may write the integral over \(K\) as an iterated integral in which the inner integral is in \(x\):
    \[\int_{\mathrm{K}} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{a}_2}^{b_2}\int_{\mathrm{a}_3}^{b_3} \bigg( \int_{\mathrm{a}_1}^{b_1} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}x \bigg) \mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y .\]
  3. Let \(y\) and \(z\) be fixed and \(G(x) = f(x, y, z)\) for \(x \in [a_1, b_1]\). The points \((x, y, z)\) lie in \(K\) and hence in \(D\), where \(f\) has a partial derivative in \(x\). By the definition of the partial derivative 1.25, \(G\) is differentiable at every point of \([a_1, b_1]\) and \(G'(x) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x, y, z)\). At the endpoints \(a_1\) and \(b_1\) this is a one-sided derivative (definition 1.9), since \(G\) is defined only on \([a_1, b_1]\), and the limit from both sides also gives the limit from one side. The function \(G\) is continuous on \([a_1, b_1]\), because \(f\) is continuous on \(D\) (step 1). The derivative \(G'\) is continuous on \([a_1, b_1]\), because \(\partial f/\partial x\) is continuous on \(K\). Both conclusions use that the distance between the points \((x, y, z)\) and \((x', y, z)\) is \(|x' - x|\).
  4. By the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.40, item 1, therefore
    \[\int_{\mathrm{a}_1}^{b_1} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}x = G(b_1) - G(a_1) = f(b_1, y, z) - f(a_1, y, z) .\]
  5. We put this into step 2 and use linearity of the integral over an interval (lemma 3.39, item 1) on the middle and on the outer integral. We get the right side of step 1. This proves (4.8) for a box.
  6. For \(y\) and \(n_{\mathrm{y}}\) we repeat steps 1 to 5, only now the inner integral is in \(y\) and the faces \(y = a_2\) and \(y = b_2\) appear. The same for \(z\) and \(n_{\mathrm{z}}\).

2. A body made of boxes.

  1. By definition 4.11 and by the first part, used on each cell of the body,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}V = \sum_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ijk}} \subseteq \mathrm{V}} \int_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ijk}}} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\mathrm{d}V = \sum_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ijk}} \subseteq \mathrm{V}} \int_{\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{ijk}}} f\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}A ,\]
    where \(S_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) is the surface of the cell \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}}\), its six faces, with the outward normals of this cell.
  2. The sum on the right is the sum of the integrals over all faces of all cells of the body. A face that is not an outer face is shared by two cells of the body that lie on its opposite sides (figure 4.17). For one cell its outward normal is \(\vek n\), for the other \(-\vek n\). The functions under the two integrals, \(f\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(f\,(-n_{\mathrm{x}})\), are therefore opposite, and by linearity (lemma 4.10, item 1, for a rectangle) the two integrals cancel.
  3. What remains are the integrals over the outer faces, each once and with the outward normal of the body. Their sum is the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) by definition 4.11, item 3.

3. A field.

  1. We use item 1 three times, with the function \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\) and the coordinate \(x\), with the function \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) and the coordinate \(y\) and with the function \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) and the coordinate \(z\), and add the equations. By linearity of the integral over each cell and over each face (lemma 4.10, item 1), the sum of the left sides is the left side of (4.9), and the sum of the right sides is the right side.

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7, Theorem 1, equations (2) and (2*) (PDF p. 479), with the proof on PDF pp. 480-482, CM (2.4.45) and (2.4.46) (PDF p. 82), SADD (1.8.6) (PDF p. 28), all for bodies bounded by a piecewise smooth surface. The proof for bodies made of boxes is a simplification of KREYSZIG's proof.

The proof shows where the theorem comes from (figure 4.17). On one box it is the fundamental theorem of calculus, used on every segment in the box parallel to the axis \(x\). The integral of the derivative along the segment is the difference of the values at the point where the segment leaves the box and at the point where it enters. The theorem on the order of integration stacks these segments into the box. In a body made of boxes the contributions of the inner faces cancel, because the shared face of two cells has opposite outward normals for the two of them. Only the surface remains. The sum on the right side of (4.9) is the scalar product \(\vek v\cdot\vek n\) (definition 2.8), so the right side adds up the part of the field that points out of the body. The theorem is also called Gauss's theorem. It needs a field that is continuously differentiable on an open set that contains the whole body. In a body made of two glued materials the displacement field has no continuous derivatives at the interface (section 1.15.6). We then use the theorem on each material separately, provided the field in each material can be written by a formula that stays continuously differentiable a little beyond the interface, for example by a polynomial. The interface then contributes one surface integral for each side.

What does the theorem say for a displacement field? Let \(\vek v = \vek u\) be the displacement field of a body. On a patch of the surface with the area \(\Delta A\), \(\vek u\cdot\vek n\) is the part of the displacement in the direction of the outward normal, that is, how far the patch moves outward. For small displacements, \(\vek u\cdot\vek n\,\Delta A\) is approximately the volume the patch sweeps as it moves, positive when it moves outward and negative when it moves inward. The right side of (4.9) is therefore approximately the change of volume of the body. On the left side is the integral of the sum \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x + \partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), which by section 1.17.4 is, for small strains, the relative change of volume of a small piece. The theorem thus says that the changes of volume of small pieces add up to the change of volume of the body, which we can compute from the displacements of the surface alone. Hence the name: divergence means moving apart. Where the divergence of the displacements is positive, neighbouring points move apart and small pieces grow.

Let us test the theorem on the hanging bar of section 4.2.3. The steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m and diameter 10 mm hangs under its own weight and is held in the idealized way. The axis \(x\) points down from the centre \(O\) of the top face. Its displacement field is (1.18),

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}} &= a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2) , \\ u_{\mathrm{y}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y , \\ u_{\mathrm{z}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,z , \end{aligned}\]

with \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\). Where the numbers \(0{,}3\) and \(0{,}6\) come from we explained in section 1.7.1. This time we take the box along the whole length of the bar, \(K = [0, L] \times [-c, c] \times [-c, c]\) with \(c = 0{,}003\) m. The components of the field are polynomials, so their partial derivatives, again polynomials, are continuous at every point of space (corollary 1.69), and we may take the whole space for \(D\).

The left side. The partial derivatives are \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = 2a\,(L - x)\), \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\) and \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\), so the divergence is \(2a\,(L - x) - 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) - 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) = 0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\). It does not depend on \(y\) and \(z\), so by definition 4.8 and by lemma 3.39, item 3, the inner integral in \(z\) equals \(2c \cdot 0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\), and the middle one in \(y\) equals \(4c^2 \cdot 0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\). The function \(Lx - x^2/2\) has the derivative \(L - x\), so by the fundamental theorem of calculus \(\int_0^L (L - x)\,\mathrm{d}x = L^2/2\), and

\[\int_{\mathrm{K}} \Big( \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}V = 4c^2 \cdot 0{,}8\,a \cdot \frac{L^2}{2} = 1{,}6\,a\,c^2 L^2 = 0{,}2811\ \text{mm}^3 .\]

The right side. The box has six faces (figure 4.18).

  1. The bottom face \(x = L\) with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The integrand is \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(L, y, z) = a L^2 - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\). The inner integral in \(z\) is \(\int_{-\mathrm{c}}^{c} (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}z = 2c\,y^2 + \tfrac23 c^3\), the outer one in \(y\) is \(2c \cdot \tfrac23 c^3 + \tfrac23 c^3 \cdot 2c = \tfrac83 c^4\). The integral over the face is therefore \(4c^2\,a L^2 - 0{,}3\,a \cdot \tfrac83 c^4 = 4\,a\,c^2 L^2 - 0{,}8\,a\,c^4\).
  2. The top face \(x = 0\) with the normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The integrand is \(-u_{\mathrm{x}}(0, y, z) = 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\), the integral over the face \(0{,}8\,a\,c^4\).
  3. The face \(y = c\) with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). The integrand is \(u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, c, z) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,c\). The integral in \(z\) gives the factor \(2c\), the integral in \(x\) the factor \(L^2/2\), together \(-0{,}6\,a\,c^2 L^2\).
  4. The face \(y = -c\) with the normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). The integrand is \(-u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, -c, z) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,c\), the same as in item 3, and the integral is again \(-0{,}6\,a\,c^2 L^2\).
  5. The faces \(z = \pm c\) with the normals \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) give the same as the faces \(y = \pm c\), each \(-0{,}6\,a\,c^2 L^2\).

The sum is \(4\,a\,c^2 L^2 - 0{,}8\,a\,c^4 + 0{,}8\,a\,c^4 - 4 \cdot 0{,}6\,a\,c^2 L^2 = 1{,}6\,a\,c^2 L^2\), the same as the left side.

What do the numbers mean (figure 4.18)? The bottom face, of area \(4c^2 = 36\ \text{mm}^2\), moves down by \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(L, 0, 0) = a L^2 = 19{,}52\) µm and sweeps \(36\ \text{mm}^2 \cdot 0{,}01952\ \text{mm} = 0{,}7027\ \text{mm}^3\), when we neglect the very small term \(0{,}8\,a\,c^4\). The four side faces move toward the axis, because the bar gets thinner, and each sweeps \(0{,}1054\ \text{mm}^3\) inward, together \(0{,}4216\ \text{mm}^3\). The top face stays in place at its centre, while its rim rises by a very small amount, and it sweeps only \(0{,}8\,a\,c^4 = 1{,}3 \cdot 10^{-8}\ \text{mm}^3\). The volume of the box grows by \(0{,}7027 - 0{,}4216 = 0{,}2811\ \text{mm}^3\). The box has the volume \(36\ \text{mm}^2 \cdot 10\,000\ \text{mm} = 360\,000\ \text{mm}^3\), so the relative change is \(0{,}2811/360\,000 = 7{,}808 \cdot 10^{-7}\). This is exactly the sum \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) at the point \(P\) at the depth of 5 m, which we computed in section 1.17.4. Why exactly at \(P\)? The sum \(0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\) is a linear function of the depth, so its average over the bar equals the value at the middle, at \(x = L/2 = 5\) m, where \(P\) lies.

4.2.6 Bodies with a curved surface

The round hanging bar is not a body made of boxes. Its side face, the mantle of a cylinder, is curved, and the outward normal on it changes from point to point. At the point \((x, y, z)\) of the mantle, where \(y^2 + z^2 = r^2\) and \(r = 5\) mm is the radius of the cross section, the outward normal is \(\vek n = (0, y/r, z/r)\) (figure 4.19). This vector is a unit vector, because \((y/r)^2 + (z/r)^2 = 1\), it has no component along the axis of the bar, and it points away from the axis. On the top face the outward normal is \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), on the bottom face \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The top and bottom faces are not rectangles either, but discs.

The divergence theorem holds for such bodies too. Precisely: let \(V\) be a closed and bounded set of points bounded by a surface made of finitely many smooth pieces, and let the components of the field \(\vek v\) be continuously differentiable on an open set that contains \(V\). Then (4.9) holds, where \(\vek n\) is the outward normal of the surface (KREYSZIG §10.7, Theorem 1, PDF p. 479, CM (2.4.46), PDF p. 82, SADD (1.8.6), PDF p. 28). KREYSZIG proves the theorem first for a body bounded above and below by the graph of a function, and then for a body that can be cut into finitely many such pieces, so that the contributions of the inner cuts cancel as with our cells (PDF pp. 480-482). For the most general bodies he says that a limit process is still needed (PDF p. 482). We will take the same route, for a class of bodies that includes the round hanging bar, and in section 4.3.7 also for bodies that we get by bending a box continuously, such as the pieces of a ball. We will not develop the limit process, because all the bodies of our examples can be cut into such pieces.

The route is as follows. In this subsection we define a body bounded above and below by a graph, and show how to cut the round bar into three such bodies. The integral over such a body will again be an iterated integral, except that the limits of the inner integral will not be constant but will depend on the outer variables. So in section 4.2.7 we show that such an integral changes continuously, and how to differentiate it with respect to a variable on which the limits depend. Then we define the integral over such a body (section 4.2.8) and over its curved surface (section 4.2.11). Finally we prove the theorem and test it on the round bar (section 4.2.12). The bodies that we cannot cut into such pieces, such as a ball, and two questions about the independence of the integral, which we will name when they come up, are treated in sections 4.2.10, 4.3.6 and 4.3.7.

Let us start with a body that is a box with a curved top and bottom lid (figure 4.20). Below it, in the plane \(z = 0\), lies the rectangle \([a, b] \times [c, d]\), which we call the shadow of the body. Above every point \((x, y)\) of the shadow the body occupies a vertical segment that starts at the height \(g(x, y)\) and ends at the height \(h(x, y)\). The bottom lid of the body is the graph of the function \(g\), the top lid the graph of the function \(h\), and the four side faces are flat, in the planes \(x = a\), \(x = b\), \(y = c\) and \(y = d\). In this section the letter \(g\) is not the gravitational acceleration but a function.

Definition 4.15 Body between two graphs (telo med dvema grafoma)

Let \(a < b\) and \(c < d\) be numbers and \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) a rectangle in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\), that is, the set of points \((x, y)\) with \(a \le x \le b\) and \(c \le y \le d\). Let \(U\) be an open set of points of the plane that contains \(R\), that is, a set that contains, together with each of its points, a disc of some radius \(r > 0\) around it. Let \(g\) and \(h\) be functions whose input is a point \((x, y)\) of \(U\) and whose output is a number, and which are continuously differentiable on \(U\): at every point of \(U\) they have the partial derivatives with respect to \(x\) and to \(y\) (definition 1.25), which are continuous at every point of \(U\). Let \(g(x, y) \le h(x, y)\) for every point \((x, y) \in R\). The set of points of space

\[V = \{ (x, y, z) : (x, y) \in R,\ g(x, y) \le z \le h(x, y) \} \tag{4.10}\]

is a body between two graphs (telo med dvema grafoma), of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R\). The graph of the function \(h\) over \(R\) is its top lid, the graph of the function \(g\) its bottom lid. We use the same name for the set obtained when the roles of the coordinates are exchanged, for example the set of points with \(a \le x \le b\), \(c \le z \le d\) and \(g(x, z) \le y \le h(x, z)\).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7, (6) (PDF p. 480), where the shadow of the body is a more general region, not only a rectangle. The restriction to a rectangle is not from the source.

The definition says what goes in. The rectangle \(R\) is the shadow of the body. The functions \(g\) and \(h\) take a point of the shadow as input, and their output is the height of the bottom and of the top lid above it. Why must they be continuously differentiable, and on an open set containing \(R\)? From their partial derivatives we will compute the normal of a lid in section 4.2.11, and in the proof of the theorem we will need them also on the edge of the shadow. A partial derivative at a point needs values of the function on both sides of the point (definition 1.25), so the functions must be defined a little beyond the edge. The inequality \(g \le h\) says that the bottom lid is not above the top lid. Equality is allowed: for the bar, the lids will meet at the edge of the shadow. The simplest body between graphs is the box \([a, b] \times [c, d] \times [g_0, h_0]\), for which \(g\) and \(h\) are constant functions with the values \(g_0 < h_0\), with zero partial derivatives.

A body over a rectangle is a special case. KREYSZIG allows the shadow, the set of points \((x, y)\) below the body, to be a more general region of the plane (KREYSZIG §10.7, (6), PDF p. 480). We will need the rectangle in the proof of the theorem, where we will exchange the order of integration in \(x\) and in \(y\). On a rectangle we may do so by theorem 4.9 on the order of integration. On more general regions we do not have this theorem. KREYSZIG avoids it by requiring the body to have this shape in the direction of all three axes, and obtains the terms with \(x\) and \(y\) from the term with \(z\) by renaming the axes (PDF pp. 480-481). How severe is our restriction? Less than it seems, because we may exchange the roles of the coordinates and cut a body into several pieces. Let us show this on the round bar.

The round hanging bar of length \(L = 10\) m, with a cross section of radius \(r = 5\) mm and the axis \(x\) down from the centre \(O\) of the top face, is the set of points with \(0 \le x \le L\) and \(y^2 + z^2 \le r^2\). Let

\[q(t) = \sqrt{r^2 - t^2} , \qquad -r \le t \le r ,\]

be the upper half of the circle of radius \(r\). At every \(y\) between \(-r\) and \(r\) the cross section of the bar occupies a vertical chord from \(z = -q(y)\) to \(z = q(y)\). Is the bar a body between the graphs of the functions \(-q(y)\) and \(q(y)\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [-r, r]\)? It is not, because \(q\) has no derivative at \(t = r\). For \(k > 0\) we have \(q(r - k) = \sqrt{2rk - k^2}\), so the slope of the segment from the point of the graph above \(r - k\) to the point above \(r\) is

\[\frac{q(r) - q(r - k)}{k} = -\frac{\sqrt{2rk - k^2}}{k} = -\sqrt{\frac{2r}{k} - 1} .\]

For \(r = 5\) mm it is \(-31{,}61\) at \(k = 0{,}01\) mm and \(-316{,}2\) at \(k = 0{,}0001\) mm. As \(k\) goes to zero, \(2r/k\) grows beyond every bound, and with it the absolute value of the slope, so there is no limit. The tangent at the point \((r, 0)\) is vertical (figure 4.21, left). For \(t > r\) the function \(q\) is not even defined, because \(r^2 - t^2 < 0\).

So we cut the bar with the planes \(y = 3\) mm and \(y = -3\) mm into three pieces (figure 4.21, right). We chose the number \(3\) because \(3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2\). The points \((y, z) = (\pm 3, \pm 4)\) in millimetres therefore lie on the circle, and \(q(\pm 3) = 4\) and \(q(\pm 4) = 3\). Let us write the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) in millimetres.

  1. The middle piece \(C\) consists of the points of the bar with \(-3 \le y \le 3\). For such \(y\), \(z\) lies between \(-q(y)\) and \(q(y)\), so \(C\) is a body between the graphs of the functions \(-q(y)\) and \(q(y)\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [-3, 3]\) in the variables \(x\) and \(y\).
  2. The right piece \(D\) consists of the points of the bar with \(y \ge 3\). For such a point \(z^2 \le 25 - y^2 \le 16\), so \(-4 \le z \le 4\) (lemma 1.28, that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square). From \(y^2 \le 25 - z^2 = q(z)^2\) it follows by the same lemma that \(y \le q(z)\). Conversely, every point with \(-4 \le z \le 4\) and \(3 \le y \le q(z)\) satisfies \(y^2 + z^2 \le q(z)^2 + z^2 = 25\). The piece \(D\) is therefore a body between the graphs of the constant function \(3\) and the function \(q(z)\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [-4, 4]\) in the variables \(x\) and \(z\). Here \(y\) is the coordinate that runs between the graphs. The condition \(3 \le q(z)\) holds because \(q(z)^2 = 25 - z^2 \ge 9\).
  3. The left piece \(E\) consists of the points of the bar with \(y \le -3\). Like \(D\), it is a body between the graphs of the functions \(-q(z)\) and \(-3\) over the same rectangle.

For the pieces to be bodies between graphs, we still have to show that \(q\) is continuously differentiable on an open interval containing \([-4, 4]\). We get rid of the root by writing the difference of two roots through the difference of their squares.

Lemma 4.16 Derivative of the upper half of a circle (odvod zgornje polovice krožnice)

Let \(r > 0\) and \(q(t) = \sqrt{r^2 - t^2}\) for \(-r < t < r\). Then \(q(t) > 0\), the function \(q\) is differentiable at every point of the open interval \((-r, r)\),

\[q'(t) = -\frac{t}{q(t)} , \tag{4.11}\]

and \(q'\) is continuous at every point of \((-r, r)\). The function \(q\) is thus continuously differentiable on \((-r, r)\).

Proof

We must show that the difference quotient of the function \(q\) converges to \(-t/q(t)\) and that this number changes continuously with \(t\).

  1. Let \(-r < t < r\). Then \(|t| < r\) and by lemma 1.28 \(t^2 < r^2\), so \(r^2 - t^2 > 0\). The square root of a positive number is positive, because its square is positive, while the square of the number \(0\) is \(0\) (theorem 1.36). Thus \(q(t) > 0\).
  2. Let \(s, t \in (-r, r)\). We have \(\big(q(s) - q(t)\big)\big(q(s) + q(t)\big) = q(s)^2 - q(t)^2 = (r^2 - s^2) - (r^2 - t^2) = t^2 - s^2\). Since \(q(s) + q(t) > 0\), we may divide by it:
    \[q(s) - q(t) = -\frac{(s - t)(s + t)}{q(s) + q(t)} .\]
  3. Continuity. The denominator in step 2 is not smaller than \(q(t)\), because \(q(s) \ge 0\). The numerator is at most \(2r\,|s - t|\) in absolute value, because \(|s + t| \le |s| + |t| < 2r\). Hence
    \[|q(s) - q(t)| \le \frac{2r}{q(t)}\,|s - t| ,\]
    which is less than \(\eta\) when \(|s - t| < \eta\,q(t)/(2r)\). The function \(q\) is thus continuous at \(t\) (definition 1.58).
  4. The difference quotient. Let \(k \neq 0\) and \(|k| < r - |t|\), so that \(t + k\) lies in \((-r, r)\). By step 2 with \(s = t + k\),
    \[\frac{q(t + k) - q(t)}{k} = -\frac{2t + k}{q(t + k) + q(t)} .\]
  5. We compare the quotient with the number \(-t/q(t)\). We write the two fractions with a common denominator and simplify the numerator:
    \[-\frac{2t + k}{q(t + k) + q(t)} + \frac{t}{q(t)} = \frac{t\,\big(q(t + k) - q(t)\big) - k\,q(t)}{\big(q(t + k) + q(t)\big)\,q(t)} .\]
    In the numerator, \(-(2t + k)\,q(t) + t\,\big(q(t + k) + q(t)\big) = t\,q(t + k) - t\,q(t) - k\,q(t)\).
  6. The denominator is not smaller than \(q(t)^2\), because \(q(t + k) \ge 0\). By step 3, \(|q(t + k) - q(t)| \le 2r\,|k|/q(t)\), and \(|t| < r\). By the triangle inequality for numbers (lemma 1.6, item 1) the absolute value of the difference in step 5 is therefore at most
    \[\frac{r \cdot 2r\,|k|/q(t) + |k|\,q(t)}{q(t)^2} = C_{\mathrm{t}}\,|k| , \qquad C_{\mathrm{t}} = \frac{2r^2 + q(t)^2}{q(t)^3} .\]
  7. For \(\eta > 0\) we take as the band \(\delta\) the smaller of the numbers \(\eta/C_{\mathrm{t}}\) and \(r - |t|\). For every \(k\) with \(0 < |k| < \delta\) the difference in step 5 is less than \(\eta\). By the definition of the derivative 1.9 and of the limit 1.5, \(q'(t) = -t/q(t)\).
  8. Continuity of the derivative. For \(s \in (-r, r)\), as in step 5,
    \[-\frac{s}{q(s)} + \frac{t}{q(t)} = \frac{t\,\big(q(s) - q(t)\big) - (s - t)\,q(t)}{q(s)\,q(t)} .\]
    By step 3, \(|q(s) - q(t)| < q(t)/2\) when \(|s - t| < q(t)^2/(4r)\), and then \(q(s) > q(t)/2\) and the denominator is greater than \(q(t)^2/2\). As in step 6, the numerator is at most \((2r^2/q(t) + q(t))\,|s - t|\). The difference is therefore at most \(2C_{\mathrm{t}}\,|s - t|\), which is less than \(\eta\) when \(|s - t|\) is smaller than \(\eta/(2C_{\mathrm{t}})\) and than \(q(t)^2/(4r)\). The derivative is continuous at \(t\).

Source: LEBL1 Example 4.1.4 (PDF p. 156) computes the derivative of the function \(\sqrt x\) with the same device of a difference of squares, and Proposition 4.1.10 (PDF p. 159) is the chain rule, from which the formula would follow. The proof is not from the sources.

For the bar \(r = 5\) mm, and the interval \([-4, 4]\) lies in \((-5, 5)\). The function \(q(y)\), taken as a function of the point \((x, y)\) on the open set of points of the plane with \(-5 < y < 5\), has the partial derivative zero with respect to \(x\) and the partial derivative \(q'(y)\) with respect to \(y\). Both are continuous, because two points of the plane differ in the coordinate \(y\) by at most their distance. The same holds for \(-q(y)\), for \(\pm q(z)\) and for the constant functions \(\pm 3\). All three pieces are therefore bodies between graphs. The cut at \(y = \pm 3\) makes sure that each piece uses the function \(q\) only on the interval \([-4, 4]\), where its derivative is at most \(4/3\) in absolute value, at \(t = \pm 4\). In the piece \(D\) the lids \(y = 3\) and \(y = q(z)\) meet at \(z = \pm 4\), because \(q(\pm 4) = 3\), which the definition allows.

The pieces touch only at the cuts. A point that lies in \(C\) and in \(D\) has \(y \le 3\) and \(y \ge 3\), so \(y = 3\), and lies on the rectangle \(0 \le x \le L\), \(-4 \le z \le 4\) in the plane \(y = 3\). An interior point of the piece \(C\), however, has \(y < 3\). A ball around it lies in \(C\), where \(y \le 3\) (section 1.15.6), and if the point had \(y = 3\), the ball would contain points with \(y > 3\). So no interior point of the piece \(C\) lies in \(D\), and likewise no interior point of the piece \(D\) lies in \(C\). The same holds for the pieces \(C\) and \(E\), while the pieces \(D\) and \(E\) have no common points.

Finally let us show that a body between graphs is closed and bounded. We will need this, because we will use the theorem on uniform continuity 4.6 on it.

Lemma 4.17 A body between two graphs is closed and bounded (telo med grafoma je zaprto in omejeno)

The body between graphs \(V\) of definition 4.15 is a closed and bounded set of points (definition 1.74).

Proof

We must show that the limit of a convergent sequence of points of \(V\) lies in \(V\) and that all points of \(V\) are at most some number away from the origin.
