  1. The functions \(g\) and \(h\) are continuous at every point of \(U\) by lemma 1.91, that a continuously differentiable function is continuous. The lemma speaks of functions of three variables, but its proof with theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step holds likewise for functions of two variables.
  2. Let the sequence of points \(P_{\mathrm{n}} = (x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}}, z_{\mathrm{n}})\) of \(V\) converge to the point \(P = (x, y, z)\). By lemma 1.66 on convergence coordinate by coordinate, \(x_{\mathrm{n}} \to x\), \(y_{\mathrm{n}} \to y\) and \(z_{\mathrm{n}} \to z\).
  3. From \(a \le x_{\mathrm{n}} \le b\) and \(c \le y_{\mathrm{n}} \le d\), by lemma 1.48 that limits preserve non-strict inequalities, item 2, it follows that \(a \le x \le b\) and \(c \le y \le d\). The point \((x, y)\) lies in \(R\).
  4. The points \((x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}})\) converge to \((x, y)\), and \(g\) is continuous at \((x, y)\). By lemma 1.68 on continuity through sequences of points, therefore, \(g(x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}}) \to g(x, y)\). Likewise \(h(x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}}) \to h(x, y)\).
  5. From \(g(x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}}) \le z_{\mathrm{n}} \le h(x_{\mathrm{n}}, y_{\mathrm{n}})\), by lemma 1.48, item 1, it follows that \(g(x, y) \le z \le h(x, y)\). The point \(P\) lies in \(V\), which is therefore closed.
  6. Boundedness. The rectangle \(R\), seen as the set of points \((x, y, 0)\) of space, is closed and bounded (section 4.2.2). The functions \(g\) and \(h\) are continuous on it, so by theorem 1.78, the extreme value theorem in space, there are numbers \(m\) and \(M\) with \(m \le g\) and \(h \le M\) on \(R\). For every point of \(V\) we therefore have \(|z| \le |m| + |M|\), and also \(|x| \le |a| + |b|\) and \(|y| \le |c| + |d|\). As for the box in section 1.13.4, \(|\overrightarrow{OP}|\) is at most the root of the sum of the squares of these three bounds.

Source: The lemma is not from the sources. The proof follows the examples of the box and the bar in section 1.13.4.

4.2.7 Differentiating an integral with respect to a parameter

Let us recall the proof of the divergence theorem for a box (theorem 4.14). We wrote the integral of the term \(\partial f/\partial x\) as an iterated integral whose inner integral is over \(x\), which we were allowed to do by theorem 4.9. The fundamental theorem of calculus then turned the integral along every segment parallel to the axis \(x\) into the difference of the values on the faces \(x = a_1\) and \(x = b_1\). For a body between graphs we can treat the term \(\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z\) in this way, because the segments parallel to the axis \(z\) are exactly the chords from the bottom to the top lid. The terms \(\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x\) and \(\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y\), however, are inside the inner integral over \(z\), whose limits \(g(x, y)\) and \(h(x, y)\) depend on \(x\) and \(y\). So we must bring the derivative with respect to \(y\) out of the integral. In doing so both the integrand and the limits change, and the motion of the limits will give terms on the lids. This section says how such an integral changes: first, that it changes continuously, which we need for the iterated integral to exist at all, and then how to differentiate it.

The inner integral of a body between graphs is the function

\[F(x, y) = \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(x, y)} f(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z ,\]

whose input is a point \((x, y)\) of the shadow and whose output is a number. When the point moves a little, the integrand changes a little, and the two limits move a little. The uniform continuity of the function \(f\) bounds the change of the integrand, as in lemma 4.7. The motion of the limits adds or removes a short piece of the interval, on which \(f\) is bounded, so its contribution is small too.

Lemma 4.18 Continuity of an integral with variable limits (zveznost integrala s spremenljivima mejama)

Let \(V\) be a body between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) (definition 4.15) and \(f\) a function that is continuous on \(V\). Then for every point \((x, y) \in R\) the integral

\[F(x, y) = \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(x, y)} f(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\]

exists, and for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|F(x', y') - F(x, y)| < \eta\) for all points \((x, y), (x', y') \in R\) with \((x' - x)^2 + (y' - y)^2 < \delta^2\).

Proof

We must show that the integral exists and that it changes little when the point moves a little. We split the intervals of integration at two nearby points into a common part and pieces at the ends.

  1. Existence. For fixed \(x\) and \(y\) the function \(z \mapsto f(x, y, z)\) is continuous on \([g(x, y), h(x, y)]\), because the distance between the points \((x, y, z)\) and \((x, y, z')\) is \(|z - z'|\). By theorem 3.38 it is integrable. If \(g(x, y) = h(x, y)\), the integral is zero by the convention of definition 3.34.
  2. Bounds. The body \(V\) is closed and bounded by lemma 4.17, so by theorem 1.78 there is a number \(M > 0\) with \(|f| \le M\) on \(V\). By the same theorem, applied to the continuous function \(h - g\) on \(R\), there is a number \(H > 0\) with \(h - g \le H\) on \(R\).
  3. We choose \(\eta > 0\). By theorem 4.6 there is a \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that \(|f(Q) - f(Q')| < \eta/(2H)\) for any two points \(Q, Q' \in V\) with \(|QQ'| < \delta_1\). By the same theorem on \(R\) there is a \(\delta_2 > 0\) such that \(|g(P') - g(P)| < \eta/(4M)\) and \(|h(P') - h(P)| < \eta/(4M)\) for any two points \(P, P' \in R\) with \(|PP'| < \delta_2\). For \(\delta\) we take the smaller of the numbers \(\delta_1\) and \(\delta_2\).
  4. Let \(P = (x, y)\) and \(P' = (x', y')\) be points of \(R\) with \(|PP'| < \delta\). We write \(g = g(P)\), \(h = h(P)\), \(g' = g(P')\) and \(h' = h(P')\), and \(z_1 = \max\{g, g'\}\) and \(z_2 = \min\{h, h'\}\). For short we also write \(f(P, z)\) for \(f(x, y, z)\).
  5. The case \(z_1 \le z_2\), when the intervals \([g, h]\) and \([g', h']\) overlap. The interval \([g, h]\) splits into \([g, z_1]\), \([z_1, z_2]\) and \([z_2, h]\), and by additivity (lemma 3.39, item 2, with the convention for pieces of length zero) \(F(P)\) is the sum of the integrals over these three pieces. Likewise \(F(P')\) splits over \([g', z_1]\), \([z_1, z_2]\) and \([z_2, h']\). Hence
    \[\begin{aligned} F(P') - F(P) = {} & \int_{\mathrm{z}_1}^{z_2} \big(f(P', z) - f(P, z)\big)\,\mathrm{d}z \\ & + \int_{\mathrm{g}'}^{z_1} f(P', z)\,\mathrm{d}z + \int_{\mathrm{z}_2}^{h'} f(P', z)\,\mathrm{d}z \\ & - \int_{\mathrm{g}}^{z_1} f(P, z)\,\mathrm{d}z - \int_{\mathrm{z}_2}^{h} f(P, z)\,\mathrm{d}z . \end{aligned}\]
  6. The points \((P, z)\) and \((P', z)\) with \(z_1 \le z \le z_2\) lie in \(V\) and are a distance \(|PP'| < \delta_1\) apart, so the first integrand is less than \(\eta/(2H)\) in absolute value. By the bound (lemma 3.39, item 3) the first integral is at most \(\eta\,(z_2 - z_1)/(2H) \le \eta/2\) in absolute value, because \(z_2 - z_1 \le h - g \le H\).
  7. By the bound, the other four integrals are at most \(M\) times the length of the interval in absolute value. Of the lengths \(z_1 - g\) and \(z_1 - g'\) one is zero and the other \(|g' - g|\), because \(z_1\) is the larger of the numbers \(g\) and \(g'\). Likewise, of the lengths \(h - z_2\) and \(h' - z_2\) one is zero and the other \(|h' - h|\). The sum of the four is therefore at most \(M\,(|g' - g| + |h' - h|) < M \cdot 2\eta/(4M) = \eta/2\).
  8. The case \(z_1 > z_2\), when the intervals do not overlap. Since \(g \le h\) and \(g' \le h'\), then \(g' > h\) or \(g > h'\). Let \(g' > h\), the other case is the same with the two points exchanged. Then \(h - g < g' - g\) and \(h' - g' < h' - h\). By the bound \(|F(P)| \le M\,(h - g)\) and \(|F(P')| \le M\,(h' - g')\), so \(|F(P') - F(P)| \le |F(P')| + |F(P)| < M\,(|g' - g| + |h' - h|) < \eta/2\).
  9. In both cases, by the triangle inequality for numbers, \(|F(P') - F(P)| < \eta/2 + \eta/2 = \eta\).

Source: The lemma is not from the sources. For constant limits it is LEBL1 Proposition 7.5.12 (PDF p. 292), as lemma 4.7.

The lemma has extended item 1 of lemma 4.7 to variable limits. The function \(F\) thus has the property of that item, so by its item 2 the middle integral \(\int_{\mathrm{c}}^d F(x, y)\,\mathrm{d}y\) exists and is a continuous function of \(x\). The iterated integral of the function \(f\) in the order \(z\), \(y\), \(x\) therefore exists. Two devices were the key: uniform continuity, which bounded the change of the integrand for all \(z\) at once, and the boundedness of the function \(f\), which bounded the contribution of the pieces at the ends.

Now the derivative. Take a function of two variables \(f(t, s)\) and its integral over \(t\) whose limits depend on \(s\):

\[G(s) = \int_{\varphi(\mathrm{s})}^{\psi(s)} f(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t .\]

We chose the letters \(t\) and \(s\) so that they do not get mixed up with the coordinates. In the proof of the theorem, \(t\) will be the coordinate \(z\), and \(s\) will be \(y\) or \(x\). When \(s\) increases by \(k\), \(G\) changes for three reasons (figure 4.22, left). The integrand changes over the whole interval, by about \(k\,\partial f/\partial s\). The upper limit moves by about \(\psi'(s)\,k\), and the interval gains a piece of this length, on which the integrand is about \(f(\psi(s), s)\). The lower limit moves by about \(\varphi'(s)\,k\), and the interval loses a piece with the integrand about \(f(\varphi(s), s)\). Divided by \(k\), this gives the three terms of the derivative.

Lemma 4.19 Differentiating an integral with respect to a parameter (odvod integrala po parametru)

Let \(\alpha < \beta\) and \(c < d\) be numbers, and let \(f\) be a function whose input is two numbers \(t\) and \(s\) from the rectangle \([\alpha, \beta] \times [c, d]\) and whose output is a number \(f(t, s)\). For every \(t \in [\alpha, \beta]\) let the function \(\sigma \mapsto f(t, \sigma)\) be differentiable at every point of the interval \([c, d]\), at the endpoints \(c\) and \(d\) with a one-sided derivative (definition 1.9). We denote its derivative at the point \(s\) by \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s)\), like the partial derivative (definition 1.25), which is the derivative with the other variable held fixed. Let the functions \(f\) and \(\partial f/\partial s\) be continuous on this rectangle.

  1. The function
    \[G(s) = \int_\alpha^\beta f(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t\]
    is differentiable at every point \(s \in (c, d)\), its derivative is
    \[G'(s) = \int_\alpha^\beta \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t , \tag{4.12}\]
    and \(G'\) is continuous on \((c, d)\).
  2. Let \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) be functions on \([c, d]\) with \(\alpha \le \varphi(s) \le \psi(s) \le \beta\) for every \(s \in [c, d]\), which are differentiable at the point \(s_0 \in (c, d)\). Then the function
    \[G(s) = \int_{\varphi(\mathrm{s})}^{\psi(s)} f(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t\]
    is differentiable at \(s_0\), and
    \[\begin{aligned} G'(s_0) = {} & \int_{\varphi(\mathrm{s}_0)}^{\psi(s_0)} \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s_0)\,\mathrm{d}t \\ & + f\big(\psi(s_0), s_0\big)\,\psi'(s_0) - f\big(\varphi(s_0), s_0\big)\,\varphi'(s_0) . \end{aligned} \tag{4.13}\]
Proof

We must show both items. For the first we write the change of the integrand with the mean value theorem and bound it uniformly for all \(t\). For the second we split the change of the function \(G\) into the change of the integrand, which the first item handles, and the pieces at the ends.

1. Constant limits.

  1. For every \(s \in [c, d]\) the functions \(t \mapsto f(t, s)\) and \(t \mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s)\) are continuous on \([\alpha, \beta]\), because the distance between the points \((t, s)\) and \((t', s)\) is \(|t - t'|\). By theorem 3.38 they are integrable, so the numbers \(G(s)\) and \(I(s) = \int_\alpha^\beta \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t\) exist.
  2. The rectangle is closed and bounded (section 4.2.2). We choose \(\eta > 0\). By theorem 4.6 there is a \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that \(\big|\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t', s') - \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s)\big| < \eta/(2(\beta - \alpha))\) for any two points of the rectangle less than \(\delta_1\) apart.
  3. Let \(s \in (c, d)\) and let \(\delta\) be the smallest of the numbers \(\delta_1\), \(s - c\) and \(d - s\). Let \(0 < |k| < \delta\), so that \(s + k\) lies in \((c, d)\).
  4. Let \(t \in [\alpha, \beta]\). The function \(\sigma \mapsto f(t, \sigma)\) is continuous on \([c, d]\), because \(f\) is continuous on the rectangle and the distance between the points \((t, \sigma)\) and \((t, \sigma')\) is \(|\sigma - \sigma'|\), as in step 1. By hypothesis it is differentiable at every point of \([c, d]\), with the derivative \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, \sigma)\). By step 3 the closed interval between \(s\) and \(s + k\) lies in \((c, d)\). By the mean value theorem 1.84 there is a number \(\sigma_{\mathrm{t}}\) between \(s\) and \(s + k\) such that
    \[f(t, s + k) - f(t, s) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, \sigma_{\mathrm{t}})\,k .\]
  5. The point \((t, \sigma_{\mathrm{t}})\) is less than \(|k| < \delta_1\) away from \((t, s)\), so by step 2
    \[\begin{aligned} & \Big| f(t, s + k) - f(t, s) - k\,\frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s) \Big| \\ & \quad = |k|\,\Big| \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, \sigma_{\mathrm{t}}) - \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s) \Big| \le \frac{\eta\,|k|}{2(\beta - \alpha)} \end{aligned}\]
    for every \(t \in [\alpha, \beta]\).
  6. The function inside the absolute value on the left is a continuous function of \(t\) (step 1 and corollary 1.64). By linearity (lemma 3.39, item 1) its integral is \(G(s + k) - G(s) - k\,I(s)\), and by the bound (item 3 of the same lemma) this is at most \(\eta\,|k|/2\) in absolute value. We divide by \(|k|\):
    \[\Big| \frac{G(s + k) - G(s)}{k} - I(s) \Big| \le \frac{\eta}{2} < \eta .\]
  7. The error \(\eta\) was arbitrary, so by the definition of the derivative 1.9 and of the limit 1.5, \(G'(s) = I(s)\).
  8. Continuity of the derivative. For \(s, s' \in (c, d)\) with \(|s' - s| < \delta_1\), by step 2 and the bound, \(|I(s') - I(s)| \le (\beta - \alpha) \cdot \eta/(2(\beta - \alpha)) < \eta\). The function \(G' = I\) is therefore continuous at every point of \((c, d)\).

2. Variable limits.

  1. For \(w \in [\alpha, \beta]\) and \(\sigma \in [c, d]\) let \(K(w, \sigma) = \int_\alpha^w f(t, \sigma)\,\mathrm{d}t\), which for \(w = \alpha\) is zero by the convention of definition 3.34. By additivity (lemma 3.39, item 2, with the same convention for pieces of length zero), for every \(\sigma \in [c, d]\)
    \[G(\sigma) = K\big(\psi(\sigma), \sigma\big) - K\big(\varphi(\sigma), \sigma\big) .\]
  2. We write \(s = s_0\) and let \(0 < |k|\), where \(|k|\) is smaller than the numbers \(s - c\) and \(d - s\). We also write \(\varphi = \varphi(s)\), \(\psi = \psi(s)\), \(\varphi_{\mathrm{k}} = \varphi(s + k)\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{k}} = \psi(s + k)\). By step 1, adding and subtracting \(K(\psi, s + k) - K(\varphi, s + k)\),
    \[\begin{aligned} G(s + k) - G(s) = {} & \big[K(\psi_{\mathrm{k}}, s + k) - K(\psi, s + k)\big] \\ & - \big[K(\varphi_{\mathrm{k}}, s + k) - K(\varphi, s + k)\big] \\ & + \int_{\varphi}^{\psi} \big(f(t, s + k) - f(t, s)\big)\,\mathrm{d}t . \end{aligned}\]
    By additivity and linearity the last term equals \(K(\psi, s + k) - K(\varphi, s + k) - K(\psi, s) + K(\varphi, s)\).
  3. The last term divided by \(k\) approaches \(\int_\varphi^\psi \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}t\). If \(\varphi < \psi\), this is the first item, applied on the rectangle \([\varphi, \psi] \times [c, d]\), which lies in \([\alpha, \beta] \times [c, d]\). If \(\varphi = \psi\), both sides are zero.
  4. The pieces at the ends. Let \(\chi\) be one of the functions \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\), \(w = \chi(s)\) and \(w_{\mathrm{k}} = \chi(s + k)\). We must show that \(\big(K(w_{\mathrm{k}}, s + k) - K(w, s + k)\big)/k\) approaches \(f(w, s)\,\chi'(s)\). We choose an error \(\eta\) with \(0 < \eta \le 1\). Larger errors need not be considered, because the band that fits the error \(1\) fits them. Let \(\eta' = \eta/\big(|\chi'(s)| + 1 + |f(w, s)|\big)\), which is not larger than \(1\). The function \(f\) is continuous at the point \((w, s)\), so there is a \(\delta_2 > 0\) such that \(|f(t, \sigma) - f(w, s)| < \eta'\) for the points \((t, \sigma)\) of the rectangle less than \(\delta_2\) away from \((w, s)\). The function \(\chi\) is differentiable at \(s\), hence continuous there (lemma 1.79), and there is a \(\delta_3 > 0\) such that \(|w_{\mathrm{k}} - w| < \delta_2/2\) for \(|k| < \delta_3\).
  5. Let \(|k|\) also be smaller than \(\delta_3\) and than \(\delta_2/2\). For every \(t\) between \(w\) and \(w_{\mathrm{k}}\) the distance between the points \((t, s + k)\) and \((w, s)\) is \(\sqrt{(t - w)^2 + k^2}\). It is not larger than \(|t - w| + |k|\), because the square of this sum is \((t - w)^2 + 2\,|t - w|\,|k| + k^2\) (lemma 1.28), so it is smaller than \(\delta_2/2 + \delta_2/2 = \delta_2\). Hence \(f(w, s) - \eta' < f(t, s + k) < f(w, s) + \eta'\).
  6. If \(w_{\mathrm{k}} > w\), then by additivity \(K(w_{\mathrm{k}}, s + k) - K(w, s + k) = \int_{\mathrm{w}}^{w_{\mathrm{k}}} f(t, s + k)\,\mathrm{d}t\). By the bound and step 5 this number lies between \((f(w, s) - \eta')(w_{\mathrm{k}} - w)\) and \((f(w, s) + \eta')(w_{\mathrm{k}} - w)\). If \(w_{\mathrm{k}} < w\), the difference is \(-\int_{\mathrm{w}_\mathrm{k}}^{w} f(t, s + k)\,\mathrm{d}t\) and lies between \((f(w, s) + \eta')(w_{\mathrm{k}} - w)\) and \((f(w, s) - \eta')(w_{\mathrm{k}} - w)\). If \(w_{\mathrm{k}} = w\), it is zero. In all three cases
    \[\big| K(w_{\mathrm{k}}, s + k) - K(w, s + k) - f(w, s)\,(w_{\mathrm{k}} - w) \big| \le \eta'\,|w_{\mathrm{k}} - w| .\]
  7. The difference quotient \((w_{\mathrm{k}} - w)/k\) of the function \(\chi\) at \(s\) converges to \(\chi'(s)\). By the definition of the limit 1.5 with the error \(\eta'\), for small enough \(|k|\) the difference \(|(w_{\mathrm{k}} - w)/k - \chi'(s)|\) is therefore smaller than \(\eta'\), and since \(\eta' \le 1\), \(|w_{\mathrm{k}} - w|/|k| < |\chi'(s)| + 1\). We divide the inequality of step 6 by \(|k|\) and use the triangle inequality for numbers:
    \[\begin{aligned} \Big| \frac{K(w_{\mathrm{k}}, s + k) - K(w, s + k)}{k} - f(w, s)\,\chi'(s) \Big| &< \eta'\,\big(|\chi'(s)| + 1\big) \\ &\quad + |f(w, s)|\,\eta' . \end{aligned}\]
    By the choice of the number \(\eta'\) in step 4 the right side equals \(\eta\). The quotient therefore approaches \(f(w, s)\,\chi'(s)\).
  8. By step 2, \((G(s + k) - G(s))/k\) is a sum of three quotients. By step 7 the first approaches \(f(\psi, s)\,\psi'(s)\), the second with the minus sign \(-f(\varphi, s)\,\varphi'(s)\), and by step 3 the third \(\int_\varphi^\psi \frac{\partial f}{\partial s}\,\mathrm{d}t\). For the error \(\eta\) we take \(|k|\) so small that each of the three quotients is less than \(\eta/3\) away from its limit. By the triangle inequality, \((G(s + k) - G(s))/k\) is then less than \(\eta\) away from the sum of the limits, which is the right side of (4.13).

Source: LEBL2 Theorem 9.1.1 (PDF pp. 65-66) for item 1, where \(f\) is given only on the rectangle. The source does not have item 2, and its proof is not from the sources.

The lemma says what the figure predicted. The first item says that with constant limits we may differentiate under the integral sign. The second adds two terms contributed by the moving limits: the value of the integrand at the limit, times the speed at which the limit moves. The proof used devices we know: the mean value theorem, as in the first item of the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.40, uniform continuity, as in theorem 3.38, and the bound of the integral over a short piece, as in the second item of the fundamental theorem of calculus. The derivative in this second item even follows from the second item of the lemma. With the integrand \(f(t, s) = f(t)\), which does not depend on \(s\), the constant lower limit \(\varphi(s) = \alpha\) and the upper limit \(\psi(s) = s\), the second item gives \(G'(s) = f(s) \cdot 1\).

Let us test the second item on the cross section of the round bar (figure 4.22, right). The square of the distance of the point \((y, z)\) of the cross section from the axis of the bar is \(y^2 + z^2\). At every \(y\) we integrate it along the chord from \(z = -q(y)\) to \(z = q(y)\):

\[\Theta(y) = \int_{-\mathrm{q}(\mathrm{y})}^{q(y)} (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}z .\]

We will meet such an integral in section 4.2.12, because the downward displacement of the hanging bar has the term \(-0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\). Here \(t = z\), \(s = y\), \(f(z, y) = y^2 + z^2\), \(\varphi = -q\) and \(\psi = q\). For the rectangle we take \([-5, 5] \times [2, 4]\) in millimetres. On it \(f\) is a polynomial with the partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial y = 2y\), and the limits \(\pm q(y)\) lie in \([-5, 5]\). At \(y = 3\) mm we have \(q(3) = 4\) mm and by (4.11) \(q'(3) = -3/4\), so \(\varphi'(3) = 3/4\). By (4.13)

\[\begin{aligned} \Theta'(3) &= \int_{-4}^{4} 2 \cdot 3\,\mathrm{d}z + (9 + 16) \cdot \Big(-\frac34\Big) - (9 + 16) \cdot \frac34 \\ &= 48 - 18{,}75 - 18{,}75 = 10{,}5\ \text{mm}^2 . \end{aligned}\]

The first term says that the integrand grows, because \(y^2\) grows with \(y\). The other two say that the chord gets shorter. When \(y\) increases by a small step, say \(0{,}01\) mm, each end of the chord moves toward the axis \(y\) by about \(0{,}75\) times as much, \(0{,}0075\) mm, at a place where the integrand is \(y^2 + q(y)^2 = r^2 = 25\ \text{mm}^2\). Let us check without the lemma. By the fundamental theorem of calculus with the function \(y^2 z + z^3/3\), whose derivative with respect to \(z\) is \(y^2 + z^2\), we get \(\Theta(y) = 2\,q(y)\,y^2 + \tfrac23\,q(y)^3\), and \(\Theta(3) = 72 + 42{,}667 = 114{,}667\ \text{mm}^3\). With SymPy we computed \(\Theta(3{,}01) = 114{,}771\ \text{mm}^3\) and the difference quotient \((\Theta(3{,}01) - \Theta(3))/0{,}01 = 10{,}44\) mm², and with the step \(0{,}001\) mm \(10{,}49\) mm². The quotients approach \(10{,}5\) mm².

4.2.8 Integral over a body between two graphs

Now we can define the integral of a function over a body between graphs as the integral over a box, with iterated integrals in the order \(z\), \(y\), \(x\). The inner integral over \(z\) exists by lemma 4.18 and has the property of item 1 of lemma 4.7. By item 2 of that lemma the middle integral over \(y\) therefore exists and is a continuous function of \(x\), and the outer integral exists by theorem 3.38.

Definition 4.20 Integral over a body between two graphs (integral po telesu med grafoma)

Let \(V\) be a body between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) (definition 4.15) and \(f\) a function that is continuous on \(V\). The integral of the function \(f\) over the body \(V\) is the number

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \bigg( \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \bigg( \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(x, y)} f(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z \bigg) \mathrm{d}y \bigg) \mathrm{d}x . \tag{4.14}\]

For a body with exchanged roles of the coordinates the inner integral is over the coordinate that runs between the graphs, and the middle and the outer one are over the coordinates of the rectangle, in the order given by the description of the body.

Source: KREYSZIG §10.3, (3) (PDF p. 453), for the double integral over a region between two curves, and §10.7 (PDF pp. 478-479), where the triple integral is defined by a subdivision into small boxes and computed by three successive integrations. LEBL2 Proposition 10.5.8 (PDF p. 126) states that the integral of the general theory over a region between two graphs in the plane equals the iterated integral, and leaves the proof to the reader. The definition by the iterated integral is not from the sources.

The round bar is not described by a single body between graphs but by three pieces. We define the integral over it as the sum of the integrals over the pieces.

Definition 4.21 Body cut into pieces (telo, razrezano na kose)

Let \(V\) be a set of points that is the union of the bodies between graphs \(V_1, \dots, V_{\mathrm{m}}\) (definition 4.15), each with its own naming of the axes, and let no interior point of any of them lie in another one. We then say that \(V\) is cut into pieces (razrezano na kose) \(V_1, \dots, V_{\mathrm{m}}\). The integral of a continuous function \(f\) over a body cut in this way is the sum of the integrals over the pieces (definition 4.20),

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m} \int_{\mathrm{V}_\mathrm{k}} f\,\mathrm{d}V .\]

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7 (PDF p. 482) cuts a body by auxiliary surfaces into pieces, for which it proves the divergence theorem separately. The definition of the integral as a sum over the pieces is not from the sources.

The definition agrees with the ones we already have. A box is a body between the graphs of constant functions, and then (4.14) is equation (4.7). A body made of boxes is cut into pieces that are its cells, and definition 4.21 gives the sum of definition 4.11, item 1. Two things remain open, however. Would another order of integration give the same number, and would another cut of the same body give the same sum? For a box and for a body made of boxes we proved both (theorem 4.9 and lemma 4.12). For a body between graphs and for a body cut into pieces both questions are answered by sections 4.2.9 and 4.2.10, in which we define the integral without iterated integrals and without a cut. The proof of the divergence theorem does not need these answers, because it uses only one order and only the given cut. Whenever we compute the integral over a body cut into pieces, we will say which cut we use.

For computing we need linearity and monotonicity.

Lemma 4.22 Properties of the integral over a body between two graphs (lastnosti integrala po telesu med grafoma)

Let \(V\) be a body between graphs or a body cut into pieces (definition 4.21), \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) continuous functions on \(V\) and \(\alpha\) a number.

  1. Linearity: \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} (f_1 + f_2)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{V}} f_1\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{V}} f_2\,\mathrm{d}V\) and \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \alpha f_1\,\mathrm{d}V = \alpha \int_{\mathrm{V}} f_1\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  2. Monotonicity: if \(f_1(P) \le f_2(P)\) for every point \(P \in V\), then \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} f_1\,\mathrm{d}V \le \int_{\mathrm{V}} f_2\,\mathrm{d}V\).
Proof

We must show both items. The proof is the proof of lemma 4.10, items 1 and 4.

  1. For a body between graphs we use, on each of the three iterated integrals, the linearity or the monotonicity of the integral over an interval (lemma 3.39, items 1 and 4), first on the inner one, then on the middle and on the outer one. We may do so because by lemma 4.18 and by lemma 4.7, item 2, all the intermediate integrals are continuous functions.
  2. For a body cut into pieces we add the equalities or inequalities of step 1 over the pieces.

Source: LEBL2 Propositions 10.1.10 and 10.1.11 (PDF p. 96) for integrable functions on a rectangle. The proof by iterated integrals is not from the sources.

The integral of the constant function \(1\) over a body is its volume. For a box this is the school volume by lemma 4.10, item 2. Let us compute the volume of the round bar with the cut into the pieces \(C\), \(D\) and \(E\) of section 4.2.6 (figure 4.21, right), with the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) in millimetres.

  1. The piece \(C\). The inner integral is \(\int_{-\mathrm{q}(\mathrm{y})}^{q(y)} 1\,\mathrm{d}z = 2\,q(y)\), the middle one \(A_{\mathrm{C}} = \int_{-3}^{3} 2\,q(y)\,\mathrm{d}y\), and the outer one \(\int_0^L A_{\mathrm{C}}\,\mathrm{d}x = L\,A_{\mathrm{C}}\).
  2. The piece \(D\). The inner integral, now over \(y\), is \(\int_3^{q(z)} 1\,\mathrm{d}y = q(z) - 3\), the middle one \(A_{\mathrm{D}} = \int_{-4}^{4} \big(q(z) - 3\big)\,\mathrm{d}z\), the outer one \(L\,A_{\mathrm{D}}\).
  3. The piece \(E\). The inner integral is \(-3 - (-q(z)) = q(z) - 3\), so the middle one is again \(A_{\mathrm{D}}\).

The numbers \(A_{\mathrm{C}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{D}}\) are the areas of the cross sections of the pieces. We cannot compute them with the tools of the book, because the function whose derivative is \(\sqrt{25 - t^2}\) needs the inverse sine function, which we have not defined. SymPy gives \(A_{\mathrm{C}} = 56{,}18\ \text{mm}^2\) and \(A_{\mathrm{D}} = 11{,}18\ \text{mm}^2\). The area of the cross section is therefore \(A = A_{\mathrm{C}} + 2A_{\mathrm{D}} = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\), which is the area of a disc \(\pi r^2\) of radius \(5\) mm from school geometry. The volume of the bar is

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} 1\,\mathrm{d}V = L\,(A_{\mathrm{C}} + 2A_{\mathrm{D}}) = L\,A = 10\,000\ \text{mm} \cdot 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2 = 785\,400\ \text{mm}^3 .\]

For a constant function \(\alpha\), by linearity \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \alpha\,\mathrm{d}V = \alpha\,L\,A\). The same holds for a function that depends only on \(x\). Its inner integrals over the pieces give its value times the area of the cross section of the piece, and the areas add up to \(A\). We will use this for the equilibrium of the whole bar in section 4.2.13.

4.2.9 Sets with volume

So far we have computed the integral over a body by a chosen recipe. For a box and for a body between graphs by iterated integrals in a chosen order, for the round bar by a cut into the pieces \(C\), \(D\) and \(E\). The questions from the end of section 4.2.8 remain. Would another order of integration give the same number? Would another cut? We could also cut the round bar by the planes \(y = 4\) mm and \(y = -4\) mm, and the pieces would have cross sections with other areas. If two cuts gave different sums, the words volume of the bar and weight of the bar would have no meaning, because the numbers would depend on our computation, not only on the bar.

We get the answer by defining the integral over a body as KREYSZIG does (§10.7, PDF p. 478). We cover the body by a grid of small boxes and add up the values of the function times the volumes of those cells that lie entirely in the body. Such a sum knows neither an order of integration nor a cut. If we show that for ever finer grids it approaches one single number, and that for a body between graphs this number equals the iterated integral in every order, both questions are settled.

The trouble comes from cells that lie in the body only partly. The sum leaves them out, so their total volume must be small for a fine grid. This is a property of the border between the body and its surroundings. In this section we describe this border precisely, name the sets that are covered by boxes of arbitrarily small total volume and the sets whose border is such, and show that the cells along the border have a small total volume for a fine grid. We define the integral in section 4.2.10.

Let us look at the cells along the boundary on the cross section of the round hanging bar, a disc of radius \(r = 5\) mm with its centre on the axis of the bar (figure 4.23). We write the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) in the plane of the cross section in millimetres. We cut the square \([-5, 5] \times [-5, 5]\), which contains the disc, by equally spaced lines parallel to the axes into square cells of side \(h\). A cell \([y_0, y_1] \times [z_0, z_1]\) lies in the disc exactly when its corner farthest from the centre lies in the disc. For a point of the cell we have \(|y| \le |y_0|\) when \(y < 0\), and \(|y| \le |y_1|\) when \(y \ge 0\), because \(y\) lies between \(y_0\) and \(y_1\). By lemma 1.28, that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, \(y^2\) is therefore not larger than the larger of the numbers \(y_0^2\) and \(y_1^2\), and the same holds for \(z\). Cells that have a point in the disc and a point outside it are grey in the figure. NumPy counted the cells:

side of the cell \(h\) cells in the disc their area grey cells their area
1 mm 60 60 mm² 36 36 mm²
0,5 mm 276 69 mm² 76 19 mm²
0,25 mm 1176 73,5 mm² 156 9,75 mm²
0,1 mm 7644 76,44 mm² 396 3,96 mm²

The area of the cells that lie in the disc grows toward the area \(A = 78{,}54\) mm², which we computed in section 4.2.8 by a cut into pieces. The area of the grey cells falls. Why does it roughly halve when the side is halved? The grey cells form a staircase along the circle. A quarter of the circle from the point \((5, 0)\) to the point \((0, 5)\) crosses \(5/h\) columns and \(5/h\) rows of cells, so there are about \(10/h\) grey cells along it, and about \(40/h\) along the whole circle. For \(h = 0{,}1\) mm this is \(400\), NumPy counted \(396\). Each has the area \(h^2\), so their total area is about \(40/h \cdot h^2 = 40\,h\), proportional to the side. The cells that lie in the disc therefore cover almost the whole disc. That this is so for every body we will meet has to be shown. The grey cells stay close to the circle, so let us start with the border between a set and its surroundings.

A grey cell contains a point in the disc and a point outside it. On the segment between them there is a point where the segment leaves the disc, a point of the circle. Every disc around this point, however small, reaches into the cross section and out of it. Recall that the ball with centre \(P\) and radius \(r\) is the set of all points that are closer to \(P\) than \(r\) (section 1.12.6), and that \(P\) is an interior point of a set if some ball around it lies entirely in the set (section 1.15.6).

Definition 4.23 Boundary point and boundary of a set (robna točka in rob množice)

Let \(W\) be a set of points of space. A point \(P\), which may or may not lie in \(W\), is a boundary point (robna točka) of the set \(W\) if for every \(r > 0\) the ball with centre \(P\) and radius \(r\) contains a point of the set \(W\) and a point that is not in \(W\). The set of all boundary points of the set \(W\) is the boundary (rob množice) of \(W\).

We define boundary points and the boundary of a set of points of the plane in the same way, with discs in place of balls.

Source: KREYSZIG §10.3, footnote 2 (PDF p. 452), for regions in the plane: a point, of the region or not, such that every disc with centre at it contains points of the region and points not of the region. LEBL1 Def. 7.2.23 (PDF p. 270), for sets in which a distance is given, defines the boundary by the closure and the interior, and Proposition 7.2.27 (PDF p. 271) shows that this is the same property as ours.

The definition looks only at the balls around the point, so it is the same for points of the set and for points outside it (figure 4.24). An interior point is not a boundary point, because some ball around it has no point outside the set. A point around which some ball has no point of the set is not a boundary point either. Are all other points boundary points? Yes. If such a point lies in the set, every ball around it contains the point itself and, since the point is not interior, a point outside the set. If it does not lie in the set, every ball around it contains the point itself, which is not in the set, and, since no ball around it is free of points of the set, a point of the set. For closed sets, like our bodies, even more holds: the boundary points lie in the set. Let us write this, and two more properties of the boundary that we will need, in a lemma.

Lemma 4.24 Boundary of a closed set and of a union (rob zaprte množice in rob unije)
  1. Let \(W\) be a closed set of points (definition 1.74) and \(P\) a point such that every ball with centre \(P\) contains a point of the set \(W\). Then \(P\) lies in \(W\). Hence every boundary point of the set \(W\) lies in \(W\), and for every point \(P\) that is not in \(W\) there is a ball with centre \(P\) that has no point of the set \(W\).
  2. Every point of the set \(W\) is an interior point of the set \(W\) or a boundary point of the set \(W\).
  3. Let \(W\) be the union of the sets of points \(W_1, \dots, W_{\mathrm{m}}\). Every boundary point of the set \(W\) is a boundary point of at least one of the sets \(W_1, \dots, W_{\mathrm{m}}\). If all of them are closed and bounded, so is \(W\).

The same holds for sets of points of the plane, with discs in place of balls. A set of points of the plane is then called closed and bounded if the set of the corresponding points \((x, y, 0)\) of space is.

Proof

We must show all three items. For the first we build, from points in ever smaller balls, a sequence that converges to \(P\).

1. A closed set.

  1. For every natural number \(n\) the ball with centre \(P\) and radius \(1/n\) contains a point of the set \(W\). We choose one and call it \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\). Then \(0 \le |P_{\mathrm{n}} P| < 1/n\).
  2. The sequence \((1/n)\) converges to \(0\) (lemma 1.39). By the squeeze lemma 1.46 with the lower sequence \(0, 0, \dots\) the sequence of distances \((|P_{\mathrm{n}} P|)\) also converges to \(0\), so by definition 1.65 the sequence of points \((P_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges to \(P\).
  3. All points \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\) lie in \(W\), and \(W\) is closed, so \(P\) lies in \(W\).
  4. For a boundary point \(P\) of the set \(W\) every ball with centre \(P\) contains a point of the set \(W\) (definition 4.23). By steps 1 to 3, \(P\) therefore lies in \(W\).
  5. Let \(P\) not lie in \(W\). By steps 1 to 3 it is then not true that every ball with centre \(P\) contains a point of the set \(W\). So there is a ball with centre \(P\) that has no point of the set \(W\).

2. Points of the set.

  1. Let the point \(P\) lie in \(W\) and not be an interior point of the set \(W\). Then no ball with centre \(P\) lies entirely in \(W\) (section 1.15.6), so every one contains a point that is not in \(W\). Every one also contains the point \(P\), which is in \(W\). By definition 4.23, \(P\) is a boundary point.

3. The union.

  1. Let \(P\) be a boundary point of the set \(W\). We argue by contradiction: suppose that \(P\) is a boundary point of none of the sets \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  2. Then for every \(k\) there is a radius \(r_{\mathrm{k}} > 0\) such that the ball with centre \(P\) and radius \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\) does not contain both a point of \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\) and a point outside \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\). It lies entirely in \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\), or it has no point of \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  3. If for some \(k\) the ball of radius \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\) lies entirely in \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\), it lies entirely in \(W\), because every point of the set \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\) is in the union. This contradicts the fact that a ball around the boundary point \(P\) of the set \(W\) contains a point that is not in \(W\).
  4. Otherwise none of the balls of radii \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\) has a point of its set \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\). Let \(r\) be the smallest of the numbers \(r_1, \dots, r_{\mathrm{m}}\). A point that is closer to \(P\) than \(r\) is closer than every \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\), so it lies in none of the \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\) and therefore not in \(W\). So the ball of radius \(r\) has no point of the set \(W\), which contradicts the fact that \(P\) is a boundary point.
  5. Closedness. Let a sequence of points \((P_{\mathrm{n}})\) from \(W\) converge to a point \(P\), and suppose that \(P\) is not in \(W\). By the fifth step of the first item, used on each \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\), there is a radius \(r_{\mathrm{k}} > 0\) such that the ball with centre \(P\) and radius \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\) has no point of \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\). Let \(r\) be the smallest of the numbers \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\). The distances \(|P_{\mathrm{n}} P|\) converge to \(0\), so there is a place \(N\) with \(|P_{\mathrm{N}} P| < r\). The point \(P_{\mathrm{N}}\) lies in some \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\) and is closer to \(P\) than \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\), which contradicts the choice of the radius \(r_{\mathrm{k}}\). So \(P\) lies in \(W\).
  6. Boundedness. If \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| \le R_{\mathrm{k}}\) for every point \(P \in W_{\mathrm{k}}\), then \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| \le R\) for every point \(P \in W\), where \(R\) is the largest of the numbers \(R_1, \dots, R_{\mathrm{m}}\).

4. The plane.

  1. The steps are the same, only the balls are discs in the plane.

Source: LEBL1 Propositions 7.2.22 and 7.2.19 (PDF p. 270): a point lies in the closure of a set exactly when every ball around it contains a point of the set, and a closed set equals its closure. Item 1 follows from both. Proposition 7.2.8 (iii) (PDF p. 266): a union of finitely many closed sets is closed. The source defines closedness by open sets. The proof by sequences and items 2 and 3 on the boundary are not from the source.

The lemma confirmed what figure 4.24 tells us. Every point of a set is interior or a boundary point, the boundary points of a closed set are its points, and a point outside a closed set has a ball around it without points of the set. The key move was a sequence of points from ever smaller balls, which converges to the centre of the balls.

What is the boundary of the cross section of the round bar, a disc of radius \(5\) mm? We expect the circle. The cross section is the set of points \((y, z)\) with \(y^2 + z^2 \le 25\). Seen as the set of points \((0, y, z)\) of space, it is given by the equation \(x = 0\) and by a non-strict inequality with a polynomial, so by lemma 1.75 it is closed, like the bar in section 1.13.4.

  1. A point \((y, z)\) with \(y^2 + z^2 > 25\) is not a boundary point. It lies outside the closed cross section, so by lemma 4.24, item 1, there is a disc around it without points of the cross section.
  2. A point \(P = (y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) with \(y_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + z_{\mathrm{P}}^2 < 25\) is not a boundary point. The set of points with \(y^2 + z^2 \ge 25\) is closed by lemma 1.75, and \(P\) does not lie in it. By lemma 4.24, item 1, there is therefore a disc around \(P\) without its points, that is, a disc that lies entirely in the cross section. The point \(P\) is interior.
  3. A point \(P = (y_{\mathrm{P}}, z_{\mathrm{P}})\) with \(y_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + z_{\mathrm{P}}^2 = 25\) is a boundary point. It lies in the cross section. For \(r > 0\) and \(t\) with \(0 < t < r/5\) the point \(((1 + t)\,y_{\mathrm{P}},\ (1 + t)\,z_{\mathrm{P}})\) lies outside the cross section, because \((1 + t)^2 \cdot 25 > 25\), and its distance from \(P\) is \(\sqrt{t^2 y_{\mathrm{P}}^2 + t^2 z_{\mathrm{P}}^2} = 5\,t < r\).

So the boundary of the cross section is the circle.

The staircase of grey cells in figure 4.23 covers the circle, and its area is about \(40\,h\) and goes to zero. The circle is thin. We can cover it by finitely many rectangles whose total area is as small as we like. Let us name this property.

Definition 4.25 Set of zero volume (množica s prostornino nič)

A set of points of space \(Z\) has zero volume (prostornina nič) if for every \(\eta > 0\) there are finitely many boxes with edges along the axes that cover \(Z\), that is, every point of the set \(Z\) lies in at least one of them, and the sum of their volumes is less than \(\eta\).

A set of points of the plane has zero area (ploščina nič) if for every \(\eta > 0\) it is covered by finitely many rectangles with edges along the axes with a total area less than \(\eta\).

Source: LEBL2 Def. 10.3.1 (PDF p. 108) allows a sequence of infinitely many rectangles and calls the notion measure zero. By Proposition 10.3.7 (PDF p. 112) a closed and bounded set of measure zero is already covered by finitely many rectangles of arbitrarily small total volume, so for such sets this is the same notion as ours.

A set of zero volume is thus a set of points that we can enclose in boxes of arbitrarily small total volume. A point has zero volume. It is covered by a cube of side \(t\) with its centre at the point, whose volume \(t^3\) is less than \(\eta\) when \(t\) is small enough. A rectangle in the plane \(z = c\) also has zero volume, for example a face of a box, made of the points \((x, y, c)\) with \(a_1 \le x \le b_1\) and \(a_2 \le y \le b_2\). It is covered by the box \([a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [c - t, c + t]\) with the volume \(2t\,(b_1 - a_1)(b_2 - a_2)\), which is less than \(\eta\) when \(t\) is less than \(\eta/(2(b_1 - a_1)(b_2 - a_2))\). A flat face has no thickness, so the box encloses it however thin the box is.

The faces of our bodies are not all flat. The top lid of a body between graphs is the graph of a continuous function, and the lateral surface of the round bar is made of such graphs. Let us show that graphs of continuous functions have zero volume, and write down two more rules that follow at once from the definition.

Lemma 4.26 Subsets, unions and graphs of zero volume (podmnožice, unije in grafi s prostornino nič)
  1. Every subset of a set of zero volume has zero volume.
  2. The union of finitely many sets of zero volume has zero volume.
  3. Let \(\varphi\) be a function that is continuous on the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\). Then the graph of the function \(\varphi\), the set of points \((x, y, \varphi(x, y))\) with \((x, y) \in R\), has zero volume. The same holds for another naming of the axes, for example for the set of points \((\varphi(y, z), y, z)\) with \((y, z)\) from a rectangle in the plane of the axes \(y\) and \(z\).

The same holds in the plane, with the area in place of the volume. The graph of a function \(\varphi\) that is continuous on the interval \([a, b]\), the set of points \((x, \varphi(x))\) with \(a \le x \le b\), has zero area, and so does the set of points \((\varphi(y), y)\).

Proof

We must show all three items. The first two follow from the definition, for the third we enclose the graph over each small rectangle in a low box.

1. A subset.

  1. Boxes that cover a set also cover each of its subsets, since every point of the subset is a point of the set.

2. A union.

  1. Let \(Z_1, \dots, Z_{\mathrm{m}}\) have zero volume and let \(\eta > 0\). For each \(k\) we choose finitely many boxes that cover \(Z_{\mathrm{k}}\) and have a total volume less than \(\eta/m\).
  2. There are finitely many of all these boxes. Every point of the union lies in some \(Z_{\mathrm{k}}\) and therefore in one of the boxes chosen for it. The total volume of all the boxes is less than \(m \cdot \eta/m = \eta\).

3. A graph.

  1. The rectangle \(R\), seen as the set of points \((x, y, 0)\), is closed and bounded (section 4.2.2). We choose \(\eta > 0\) and let \(\omega = \eta/(4(b - a)(d - c))\). By theorem 4.6 there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|\varphi(P) - \varphi(Q)| < \omega\) for any points \(P, Q \in R\) with \(|PQ| < \delta\).
  2. By the Archimedean property 1.35 there is a natural number \(n\) such that \(n\,\delta/2\) is larger than \(b - a\) and than \(d - c\). We divide the intervals \([a, b]\) and \([c, d]\) into \(n\) equal pieces, which are shorter than \(\delta/2\), and get the rectangles \(R_{\mathrm{ij}} = [x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}] \times [y_{\mathrm{j}-1}, y_{\mathrm{j}}]\). Two points of the same rectangle \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are closer than \(\delta\). The differences of their coordinates are less than \(\delta/2\) in absolute value, by lemma 1.28 their squares are less than \(\delta^2/4\), the square of the distance is therefore less than \(\delta^2/2\), and by the same lemma the distance is less than \(\delta\).
  3. Let \(P_{\mathrm{ij}} = (x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{j}})\) be a corner of the rectangle \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\). By steps 1 and 2, for every point \((x, y) \in R_{\mathrm{ij}}\)
    \[\varphi(P_{\mathrm{ij}}) - \omega < \varphi(x, y) < \varphi(P_{\mathrm{ij}}) + \omega ,\]
    so the point \((x, y, \varphi(x, y))\) lies in the box \(K_{\mathrm{ij}} = R_{\mathrm{ij}} \times [\varphi(P_{\mathrm{ij}}) - \omega,\ \varphi(P_{\mathrm{ij}}) + \omega]\).
  4. Every point \((x, y)\) of the rectangle \(R\) lies in at least one of the rectangles \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\), because \(x\) lies in one of the pieces of the interval \([a, b]\) and \(y\) in one of the pieces of the interval \([c, d]\). The boxes \(K_{\mathrm{ij}}\) therefore cover the graph.
  5. The box \(K_{\mathrm{ij}}\) has the volume \(\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}} \cdot 2\omega\). By distributivity and the telescoping sum, as in step 6 of the proof of theorem 4.9, the sum of the areas \(\Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\) is \((b - a)(d - c)\). The total volume of the boxes is therefore \(2\omega\,(b - a)(d - c) = \eta/2 < \eta\).
  6. For another naming of the axes the steps are the same, only the coordinates exchange roles.

4. The plane.

  1. Items 1 and 2 are the same, with rectangles in place of boxes.
  2. For the graph of the function \(\varphi\) on \([a, b]\) we take \(\omega = \eta/(4(b - a))\) and the band \(\delta\) that theorem 3.37 on uniform continuity on a closed interval gives for the error \(\omega\). We divide the interval into pieces shorter than \(\delta\) and enclose the graph over the piece \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\) in the rectangle \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}] \times [\varphi(x_{\mathrm{i}}) - \omega,\ \varphi(x_{\mathrm{i}}) + \omega]\). The total area of the rectangles is \(2\omega\,(b - a) = \eta/2 < \eta\).

Source: LEBL2 (PDF p. 108) states that a subset of a set of measure zero is again such a set, and Proposition 10.3.4 (PDF p. 110) that a countable union of sets of measure zero is such a set. The proof for finitely many boxes and item 3 are not from the source.

The proof of item 3 showed why a graph has zero volume (figure 4.25). Over a small rectangle a continuous function changes by less than \(\omega\), so the graph over it lies in a box of height \(2\omega\). The total volume of the boxes is \(2\omega\) times the area of the rectangle \(R\), and it goes to zero with \(\omega\). Uniform continuity made sure that one single height \(2\omega\) worked for all the rectangles at once.

Now we can say which sets we will integrate over.

Definition 4.27 Set with volume (množica s prostornino)

A set of points of space \(W\) is a set with volume (množica s prostornino) if it is closed and bounded (definition 1.74) and its boundary (definition 4.23) has zero volume (definition 4.25).

A set of points of the plane \(M\) is a set with area (množica s ploščino) if it is closed and bounded when we view each of its points \((x, y)\) as the point \((x, y, 0)\) of space, and its boundary, determined in the plane with discs, has zero area.

Source: LEBL2 (PDF p. 123) calls a bounded set Jordan measurable if its characteristic function is integrable, and in Proposition 10.5.1 (PDF p. 123) shows that this is so exactly when its boundary has measure zero. The source does not require closedness.

The definition requires two things, and we will need both. Closedness and boundedness will give the largest value and uniform continuity of a continuous function on the set (theorems 1.78 and 4.6). A boundary of zero volume will make sure that the cells along the boundary have a small total volume. The source does not require closedness and also integrates functions that are not continuous, which we will not need. Our bodies together with their surfaces are closed sets (section 1.13.4), so the requirement does not restrict us.

Why this agreement in the plane? We defined closedness and boundedness only for sets of points of space, so we view the points of the plane as the points \((x, y, 0)\). The distance between the points \((x, y, 0)\) and \((x', y', 0)\) is \(\sqrt{(x' - x)^2 + (y' - y)^2}\), equal to the distance in the plane, so theorems 1.78 on the largest value and 4.6 on uniform continuity also hold for continuous functions on a closed and bounded set of the plane. This is how we already treated the rectangle in section 4.2.2 and, above, the cross section of the bar. The boundary, however, we determine in the plane. In space every ball around the point \((x, y, 0)\) contains points with \(z \neq 0\), which are not in \(M\), so in space every point of the set \(M\) would be a boundary point. A disc in the plane does not contain these points. We do the same in the plane of two other axes, for example with the cross section of the bar in the plane \(x = 0\).

Let us check the definition on two sets we know.

The box \(K = [a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\) is a set with volume. It is closed and bounded by section 1.13.4.

  1. A point \(P\) with \(a_1 < x_{\mathrm{P}} < b_1\), \(a_2 < y_{\mathrm{P}} < b_2\) and \(a_3 < z_{\mathrm{P}} < b_3\) is not a boundary point. Let \(\rho\) be the smallest of the six distances \(x_{\mathrm{P}} - a_1\), \(b_1 - x_{\mathrm{P}}\), \(y_{\mathrm{P}} - a_2\), \(b_2 - y_{\mathrm{P}}\), \(z_{\mathrm{P}} - a_3\) and \(b_3 - z_{\mathrm{P}}\). A point that is closer to \(P\) than \(\rho\) differs from \(P\) by less than \(\rho\) in every coordinate (step 2 of the proof of lemma 1.66), so it lies in \(K\). The ball of radius \(\rho\) has no points outside \(K\).
  2. A boundary point lies in \(K\) by lemma 4.24, item 1, so by step 1 at least one of its coordinates equals an end point. It lies on one of the six faces of the box.
  3. Every face is the graph of a constant function over a rectangle. The face \(x = a_1\), for example, is the set of points \((a_1, y, z)\) with \((y, z) \in [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\). By lemma 4.26, item 3, it has zero volume, by item 2 of the same lemma so does the union of the six faces, and by item 1 so does the boundary, which lies in it.

In the same way a rectangle with edges along the axes is a set with area.

The cross section of the round bar, a disc of radius \(5\) mm, is also a set with area. It is closed and bounded, and its boundary is the circle. We cut the circle as we cut the bar in section 4.2.6. A point \((y, z)\) of the circle with \(|y| \le 3\) has \(z^2 = 25 - y^2\), so by theorem 1.36 on the existence of square roots \(|z| = q(y)\), where \(q(t) = \sqrt{25 - t^2}\), and the point lies on the graph of the function \(q\) or \(-q\) over \([-3, 3]\). A point with \(|y| > 3\) has \(z^2 < 16\), so \(|z| < 4\), and in the same way \(|y| = q(z)\), so it lies on the graph \(y = q(z)\) or \(y = -q(z)\) over \([-4, 4]\). The function \(q\) is continuous on \((-5, 5)\), which contains \([-4, 4]\), by lemma 4.16. By lemma 4.26, item 3 in the plane, the four graphs have zero area, and by items 2 and 1 so does the circle.

Is the bar itself, a cylinder of length \(10\) m, a set with volume? Its surface is made of the lids of the pieces \(C\), \(D\) and \(E\), which are graphs, and of flat faces. We will show this in section 4.2.10 for every body between graphs and for every body cut into such bodies.

Let us return to the cells. Recall the words from section 4.2.3. A grid of the box \(K = [a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\) is given by partitions \(D_1 = \{x_0, \dots, x_{\mathrm{l}}\}\), \(D_2 = \{y_0, \dots, y_{\mathrm{m}}\}\) and \(D_3 = \{z_0, \dots, z_{\mathrm{n}}\}\) of its edges. Its cells are the boxes \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}} = [x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}] \times [y_{\mathrm{j}-1}, y_{\mathrm{j}}] \times [z_{\mathrm{k}-1}, z_{\mathrm{k}}]\) with the volumes \(\Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}} = \Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\,\Delta z_{\mathrm{k}}\). For a set of points \(W\) in the box \(K\) a cell lies in \(W\), written \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}} \subseteq W\), if all its points are in \(W\). A cell that has a point in \(W\) lies in \(W\) or else also has a point outside \(W\). Cells of the second kind are grey in figure 4.23. In the plane the cells are rectangles \(K_{\mathrm{ij}} = [x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}] \times [y_{\mathrm{j}-1}, y_{\mathrm{j}}]\) with the areas \(\Delta A_{\mathrm{ij}} = \Delta x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta y_{\mathrm{j}}\).

We will compare cells with boxes that are not cells of the grid, for example with boxes that cover the boundary. We need a rule for how the volumes of the cells that lie in a given box add up.

Lemma 4.28 Cells in a box (celice v kvadru)

Let a grid of a box \(K\) with the partitions \(D_1\), \(D_2\) and \(D_3\) be given, and a box \(B = [\alpha_1, \beta_1] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2] \times [\alpha_3, \beta_3]\) with edges along the axes.

  1. The cell \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) lies in \(B\) exactly when the piece \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\) lies in \([\alpha_1, \beta_1]\), the piece \([y_{\mathrm{j}-1}, y_{\mathrm{j}}]\) in \([\alpha_2, \beta_2]\) and the piece \([z_{\mathrm{k}-1}, z_{\mathrm{k}}]\) in \([\alpha_3, \beta_3]\).
  2. The cells of the grid that lie in \(B\) have a total volume of at most \(V_{\mathrm{B}}\).
  3. If the numbers \(\alpha_1\) and \(\beta_1\) are points of the partition \(D_1\), \(\alpha_2\) and \(\beta_2\) points of the partition \(D_2\), and \(\alpha_3\) and \(\beta_3\) points of the partition \(D_3\), this total volume equals \(V_{\mathrm{B}}\).

The same holds in the plane, with rectangles and areas.

Proof

We must show all three items. The cells in \(B\) are all combinations of the pieces that lie in the edges of the box \(B\), and the pieces in an edge add up to a telescoping sum.

  1. If every piece lies in the corresponding edge of the box \(B\), every point of the cell has all three coordinates in the edges of the box \(B\) and lies in \(B\). Conversely, let the cell lie in \(B\) and let \(x\) be a number from the piece \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\). The point \((x, y_{\mathrm{j}-1}, z_{\mathrm{k}-1})\) lies in the cell, hence in \(B\), so \(\alpha_1 \le x \le \beta_1\). So the piece lies in \([\alpha_1, \beta_1]\). The same for the other two pieces.
  2. The pieces of the partition \(D_1\) that lie in \([\alpha_1, \beta_1]\) follow each other without gaps. If pieces with indices \(i_0 < i_1\) lie in it, then for every \(i\) between them \(x_{\mathrm{i}-1} \ge x_{\mathrm{i}_0 - 1} \ge \alpha_1\) and \(x_{\mathrm{i}} \le x_{\mathrm{i}_1} \le \beta_1\), because the points of a partition increase. Let \(i_0\) be the smallest and \(i_1\) the largest such index. The sum of the lengths of these pieces is a telescoping sum (section 3.5.2)
    \[L_1 = \sum_{\mathrm{i} = \mathrm{i}_0}^{i_1} \Delta x_{\mathrm{i}} = x_{\mathrm{i}_1} - x_{\mathrm{i}_0 - 1} \le \beta_1 - \alpha_1 .\]
    If no piece lies in \([\alpha_1, \beta_1]\), then \(L_1 = 0\). In the same way we define \(L_2 \le \beta_2 - \alpha_2\) and \(L_3 \le \beta_3 - \alpha_3\).
  3. By step 1 the cells in \(B\) are exactly the cells \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) for which all three pieces lie in the edges of the box \(B\). By distributivity, as in step 6 of the proof of theorem 4.9, the sum of their volumes is \(L_1 L_2 L_3\). All the numbers are nonnegative, so by step 2 this product is at most \((\beta_1 - \alpha_1)(\beta_2 - \alpha_2)(\beta_3 - \alpha_3) = V_{\mathrm{B}}\).
  4. Let \(\alpha_1 = x_{\mathrm{p}}\) and \(\beta_1 = x_{\mathrm{q}}\) be points of the partition \(D_1\), with \(p < q\). Exactly the pieces with indices from \(p + 1\) to \(q\) lie in \([\alpha_1, \beta_1]\), so \(L_1 = x_{\mathrm{q}} - x_{\mathrm{p}} = \beta_1 - \alpha_1\). In the same way \(L_2 = \beta_2 - \alpha_2\) and \(L_3 = \beta_3 - \alpha_3\), and the product from step 3 is \(V_{\mathrm{B}}\).
  5. In the plane the steps are the same, with two partitions and two lengths.

Source: The lemma is not from the sources.

Now let us show that the cells along the boundary have a small total volume for a fine grid. The idea has two steps (figure 4.26). A cell that has a point in \(W\) and a point outside \(W\) contains a boundary point, because the segment between them leaves \(W\) somewhere. The boundary, in turn, is covered by boxes of small total volume, and a small cell that has a point in one of them lies in this box, slightly enlarged.

Lemma 4.29 Boundary cells (robne celice)

A cell of a grid is a boundary cell (robna celica) of the set \(W\) if it contains a point of the set \(W\) and a point that is not in \(W\).

  1. Let the set of points \(Z\) have zero volume. For every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that for every grid of a box in which all pieces of the partitions are shorter than \(\delta\), the cells that contain at least one point of the set \(Z\) have a total volume less than \(\eta\).
  2. If the set \(W\) is closed, every boundary cell of the set \(W\) contains a boundary point of the set \(W\).
  3. Let \(W\) be a set with volume. For every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that for every grid of a box that contains \(W\), in which all pieces of the partitions are shorter than \(\delta\), the boundary cells of the set \(W\) have a total volume less than \(\eta\).

The same holds in the plane, with rectangles and areas.

Proof

We must show all three items. In the first we enclose the cells in slightly enlarged boxes that cover \(Z\), in the second we find a boundary point by a supremum on a segment, and the third follows from the first two.

1. Cells along a set of zero volume.

  1. We choose \(\eta > 0\). If \(Z\) is empty, no cell has a point of \(Z\), and every \(\delta\) works. Let \(Z\) not be empty. Since it has zero volume, it is covered by \(p \ge 1\) boxes \(B_1, \dots, B_{\mathrm{p}}\) with a total volume less than \(\eta/2\).
  2. Let \(\Lambda\) be a number that is not smaller than any edge of any of the boxes \(B_{\mathrm{l}}\). For \(\delta\) we take a positive number that is less than \(1\) and than \(\eta/(12\,p\,(\Lambda + 2)^2)\).
  3. For the box \(B_{\mathrm{l}} = [\alpha_1, \beta_1] \times [\alpha_2, \beta_2] \times [\alpha_3, \beta_3]\) let \(B_{\mathrm{l}}^\delta = [\alpha_1 - \delta, \beta_1 + \delta] \times [\alpha_2 - \delta, \beta_2 + \delta] \times [\alpha_3 - \delta, \beta_3 + \delta]\) be the box enlarged by \(\delta\) on all sides.
  4. Let all pieces of the partitions be shorter than \(\delta\) and let the cell \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) contain a point \(Q \in Z\). The point \(Q\) lies in some box \(B_{\mathrm{l}}\). For every point of the cell, its coordinate \(x\) and the coordinate \(x_{\mathrm{Q}}\) are on the same piece \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\), so they differ by less than \(\delta\). Since \(\alpha_1 \le x_{\mathrm{Q}} \le \beta_1\), we have \(\alpha_1 - \delta < x < \beta_1 + \delta\). The same for \(y\) and \(z\). The cell therefore lies in \(B_{\mathrm{l}}^\delta\).
  5. By lemma 4.28, item 2, the cells that lie in \(B_{\mathrm{l}}^\delta\) have a total volume of at most \(V_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{l}^\delta}\). By step 4 every cell with a point of \(Z\) lies in at least one of the boxes \(B_{\mathrm{l}}^\delta\), so the total volume of such cells is at most \(V_{\mathrm{B}_1^\delta} + \dots + V_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{p}^\delta}\). A cell that lies in several boxes is counted several times on the right, which only makes the right side larger.
  6. Let us estimate by how much the enlargement increases the volume. Let \(s_1, s_2, s_3\) be the edges of the box \(B_{\mathrm{l}}\) and \(s_{\mathrm{i}}' = s_{\mathrm{i}} + 2\delta\) the edges of the box \(B_{\mathrm{l}}^\delta\). Then
    \[s_1' s_2' s_3' - s_1 s_2 s_3 = (s_1' - s_1)\,s_2' s_3' + s_1\,(s_2' - s_2)\,s_3' + s_1 s_2\,(s_3' - s_3) ,\]
    which we check by multiplying out the right side: the terms \(s_1 s_2' s_3'\) and \(s_1 s_2 s_3'\) cancel, and the left side remains. Each difference is \(2\delta\), each \(s_{\mathrm{i}}\) is at most \(\Lambda\), and each \(s_{\mathrm{i}}'\) is less than \(\Lambda + 2\), because \(\delta < 1\). Therefore \(V_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{l}^\delta} - V_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{l}} < 3 \cdot 2\delta\,(\Lambda + 2)^2 = 6\delta\,(\Lambda + 2)^2 < \eta/(2p)\).
  7. By steps 5 and 6 the total volume of the cells with a point of \(Z\) is less than \(V_{\mathrm{B}_1} + \dots + V_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{p}} + p \cdot \eta/(2p) < \eta/2 + \eta/2 = \eta\).

2. A boundary cell contains a boundary point.

  1. Let the boundary cell \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) contain a point \(P \in W\) and a point \(Q\) that is not in \(W\). The points are different, so \(|PQ| > 0\). For \(t \in [0, 1]\) let \(P_{\mathrm{t}}\) be the point with the coordinates \(x_{\mathrm{P}} + t\,(x_{\mathrm{Q}} - x_{\mathrm{P}})\), \(y_{\mathrm{P}} + t\,(y_{\mathrm{Q}} - y_{\mathrm{P}})\) and \(z_{\mathrm{P}} + t\,(z_{\mathrm{Q}} - z_{\mathrm{P}})\). Since \(x_{\mathrm{P}} + t\,(x_{\mathrm{Q}} - x_{\mathrm{P}}) = (1 - t)\,x_{\mathrm{P}} + t\,x_{\mathrm{Q}}\) and \(1 - t\) and \(t\) are nonnegative numbers with the sum \(1\), this coordinate lies between \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{Q}}\), hence on the piece \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\). The same for \(y\) and \(z\). All points \(P_{\mathrm{t}}\) therefore lie in the cell, \(P_0 = P\) and \(P_1 = Q\).
  2. Let \(T\) be the set of all \(t \in [0, 1]\) for which \(P_{\mathrm{t}}\) lies in \(W\). It contains \(0\) and is bounded above by \(1\). By the completeness axiom 1.32 it has a supremum \(t^*\), and \(0 \le t^* \le 1\). Let \(B = P_{\mathrm{t}^*}\).
  3. The point \(B\) lies in \(W\). By theorem 1.33, item 2, for every natural number \(n\) there is a \(t_{\mathrm{n}} \in T\) with \(t^* - 1/n < t_{\mathrm{n}} \le t^*\). By the squeeze lemma 1.46 the sequence \((t_{\mathrm{n}})\) converges to \(t^*\). By lemma 1.60 on limit laws for sequences the coordinates of the points \(P_{\mathrm{t}_\mathrm{n}}\) converge to the coordinates of the point \(B\), so by lemma 1.66 the points \(P_{\mathrm{t}_\mathrm{n}}\) converge to \(B\). All of them lie in \(W\), which is closed, so \(B\) lies in \(W\).
  4. Hence \(t^* \in T\), and \(t^* < 1\), because \(P_1 = Q\) is not in \(W\).
  5. The point \(B\) is a boundary point. Let \(r > 0\). The ball with centre \(B\) and radius \(r\) contains the point \(B\) of \(W\). Let \(t\) be the smaller of the numbers \(1\) and \(t^* + r/(2|PQ|)\). Both are larger than \(t^*\) (step 4), so \(t > t^*\), so \(t\) is not in \(T\), and the point \(P_{\mathrm{t}}\) is not in \(W\). The vector from \(B\) to \(P_{\mathrm{t}}\) has the components \((t - t^*)(x_{\mathrm{Q}} - x_{\mathrm{P}})\), \((t - t^*)(y_{\mathrm{Q}} - y_{\mathrm{P}})\) and \((t - t^*)(z_{\mathrm{Q}} - z_{\mathrm{P}})\), so by (1.10) the square of its length is \((t - t^*)^2\,|PQ|^2\). The nonnegative number \((t - t^*)\,|PQ|\) has this square, so by theorem 1.36 the length is \((t - t^*)\,|PQ| \le r/2 < r\). So the ball also contains the point \(P_{\mathrm{t}}\), which is not in \(W\). By definition 4.23, \(B\) is a boundary point of the set \(W\), and by step 1 it lies in the cell.

3. Boundary cells of a set with volume.

  1. A set with volume \(W\) is closed, and its boundary has zero volume (definition 4.27). For \(\eta > 0\) we take the \(\delta\) that the first item gives for the boundary of the set \(W\) in place of \(Z\).
  2. For a grid with pieces shorter than \(\delta\), every boundary cell of the set \(W\) contains a boundary point by the second item. So the boundary cells are among the cells of the first item, which have a total volume less than \(\eta\).

4. The plane.

  1. The steps are the same, with two coordinates. In step 6 of the first item there are two terms, \(s_1' s_2' - s_1 s_2 = (s_1' - s_1)\,s_2' + s_1\,(s_2' - s_2)\), so a \(\delta\) less than \(1\) and than \(\eta/(8\,p\,(\Lambda + 2))\) suffices.

Source: The lemma is not from the sources. LEBL2 in the proof of Proposition 10.5.3 (PDF pp. 124-125) likewise compares the rectangles of a partition that lie in the set with those that meet it.

The first item showed how a grid meets a cover. The grid does not know the boxes \(B_{\mathrm{l}}\) that cover the boundary, but since the cells are small, every cell that touches the boundary lies in a box enlarged by \(\delta\), and the enlargement increases the volume only a little. The second item found a boundary point by a supremum. The last point of the segment that still lies in \(W\) is a boundary point, because right after it there are points outside \(W\). On the cross section of the bar we see this in the table. The circle is covered by a staircase of grey cells with an area of about \(40\,h\), which for \(h = 0{,}1\) mm is only \(3{,}96\) mm².

With this we have what we need for the definition of the integral. For a set with volume the cells along the boundary have an arbitrarily small total volume for a fine enough grid, so the sum may leave them out. The next section tells how.

4.2.10 The integral without an order

Recall what theorem 4.9 on the order of integration says in item 1. We cut a box by a grid into cells, choose a point in each cell and add up the values of the function at these points times the volumes of the cells. For ever finer grids these sums approach the iterated integral, in any order. For a set \(W\) that is not a box we do the same, except that we add up only the cells that lie in \(W\). We leave out the boundary cells. For a set with volume they have a small total volume for a fine grid by lemma 4.29, so with them we leave out only a small part of the set. We must also leave out the boundary cells because the function may not even be defined outside \(W\), and in a boundary cell we could choose a point outside \(W\).

Definition 4.30 Integral over a set with volume (integral po množici s prostornino)

Let \(W\) be a set with volume (definition 4.27) and \(f\) a function that is continuous on \(W\) (definition 1.67). A number \(I\) is the integral (integral) of the function \(f\) over the set \(W\) if for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) with the following property. For every box that contains \(W\), for every grid of it in which all pieces of the partitions are shorter than \(\delta\), and for every choice of a point \(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) in each cell \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) that lies in \(W\),

\[\Big| \sum_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ijk}} \subseteq \mathrm{W}} f(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}})\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}} - I \Big| < \eta . \tag{4.15}\]

The sum runs over the cells that lie in \(W\), and it is zero if there are no such cells. We write the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\). The integral of the constant function \(1\) is the volume (prostornina) of the set \(W\), \(V_{\mathrm{W}} = \int_{\mathrm{W}} 1\,\mathrm{d}V\).

In the plane \(M\) is a set with area, the cells are rectangles \(K_{\mathrm{ij}}\) with the areas \(\Delta A_{\mathrm{ij}}\), the sum in (4.15) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ij}} \subseteq \mathrm{M}} f(Q_{\mathrm{ij}})\,\Delta A_{\mathrm{ij}}\), we write the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{M}} f\,\mathrm{d}A\), and the area (ploščina) of the set \(M\) is \(A_{\mathrm{M}} = \int_{\mathrm{M}} 1\,\mathrm{d}A\).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7 (PDF pp. 478-479) defines the triple integral as the limit of sums over the boxes of a grid that lie entirely in the body, and §10.3 (PDF pp. 452-453) the double integral likewise with rectangles that lie entirely in the region. LEBL2 Def. 10.5.4 (PDF pp. 124-125) extends the function by zero outside the set and integrates over a rectangle, and defines the volume of a set on PDF p. 123.

What goes in and what comes out? In go a set with volume \(W\) and a continuous function \(f\) on it, out comes one number. The definition mentions neither an order of integration nor a cut, only the cells of grids that lie in \(W\). The requirement holds for all grids of all boxes that contain \(W\), not only for some chosen sequence of grids. This is exactly why the number will belong to the set and not to our choice of grid. For the function \(1\) the sum (4.15) is the total volume of the cells that lie in \(W\). For the cross section of the round bar these are the areas of the blue cells from the table in section 4.2.9, \(60\), \(69\), \(73{,}5\) and \(76{,}44\) mm², which approach \(78{,}54\) mm².

The symbol \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\) already has a meaning for a box, for a body made of boxes, for a body between graphs and for a body cut into pieces. That the new definition gives the same number for all these bodies we show in the rest of this section. Until then we will say for every integral by which definition we take it.

The definition states that the number \(I\) is the integral if it has the property. Does such a number exist at all, and is there only one? For a general set we have no iterated integral that could be a candidate, so we find the number by a supremum, as we found the integral over an interval by the supremum of the lower sums in section 3.5.3. For a nonnegative function we take, in each cell that lies in \(W\), the smallest value of the function on the cell and add up the products with the volumes of the cells. This gives a lower sum. When we refine the grid, the lower sum does not decrease (figure 4.27). Every old cell in \(W\) splits into new cells, which also lie in \(W\) and have smallest values at least as large. New cells that lie in \(W\) can appear only in old boundary cells, and they contribute nonnegative terms. The supremum of the lower sums is the candidate for the integral. That the lower sum of every fine enough grid is close to it follows from two estimates. When a fine grid is refined, the values on the old cells change little, because the function is uniformly continuous, and the new cells lie in boundary cells, which have a small total volume.

Theorem 4.31 Existence of the integral over a set with volume (obstoj integrala po množici s prostornino)

Let \(W\) be a set with volume and \(f\) a function that is continuous on \(W\). Then the function \(f\) has exactly one integral over the set \(W\) (definition 4.30), the number \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\). The same holds in the plane.

Proof

We must show that such a number exists and that there is only one. We show existence first for nonnegative functions, with lower sums and the completeness axiom, and then for all continuous functions. In the proof \(G\) denotes grids, \(C\) cells of the grid \(G\) and \(C'\) cells of a finer grid.

1. The empty set.

  1. If \(W\) is empty, no cell lies in it, and every sum (4.15) is zero. The number \(0\) then has the property of the definition. From now on let \(W\) not be empty.

2. A box that contains all the cells.

  1. The set \(W\) is bounded, so there is a number \(R\) with \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| \le R\) for every point \(P \in W\). No coordinate is larger in absolute value than the distance from the origin (step 2 of the proof of lemma 1.66), so \(W\) lies in the cube \(K_0 = [-R - 1, R + 1] \times [-R - 1, R + 1] \times [-R - 1, R + 1]\) with the volume \(V_0 = (2R + 2)^3\).
  2. Let \(G\) be a grid of a box that contains \(W\). The cells of the grid \(G\) that lie in \(W\) lie in \(K_0\), so by lemma 4.28, item 2, their total volume is at most \(V_0\).

3. Lower sums of a nonnegative function. Up to the end of the sixth part let \(f(P) \ge 0\) for every point \(P \in W\).

  1. Let \(G\) be a grid of a box that contains \(W\), and \(C\) a cell of it that lies in \(W\). The cell is nonempty, closed and bounded (section 1.13.4), and \(f\) is continuous on it, because continuity on a part of a set checks only a part of the points. By theorem 1.78, \(f\) has a smallest value \(m_{\mathrm{C}}\) on \(C\). The lower sum of the function \(f\) for the grid \(G\) is the number
    \[s(f, G) = \sum_{\mathrm{C} \subseteq \mathrm{W}} m_{\mathrm{C}}\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{C}} .\]
  2. By theorem 1.78, \(f\) has a largest value \(M\) on \(W\). Since \(0 \le m_{\mathrm{C}} \le M\), by step 2 of the second part \(0 \le s(f, G) \le M\,V_0\).
  3. The set of all lower sums for all grids of all boxes that contain \(W\) is nonempty, because the cube \(K_0\) has a grid with a single cell, and it is bounded above by \(M\,V_0\). By the completeness axiom 1.32 it has a supremum, which we call \(I\). For every grid \(G\), \(s(f, G) \le I\).

4. Extension and refinement of a grid.

  1. Extension. Let \(G\) be a grid of a box \(K\) that contains \(W\), and \(K'\) a box that contains \(K\). We add the end points of the edges of the box \(K'\) to the partitions of the grid \(G\) and get a grid \(G'\) of the box \(K'\). The cells of the grid \(G\) are cells of the grid \(G'\). Every new cell has a piece outside the corresponding edge of the box \(K\), for example the piece \([a_1', a_1]\) to the left of the edge \([a_1, b_1]\). Every cell that lies in a new cell contains a point whose coordinate lies strictly inside this piece, and this point is not in \(K\), hence not in \(W\). So no new cell and no cell that lies in a new cell lies in \(W\). The lower sum and the sums (4.15) for the grid \(G'\) are the same as for \(G\).
  2. Refinement. Let \(H\) be a grid of the same box as \(G'\) whose partitions contain all points of the partitions of the grid \(G'\). Between two consecutive points of a partition of the grid \(H\) there is no point of the partitions of the grid \(G'\), so a piece of the grid \(H\) lies in a piece of the grid \(G'\), and every cell \(C'\) of the grid \(H\) lies in a cell of the grid \(G'\). There is only one such cell, because two pieces of the same partition overlap at most in an end point. The cells \(C'\) that lie in a cell \(C\) of the grid \(G'\) have, by lemma 4.28, item 3, the total volume \(\Delta V_{\mathrm{C}}\), because the end points of the edges of the cell \(C\) are points of the partitions of the grid \(H\).
  3. The lower sum does not fall under refinement. If a cell \(C\) of the grid \(G'\) lies in \(W\), the cells \(C'\) in it also lie in \(W\), and their smallest values are at least \(m_{\mathrm{C}}\), because \(C'\) is a part of the cell \(C\). By step 2 their contribution to \(s(f, H)\) is at least \(m_{\mathrm{C}}\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{C}}\). The other cells of the grid \(H\) that lie in \(W\) contribute nonnegative terms, because \(f \ge 0\). Therefore \(s(f, G') \le s(f, H)\).

5. Fine grids have lower sums close to \(I\).

  1. We choose \(\eta > 0\). By theorem 1.33, item 2, there is a grid \(G_*\) of some box \(K_*\) that contains \(W\) with \(s(f, G_*) > I - \eta/3\).
  2. By theorem 4.6 there is a \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that \(|f(P) - f(Q)| < \eta/(3V_0)\) for any points \(P, Q \in W\) with \(|PQ| < \delta_1\). By lemma 4.29, item 3, there is a \(\delta_2 > 0\) such that for every grid of a box that contains \(W\), with pieces shorter than \(\delta_2\), the boundary cells of the set \(W\) have a total volume less than \(\eta/(3M + 3)\). Let \(\delta\) be less than the numbers \(\delta_1/2\) and \(\delta_2\).
  3. Let \(G\) be a grid of a box \(K\) that contains \(W\), with pieces shorter than \(\delta\). Two points of the same cell are closer than \(\delta_1\), as in step 2 of the proof of theorem 4.9. On a cell \(C\) that lies in \(W\) every value of the function \(f\) is therefore less than \(m_{\mathrm{C}} + \eta/(3V_0)\).
  4. Let \(K'\) be a box that contains \(K\) and \(K_*\): on each axis it reaches from the smaller to the larger end point of the two edges. By step 1 of the fourth part we extend the grids \(G\) and \(G_*\) to grids \(G'\) and \(G_*'\) of the box \(K'\) with the same lower sums. Let \(H\) be the grid of the box \(K'\) whose partitions are the unions of the partitions of the grids \(G'\) and \(G_*'\). By step 3 of the fourth part, \(s(f, H) \ge s(f, G_*') = s(f, G_*) > I - \eta/3\).
  5. Let us also estimate \(s(f, H)\) from above. We sort the cells of the grid \(H\) that lie in \(W\) by the cells of the grid \(G'\) in which they lie (step 2 of the fourth part). If a cell \(C\) of the grid \(G'\) lies in \(W\), it is by step 1 of the fourth part a cell of the grid \(G\), and by step 3 all values on it are less than \(m_{\mathrm{C}} + \eta/(3V_0)\).
