The cells \(C'\) in it therefore have smallest values less than this number, and by step 2 of the fourth part the total volume \(\Delta V_{\mathrm{C}}\). Their contribution is at most \(m_{\mathrm{C}}\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{C}} + \eta\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{C}}/(3V_0)\).
  6. Let a cell \(C\) of the grid \(G'\) not lie in \(W\) but contain a cell \(C'\) of the grid \(H\) that lies in \(W\). Then \(C\) has points in \(W\) and a point outside \(W\), so it is a boundary cell. By step 1 of the fourth part it is not a new cell of the extension, so it is a boundary cell of the grid \(G\). The cells \(C'\) in it have, by lemma 4.28, item 2, a total volume of at most \(\Delta V_{\mathrm{C}}\), and their smallest values are at most \(M\). Their contribution is at most \(M\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{C}}\).
  7. We add up over the cells of the grid \(G'\). The total volume of the cells of the grid \(G\) that lie in \(W\) is at most \(V_0\) by step 2 of the second part, and the total volume of the boundary cells of the grid \(G\) is less than \(\eta/(3M + 3)\) by step 2 of this part. Therefore
    \[s(f, H) \le s(f, G) + \frac{\eta}{3V_0}\,V_0 + M\,\frac{\eta}{3M + 3} < s(f, G) + \frac{2\eta}{3} .\]
  8. From steps 4 and 7 it follows that \(s(f, G) > s(f, H) - 2\eta/3 > I - \eta\). By step 3 of the third part, \(s(f, G) \le I\).

6. Sums over cells of a nonnegative function.

  1. Let \(G\) be the grid of step 3 of the fifth part and \(Q_{\mathrm{C}}\) a point in a cell \(C\) that lies in \(W\). By the same step \(m_{\mathrm{C}} \le f(Q_{\mathrm{C}}) < m_{\mathrm{C}} + \eta/(3V_0)\). We multiply by \(\Delta V_{\mathrm{C}}\) and add up. By step 2 of the second part the sum (4.15), which we call \(\Sigma\), lies between \(s(f, G)\) and \(s(f, G) + \eta/3\).
  2. By step 8 of the fifth part therefore \(I - \eta < \Sigma < I + \eta/3\), so \(|\Sigma - I| < \eta\). The number \(I\) has the property of definition 4.30, with the \(\delta\) of step 2 of the fifth part.

7. Any continuous function.

  1. By theorem 1.78, \(f\) has a smallest value \(m_0\) on \(W\). The function \(f - m_0\) is continuous (corollary 1.69, item 1) and nonnegative, and so is the constant function \(1\). By parts 3 to 6 there are numbers \(I_1\) and \(V\) with the property of the definition, the first for the function \(f - m_0\), the second for the function \(1\).
  2. Let \(I = I_1 + m_0 V\). For the same grid and the same points, the sum (4.15) for \(f\) equals the sum for \(f - m_0\) plus \(m_0 \sum_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ijk}} \subseteq \mathrm{W}} \Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}}\), where the last sum is the sum (4.15) for the function \(1\).
  3. We choose \(\eta > 0\). Let \(\delta\) be less than the band that the property of the number \(I_1\) gives for the error \(\eta/2\), and less than the band that the property of the number \(V\) gives for the error \(\eta/(2|m_0| + 2)\). For a grid with pieces shorter than \(\delta\), by step 2 and by the triangle inequality for numbers (lemma 1.6, item 1), the sum for \(f\) differs from \(I\) by less than \(\eta/2 + |m_0|\,\eta/(2|m_0| + 2) < \eta\).

8. Only one number.

  1. Let the numbers \(I\) and \(I'\) have the property of the definition. We choose \(\eta > 0\) and take a \(\delta\) that is less than the bands that the properties of the numbers \(I\) and \(I'\) give for the error \(\eta/2\).
  2. By the Archimedean property 1.35 there is a grid of the cube \(K_0\) with equal pieces shorter than \(\delta\). We choose a point in each cell that lies in \(W\), and let \(\Sigma\) be the sum (4.15).
  3. By the triangle inequality, \(|I - I'| \le |I - \Sigma| + |\Sigma - I'| < \eta\). The error was arbitrary, so by lemma 1.34 \(|I - I'| = 0\).

9. The plane.

  1. The steps are the same, with rectangles in place of boxes and areas in place of volumes. In step 3 of the fifth part the square of the distance of two points of the same cell is less than \(2 \cdot \delta_1^2/4\).

Source: LEBL2 Proposition 10.5.5 (PDF p. 125): a bounded continuous function on a bounded Jordan measurable set is integrable. KREYSZIG (PDF pp. 453 and 478) states that the sums converge to a number that does not depend on the choice of the grids and the points, and leaves the proof to other books. The proof by lower sums over the cells that lie in the set is not from the sources.

The proof repeated the path by which we arrived at the integral over an interval in section 3.5.3. The lower sums of a nonnegative function are bounded, so they have a supremum, and they do not fall under refinement. Two moves are new. We compared grids of different boxes by extending them to a common box, which does not change the cells in \(W\). And we bounded the cells that newly appear in \(W\) under refinement by the boundary cells, which have a small total volume by lemma 4.29. Nowhere did we integrate over one variable at a time, so no order of integration appears in the proof.

For computing we need rules like those we know for the integral over a box. New is the rule for a set made of parts (figure 4.28). In a cut the cells fall into three groups. A cell that lies in one part contributes to the sum of that part. A cell cannot lie in two parts at once, because its centre would be an interior point of one part that lies in the other, which a cut does not allow. A cell that lies in the union but in no part crosses the cut and is a boundary cell of a part that it crosses. There are few such cells.

Lemma 4.32 Properties of the integral over a set with volume (lastnosti integrala po množici s prostornino)

Let \(W\) be a set with volume, \(f\) and \(g\) functions that are continuous on \(W\), and \(\alpha\) a number. The integrals are integrals of definition 4.30.

  1. Linearity: \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} (f + g)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{W}} g\,\mathrm{d}V\) and \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} \alpha f\,\mathrm{d}V = \alpha \int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  2. Monotonicity: if \(f(P) \le g(P)\) for every point \(P \in W\), then \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V \le \int_{\mathrm{W}} g\,\mathrm{d}V\). If \(W_1 \subseteq W\) is a set with volume and \(f(P) \ge 0\) for every point \(P \in W\), then \(\int_{\mathrm{W}_1} f\,\mathrm{d}V \le \int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\). In particular \(V_{\mathrm{W}_1} \le V_{\mathrm{W}}\).
  3. Bound: if \(|f(P)| \le c\) for every point \(P \in W\), for example with \(c = \max_{\mathrm{W}} |f|\), then \(\big|\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\big| \le c\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\).
  4. Additivity: let \(W_1, \dots, W_{\mathrm{m}}\) be sets with volume, and let no interior point of any of them lie in another. Then their union \(W_1 \cup \dots \cup W_{\mathrm{m}}\) is a set with volume, and for every function \(f\) that is continuous on the union
    \[\int_{\mathrm{W}_1 \cup \dots \cup \mathrm{W}_\mathrm{m}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{W}_1} f\,\mathrm{d}V + \dots + \int_{\mathrm{W}_\mathrm{m}} f\,\mathrm{d}V . \tag{4.16}\]
  5. A set of zero volume: if \(W\) also has zero volume (definition 4.25), then \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\). In particular \(V_{\mathrm{W}} = 0\).
  6. A box and a body made of boxes: a box \(K\) and a body made of boxes \(V\) (definition 4.11) are sets with volume. For a function that is continuous on \(K\), the integral over \(K\) of definition 4.30 equals the integral over a box of definition 4.8, and \(V_{\mathrm{K}}\) is the product of the lengths of the edges. For a function that is continuous on \(V\), the integral over \(V\) of definition 4.30 equals the sum of definition 4.11, item 1.
  7. Estimate by cells: for every grid of a box that contains \(W\),
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ijk}} \subseteq \mathrm{W}} \Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}} \le V_{\mathrm{W}} \le \sum_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ijk}} \subseteq \mathrm{W}} \Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}} + \sum_{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{ijk}} \text{ boundary}} \Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}} ,\]
    where the last sum runs over the boundary cells of the set \(W\).

The same holds in the plane, with the area in place of the volume.

Proof

We must show seven items. In all of them we compare the sums (4.15) for the same grid and the same points and use that the integral is the only number with the property of the definition (theorem 4.31).

1. Linearity.

  1. The functions \(f + g\) and \(\alpha f\) are continuous on \(W\) (corollary 1.69, item 1), so their integrals exist.
  2. For the same grid and the same points, the sum (4.15) for \(f + g\) is the sum of the two sums for \(f\) and for \(g\).
  3. We choose \(\eta > 0\) and take a \(\delta\) that is less than the bands that the definition gives the integrals of the functions \(f\) and \(g\) for the error \(\eta/2\). For a grid with pieces shorter than \(\delta\), by step 2 and by the triangle inequality for numbers, the sum for \(f + g\) differs from the number \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{W}} g\,\mathrm{d}V\) by less than \(\eta\). So this number has the property of the definition for the function \(f + g\), and by theorem 4.31 it equals \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} (f + g)\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  4. The sum for \(\alpha f\) is \(\alpha\) times the sum for \(f\), so by lemma 1.6, item 2, its distance from \(\alpha \int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\) is \(|\alpha|\) times the distance of the sum for \(f\) from \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\). The band that the definition gives for the error \(\eta/(|\alpha| + 1)\) therefore gives a distance less than \(\eta\).

2. Monotonicity.

  1. Let \(f \le g\) on \(W\) and \(\eta > 0\). A box that contains \(W\) exists, because \(W\) is bounded (step 1 of the second part of the proof of theorem 4.31). By the Archimedean property 1.35 there is a grid of it with pieces shorter than the bands that the definition gives both integrals for the error \(\eta\). With the same points the term \(f(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}})\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) is not larger than the term \(g(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}})\,\Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}}\), so the sum \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{f}}\) for \(f\) is not larger than the sum \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{g}}\) for \(g\), and
    \[\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V < \Sigma_{\mathrm{f}} + \eta \le \Sigma_{\mathrm{g}} + \eta < \int_{\mathrm{W}} g\,\mathrm{d}V + 2\eta .\]
  2. So the number \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V - \int_{\mathrm{W}} g\,\mathrm{d}V\) is less than \(2\eta\) for every \(\eta > 0\), and by lemma 1.34 it is at most \(0\).
  3. Let \(W_1 \subseteq W\) be a set with volume and \(f \ge 0\) on \(W\). A box that contains \(W\) also contains \(W_1\), and a cell that lies in \(W_1\) also lies in \(W\). We choose points in the cells that lie in \(W\). The sum over the cells in \(W\) is the sum over the cells in \(W_1\) plus the nonnegative terms of the cells that lie in \(W\) but not in \(W_1\). As in steps 1 and 2 it follows that \(\int_{\mathrm{W}_1} f\,\mathrm{d}V \le \int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\). For \(f = 1\) this is \(V_{\mathrm{W}_1} \le V_{\mathrm{W}}\).

3. Bound.

  1. From \(|f(P)| \le c\) it follows that \(-c \le f(P) \le c\) for every point \(P \in W\).
  2. By item 1, \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} c\,\mathrm{d}V = c \int_{\mathrm{W}} 1\,\mathrm{d}V = c\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\) and \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} (-c)\,\mathrm{d}V = -c\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\). By item 2, \(-c\,V_{\mathrm{W}} \le \int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V \le c\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\), which written with the absolute value is \(\big|\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\big| \le c\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\).
  3. If \(W\) is not empty, \(f\) has by theorem 1.78 a largest value \(M\) and a smallest value \(m\) on \(W\). The larger of the numbers \(|M|\) and \(|m|\) is the value of \(|f|\) at one of the points and a bound for \(|f(P)|\), because \(m \le f(P) \le M\). This is \(\max_{\mathrm{W}} |f|\).

4. Additivity.

  1. The union \(W = W_1 \cup \dots \cup W_{\mathrm{m}}\) is closed and bounded by lemma 4.24, item 3. By the same item every boundary point of the set \(W\) is a boundary point of one of the sets \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\). The boundaries of the sets \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\) have zero volume, so by lemma 4.26, item 2, so does their union, and by item 1 of the same lemma so does the boundary of the set \(W\), which lies in this union. The set \(W\) has volume.
  2. No cell lies in two of the sets \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\). Suppose that a cell lies in \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\) and in \(W_{\mathrm{l}}\) with \(k \ne l\). Let \(S\) be its centre and \(\rho\) half of its shortest edge. A point that is closer to \(S\) than \(\rho\) differs from \(S\) by less than \(\rho\) in every coordinate (step 2 of the proof of lemma 1.66), so it lies in the cell. The ball with centre \(S\) and radius \(\rho\) therefore lies in \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\), and \(S\) is an interior point of the set \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\) that lies in \(W_{\mathrm{l}}\). This contradicts the assumption.
  3. A cell that lies in \(W\) but in none of the sets \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\) is a boundary cell of one of them. Its point \(P\) lies in some \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\), and since the cell does not lie in \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\), it also has a point outside \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  4. Let \(c\) be the bound for \(|f|\) on \(W\) from item 3 (for an empty \(W\), \(c = 0\)). We choose \(\eta > 0\). We take a \(\delta\) that is less than the bands that the definition gives the integrals over \(W_1, \dots, W_{\mathrm{m}}\) for the error \(\eta/(3m)\), less than the band it gives the integral over \(W\) for the error \(\eta/3\), and less than the bands that lemma 4.29, item 3, gives the sets \(W_1, \dots, W_{\mathrm{m}}\) for the total volume \(\eta/(3m\,(c + 1))\).
  5. Let a grid of a box that contains \(W\), and hence every \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\), have pieces shorter than \(\delta\). In each cell that lies in \(W\) we choose a point. By step 2 every cell that lies in one of the sets \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\) lies in exactly one of them, and it lies in \(W\). The sum \(\Sigma\) over the cells in \(W\) is therefore the sum of the sums \(\Sigma_1, \dots, \Sigma_{\mathrm{m}}\) over the cells in \(W_1, \dots, W_{\mathrm{m}}\) and of the sum over the cells that lie in \(W\) but in no \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\). By step 3 these are boundary cells of the sets \(W_{\mathrm{k}}\) with a total volume less than \(m \cdot \eta/(3m\,(c + 1))\), so the last sum is less than \(\eta/3\) in absolute value.
  6. By the triangle inequality for numbers
    \[\begin{aligned} & \Big| \int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V - \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m} \int_{\mathrm{W}_\mathrm{k}} f\,\mathrm{d}V \Big| \\ & \quad \le \Big| \int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V - \Sigma \Big| + \Big| \Sigma - \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m} \Sigma_{\mathrm{k}} \Big| \\ & \qquad + \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m} \Big| \Sigma_{\mathrm{k}} - \int_{\mathrm{W}_\mathrm{k}} f\,\mathrm{d}V \Big| \\ & \quad < \frac{\eta}{3} + \frac{\eta}{3} + m\,\frac{\eta}{3m} = \eta . \end{aligned}\]
    The error was arbitrary, so by lemma 1.34 the left side is zero.

5. A set of zero volume.

  1. Let \(W\) also have zero volume and let \(c\) be the bound for \(|f|\) from item 3. We choose \(\eta > 0\). By lemma 4.29, item 1, used for \(Z = W\), there is a \(\delta\) such that for a grid with pieces shorter than \(\delta\) the cells with a point of \(W\) have a total volume less than \(\eta/(c + 1)\).
  2. A cell that lies in \(W\) contains a point of \(W\). The sum (4.15) is therefore less than \(c\,\eta/(c + 1) < \eta\) in absolute value. The number \(0\) has the property of the definition, and by theorem 4.31 \(\int_{\mathrm{W}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\).

6. A box and a body made of boxes.

  1. The box \(K\) is a set with volume, as we showed in section 4.2.9. All cells of a grid of the box \(K\) lie in \(K\), so for a grid of the box \(K\) the sum (4.15) is the Riemann sum of theorem 4.9.
  2. We choose \(\eta > 0\). By theorem 4.9, item 1, with the error \(\eta/(2V_{\mathrm{K}})\), there is a \(\delta_1\) such that such a sum for pieces shorter than \(\delta_1\) differs from the integral over the box by at most \(\eta/2\). By definition 4.30 there is a \(\delta_2\) for the error \(\eta/2\). A grid of the box \(K\) with equal pieces shorter than both bands gives a sum that differs from both numbers by at most \(\eta/2\), so the numbers differ by at most \(\eta\). By lemma 1.34 they are equal. For \(f = 1\) the integral over the box equals the product of the lengths of the edges by lemma 4.10, item 2.
  3. A body made of boxes \(V\) is the union of cells of some grid. Two different cells differ in at least one piece, for example in the pieces \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\) and \([x_{\mathrm{i}'-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}'}]\) with \(i < i'\). An interior point of the first cell has an \(x\) coordinate less than \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\), because a ball around a point with the coordinate \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\) contains points with a larger coordinate \(x\), which are not in the cell. Points of the second cell have \(x \ge x_{\mathrm{i}'-1} \ge x_{\mathrm{i}}\). So no interior point of the first cell lies in the second, and likewise no interior point of the second lies in the first.
  4. By item 4, \(V\) is a set with volume and the integral over it is the sum of the integrals over the cells, and these are by step 2 the integrals over boxes of definition 4.8. This is the sum of definition 4.11, item 1.

7. Estimate by cells.

  1. Let \(G\) be a grid of a box \(K\) that contains \(W\), and \(\eta > 0\). Let \(\delta\) be the band that the definition gives the integral of the function \(1\) over \(W\) for the error \(\eta\). We add to the partitions of the grid \(G\) the points of partitions of the edges into equal pieces shorter than \(\delta\) (Archimedean property), and get a grid \(H\) of the same box with pieces shorter than \(\delta\) that contains all points of the partitions of the grid \(G\).
  2. The sum (4.15) for the function \(1\) and the grid \(H\) is the total volume of the cells of the grid \(H\) that lie in \(W\), and it differs from \(V_{\mathrm{W}}\) by less than \(\eta\).
  3. A cell of the grid \(G\) that lies in \(W\) is the union of the cells of the grid \(H\) that lie in it and therefore in \(W\). By lemma 4.28, item 3, these have a total volume equal to its volume. So the total volume of the cells of the grid \(G\) in \(W\) is not larger than the total volume of the cells of the grid \(H\) in \(W\), which is less than \(V_{\mathrm{W}} + \eta\).
  4. A cell of the grid \(H\) that lies in \(W\) lies in a cell of the grid \(G\) (step 2 of the fourth part of the proof of theorem 4.31), which has a point in \(W\), so it lies in \(W\) or is a boundary cell. The cells of the grid \(H\) in one cell of the grid \(G\) have, by lemma 4.28, item 2, a total volume of at most its volume. Therefore \(V_{\mathrm{W}} - \eta\) is less than the total volume of the cells of the grid \(G\) that lie in \(W\) or are boundary cells.
  5. The error was arbitrary, so by lemma 1.34 both inequalities follow from steps 3 and 4.

8. The plane.

  1. The steps are the same, with rectangles and areas.

Source: KREYSZIG §10.3, (1) (PDF p. 453), for double integrals: linearity and additivity for a region divided into two parts (Fig. 228). LEBL2 Proposition 10.5.2 (PDF p. 123) for unions, Proposition 10.5.7 (PDF p. 125) for additivity over disjoint sets. The proof is not from the sources.

Item 7 tells how to estimate a volume by a grid. For the cross section of the round bar, the grids of the table in section 4.2.9 give the estimates of the area \(A\) of the cross section

\[\begin{aligned} 60 &\le A \le 96 , & 69 &\le A \le 88 , \\ 73{,}5 &\le A \le 83{,}25 , & 76{,}44 &\le A \le 80{,}4 , \end{aligned}\]

in square millimetres. The difference between the bounds is the area of the boundary cells, which is arbitrarily small for a fine grid by lemma 4.29. Item 4 is the rule for a cut: the integral over the union of pieces is the sum of the integrals over the pieces, if no interior point of one piece lies in another.

What remains is the link with the iterated integral. Let us take a body between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R\) and cut it by a grid whose partitions of the edges \([a, b]\) and \([c, d]\) cut \(R\) into rectangles \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\). Over each \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\) stands a column of cells (figure 4.29). The cells of the column that lie in the body fill almost the whole vertical chord from \(g\) to \(h\) over a chosen point \(p\) of the rectangle \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\). At each end at most as much is missing as \(g\) or \(h\) changes on \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\), plus one cell. The sum over the column is therefore close to the inner integral \(F(p) = \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{p})}^{h(p)} f\,\mathrm{d}z\) times the area of the rectangle \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The sum over the columns is a Riemann sum of the continuous function \(F\) on the rectangle \(R\), which approaches the iterated integral by theorem 4.9.

Theorem 4.33 Integral over a body between two graphs without an order (integral po telesu med grafoma brez vrstnega reda)

Let \(V\) be a body between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) (definition 4.15), with any naming of the axes. Then \(V\) is a set with volume, and for every function \(f\) that is continuous on \(V\) the integral of definition 4.30 equals the iterated integral of definition 4.20:

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(x, y)} f(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x . \tag{4.17}\]

The same holds in the plane. If \(g\) and \(h\) are continuous functions on \([a, b]\) with \(g(x) \le h(x)\), the region \(M\) of the points \((x, y)\) with \(a \le x \le b\) and \(g(x) \le y \le h(x)\) is a set with area, and for every function \(f\) continuous on \(M\), \(\int_{\mathrm{M}} f\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x})}^{h(x)} f(x, y)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x\). This also holds with the roles of the coordinates exchanged.

Proof

We must show that the boundary of the body has zero volume and that the sum (4.15) for a suitable fine grid is close to the iterated integral. We write the proof for a body in which the coordinate \(z\) runs between the graphs.

1. The body has volume.

  1. The body \(V\) is closed and bounded by lemma 4.17. The functions \(g\) and \(h\) are continuous on the open set \(U\) from the definition of the body, as in step 1 of the proof of that lemma.
  2. Interior points. Let \(P = (x_0, y_0, z_0)\) be a point with \(a < x_0 < b\), \(c < y_0 < d\) and \(g(x_0, y_0) < z_0 < h(x_0, y_0)\). Let \(\varepsilon\) be a positive number less than the positive numbers \(z_0 - g(x_0, y_0)\) and \(h(x_0, y_0) - z_0\). By the continuity of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) at the point \((x_0, y_0)\) there is a \(\rho > 0\) such that at points of \(U\) closer to \((x_0, y_0)\) than \(\rho\), \(g\) and \(h\) differ from their values at \((x_0, y_0)\) by less than \(\varepsilon/2\). Let \(r\) be the smallest of the numbers \(\rho\), \(x_0 - a\), \(b - x_0\), \(y_0 - c\), \(d - y_0\) and \(\varepsilon/2\).
  3. Let \(Q = (x, y, z)\) be a point with \(|PQ| < r\). Every difference of coordinates is less than \(r\), so \(a < x < b\), \(c < y < d\) and \(|z - z_0| < \varepsilon/2\). Since \((x - x_0)^2 + (y - y_0)^2 \le |PQ|^2\), by lemma 1.28 the point \((x, y)\) is closer to \((x_0, y_0)\) than \(\rho\). Therefore
    \[g(x, y) < g(x_0, y_0) + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \le z_0 - \frac{\varepsilon}{2} < z < z_0 + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \le h(x_0, y_0) - \frac{\varepsilon}{2} < h(x, y) ,\]
    and \(Q\) lies in \(V\). The point \(P\) is an interior point of the body \(V\), so it is not a boundary point.
  4. The boundary. A boundary point of the body \(V\) lies in \(V\) by lemma 4.24, item 1, and by step 3 it has \(x_0 = a\) or \(x_0 = b\) or \(y_0 = c\) or \(y_0 = d\) or \(z_0 = g(x_0, y_0)\) or \(z_0 = h(x_0, y_0)\). The boundary therefore lies in the union of the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over \(R\) and of the four side pieces on which \(x = a\), \(x = b\), \(y = c\) or \(y = d\).
  5. The graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over \(R\) have zero volume by lemma 4.26, item 3.
  6. The side pieces. By theorem 1.78 there are numbers \(m\) and \(M'\) with \(m \le g\) and \(h \le M'\) on \(R\). The piece with \(x = a\) lies in the box \([a, a + t] \times [c, d] \times [m - 1, M' + 1]\) for every \(t > 0\). Its volume \(t\,(d - c)(M' - m + 2)\) is less than \(\eta\) when \(t\) is small enough, so the piece has zero volume. The same for the other three pieces.
  7. By lemma 4.26, items 2 and 1, the boundary has zero volume. The body \(V\) is a set with volume.

2. Choice of the numbers.

  1. Let \(f\) be continuous on \(V\). By theorem 4.31 the integral \(J = \int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\) of definition 4.30 exists. We call the iterated integral on the right side of (4.17) \(I\), and the inner integral \(F(x, y) = \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(x, y)} f(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\). By lemma 4.18, \(F\) has the property of item 1 of lemma 4.7, so it is continuous on \(R\).
  2. By theorem 1.78 there are numbers \(M > 0\) and \(H\) with \(|f| \le M\) on \(V\) and \(h - g \le H\) on \(R\). We need a positive \(M\) for the strict inequalities in the third part. Let \(A_{\mathrm{R}} = (b - a)(d - c)\) be the area of the rectangle \(R\).
  3. We choose \(\eta > 0\). Let \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{f}} = \eta/(9\,(H + 1)\,A_{\mathrm{R}})\) and \(\omega = \eta/(18\,(M + 1)\,A_{\mathrm{R}})\). By theorem 4.6 there is a \(\delta_{\mathrm{f}} > 0\) such that \(|f(P) - f(Q)| < \varepsilon_{\mathrm{f}}\) for points \(P, Q \in V\) with \(|PQ| < \delta_{\mathrm{f}}\), and a \(\delta_{\mathrm{g}} > 0\) such that \(g\) and \(h\) differ by less than \(\omega\) at points of the rectangle \(R\) closer than \(\delta_{\mathrm{g}}\). By theorem 4.9, item 1, used for the rectangle, the function \(F\) and the error \(\eta/(3A_{\mathrm{R}})\), there is a \(\delta_{\mathrm{F}}\) such that a Riemann sum of the function \(F\) for a grid of the rectangle \(R\) with pieces shorter than \(\delta_{\mathrm{F}}\) differs from \(I\) by at most \(\eta/3\). By definition 4.30 there is a \(\delta_{\mathrm{J}}\) for the integral \(J\) and the error \(\eta/3\).
  4. Let \(\delta\) be a positive number less than \(\delta_{\mathrm{f}}\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{g}}\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{F}}\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{J}}\) and \(\omega\). The box \(K = [a, b] \times [c, d] \times [m - 1, M' + 1]\) contains \(V\). By the Archimedean property 1.35 we divide its edges into equal pieces shorter than \(\delta/2\). Two points of the same rectangle \(R_{\mathrm{ij}} = [x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}] \times [y_{\mathrm{j}-1}, y_{\mathrm{j}}]\) are then closer than \(\delta\), as in step 2 of the proof of lemma 4.26, item 3.

3. One column.

  1. Let \(p = (x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{j}})\) be a corner of the rectangle \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\). In each cell \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}} = R_{\mathrm{ij}} \times [z_{\mathrm{k}-1}, z_{\mathrm{k}}]\) that lies in \(V\) we choose the point \(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}} = (x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{j}}, z_{\mathrm{k}})\). We compare the sum over these cells \(S_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} f(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}})\,\Delta z_{\mathrm{k}}\) with the number \(F(p)\).
  2. Let \(g_{\mathrm{ij}}\) be the largest value of the function \(g\) and \(h_{\mathrm{ij}}\) the smallest value of the function \(h\) on \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (theorem 1.78). The cell \(K_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) lies in \(V\) exactly when \(g_{\mathrm{ij}} \le z_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) and \(z_{\mathrm{k}} \le h_{\mathrm{ij}}\). If this holds, then for every point of the cell \(g(x, y) \le g_{\mathrm{ij}} \le z_{\mathrm{k}-1} \le z \le z_{\mathrm{k}} \le h_{\mathrm{ij}} \le h(x, y)\). Conversely, if the cell lies in \(V\), its point \((x, y, z_{\mathrm{k}-1})\), where \(g\) attains \(g_{\mathrm{ij}}\), also lies in \(V\), so \(g_{\mathrm{ij}} \le z_{\mathrm{k}-1}\), and likewise \(z_{\mathrm{k}} \le h_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
  3. Since the point \(p\) and the point where \(g\) attains \(g_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are closer than \(\delta_{\mathrm{g}}\), we have \(g(p) \le g_{\mathrm{ij}} < g(p) + \omega\). Likewise \(h(p) - \omega < h_{\mathrm{ij}} \le h(p)\).
  4. The first case: no cell of the column lies in \(V\), and \(S_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\). Then \(h_{\mathrm{ij}} - g_{\mathrm{ij}} < \delta\). Indeed, suppose that \(h_{\mathrm{ij}} - g_{\mathrm{ij}} \ge \delta\). Let \(z_{\mathrm{k}}\) be the smallest point of the partition that is not less than \(g_{\mathrm{ij}}\). Since \(z_0 = m - 1 < g_{\mathrm{ij}}\), we have \(k \ge 1\) and \(z_{\mathrm{k}-1} < g_{\mathrm{ij}}\), so \(z_{\mathrm{k}} < g_{\mathrm{ij}} + \delta/2\), because the pieces are shorter than \(\delta/2\). Since \(z_{\mathrm{k}} < h_{\mathrm{ij}} \le M' < M' + 1\), there is a next point \(z_{\mathrm{k}+1} < z_{\mathrm{k}} + \delta/2 < g_{\mathrm{ij}} + \delta \le h_{\mathrm{ij}}\). By step 2 the cell with the piece \([z_{\mathrm{k}}, z_{\mathrm{k}+1}]\) would lie in \(V\), which contradicts the assumption of the case. By step 3 therefore \(h(p) - g(p) < h_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega - (g_{\mathrm{ij}} - \omega) < \delta + 2\omega\). By the bound (lemma 3.39, item 3), \(|S_{\mathrm{ij}} - F(p)| = |F(p)| \le M\,(h(p) - g(p)) < M\,(\delta + 2\omega)\).
  5. The second case: the cells of the column with indices from \(k_0\) to \(k_1\) lie in \(V\). The cells between them lie in \(V\) by step 2, because the points of the partition increase. Let \(\alpha = z_{\mathrm{k}_0 - 1}\) and \(\beta = z_{\mathrm{k}_1}\). Then \(g_{\mathrm{ij}} \le \alpha < g_{\mathrm{ij}} + \delta\). The first inequality follows from step 2. Since \(\alpha \ge g_{\mathrm{ij}} \ge m > m - 1 = z_0\), the cell with the piece \([z_{\mathrm{k}_0 - 1}, z_{\mathrm{k}_0}]\) has a predecessor with the piece \([z_{\mathrm{k}_0 - 2}, \alpha]\). It does not lie in \(V\), because \(k_0\) is the smallest index, and its upper end is \(\alpha \le \beta \le h_{\mathrm{ij}}\). By step 2 therefore \(z_{\mathrm{k}_0 - 2} < g_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and \(\alpha < z_{\mathrm{k}_0 - 2} + \delta/2 < g_{\mathrm{ij}} + \delta\). Likewise \(h_{\mathrm{ij}} - \delta < \beta \le h_{\mathrm{ij}}\). By step 3 therefore \(0 \le \alpha - g(p) < \omega + \delta\) and \(0 \le h(p) - \beta < \omega + \delta\).
  6. For \(z\) from the piece \([z_{\mathrm{k}-1}, z_{\mathrm{k}}]\) with \(k_0 \le k \le k_1\) the point \((x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{j}}, z)\) lies in \(V\), because \(g(p) \le \alpha \le z \le \beta \le h(p)\), and it is closer to \(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}}\) than \(\delta < \delta_{\mathrm{f}}\). Therefore \(|f(x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{j}}, z) - f(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}})| < \varepsilon_{\mathrm{f}}\), and by the bound
    \[\Big| \int_{\mathrm{z}_{\mathrm{k}-1}}^{z_{\mathrm{k}}} f(x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{j}}, z)\,\mathrm{d}z - f(Q_{\mathrm{ijk}})\,\Delta z_{\mathrm{k}} \Big| \le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{f}}\,\Delta z_{\mathrm{k}} .\]
    We add up over \(k\) and use additivity (lemma 3.39, item 2) and the triangle inequality for numbers: \(\big|\int_\alpha^\beta f(x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{j}}, z)\,\mathrm{d}z - S_{\mathrm{ij}}\big| \le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{f}}\,(\beta - \alpha) \le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{f}} H\).
  7. By additivity \(F(p) = \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{p})}^{\alpha} + \int_\alpha^\beta + \int_\beta^{h(p)}\), all with the integrand \(f(x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{j}}, z)\). The first and the last part are less than \(M\,(\omega + \delta)\) in absolute value by the bound and step 5. By the triangle inequality, \(|S_{\mathrm{ij}} - F(p)| < \varepsilon_{\mathrm{f}} H + 2M\,(\omega + \delta)\).
  8. In both cases \(|S_{\mathrm{ij}} - F(p)| < \varepsilon_{\mathrm{f}} H + 2M\,(\omega + \delta)\), because \(M\,(\delta + 2\omega)\) is at most \(2M\,(\omega + \delta)\).

4. All columns.

  1. The partitions of the edges \([a, b]\) and \([c, d]\) cut \(R\) into the rectangles \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\), so every cell lies over exactly one of them. Since \(\Delta V_{\mathrm{ijk}} = \Delta A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\Delta z_{\mathrm{k}}\), where \(\Delta A_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is the area of the rectangle \(R_{\mathrm{ij}}\), the sum (4.15) with the chosen points equals \(\Sigma = \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}} S_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\Delta A_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
  2. By the third part and by the triangle inequality
    \[\Big| \Sigma - \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}} F(x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{j}})\,\Delta A_{\mathrm{ij}} \Big| < \big( \varepsilon_{\mathrm{f}} H + 2M\,(\omega + \delta) \big)\,A_{\mathrm{R}} < \frac{\eta}{9} + \frac{4M\,\eta}{18\,(M + 1)} < \frac{\eta}{3} ,\]
    because \(\delta < \omega\) and the areas \(\Delta A_{\mathrm{ij}}\) add up to \(A_{\mathrm{R}}\).

5. Conclusion.

  1. The sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j}} F(x_{\mathrm{i}}, y_{\mathrm{j}})\,\Delta A_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is a Riemann sum of the function \(F\) for a grid of the rectangle \(R\) with pieces shorter than \(\delta_{\mathrm{F}}\), so it differs from \(I\) by at most \(\eta/3\) (step 3 of the second part).
  2. The grid is a grid of a box that contains \(V\), with pieces shorter than \(\delta_{\mathrm{J}}\), so \(|\Sigma - J| < \eta/3\).
  3. By the triangle inequality, \(|J - I| < \eta/3 + \eta/3 + \eta/3 = \eta\). The error was arbitrary, so by lemma 1.34 \(J = I\).

6. Other namings of the axes and the plane.

  1. For another naming of the axes the steps are the same, only the coordinates exchange roles. Definition 4.30 treats all three coordinates alike, so it does not change.
  2. In the plane the region \(M\) is closed and bounded by the proof of lemma 4.17 with one coordinate less. Its boundary lies in the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) and in the segments \(x = a\) and \(x = b\), which have zero area. The columns stand over the pieces \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}]\). The function \(F(x) = \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x})}^{h(x)} f(x, y)\,\mathrm{d}y\) is continuous on \([a, b]\) by the proof of lemma 4.18 in which the points \((x, y)\) of the rectangle are replaced by numbers \(x\), and in place of theorem 4.9 we use theorem 3.38, item 3.

Source: LEBL2 Proposition 10.5.8 (PDF p. 126) for a region between the graphs of continuous functions in the plane, with the proof left to the reader. KREYSZIG §10.3, (3) (PDF p. 453), and §10.7 (PDF p. 479) use the iterated integral for computing, without proof. The proof is not from the sources.

The proof used only the continuity of the functions \(g\) and \(h\), not their derivatives. We need the derivatives for the lids and for the divergence theorem, not for the integral over the body. The key step was the third one. The column of cells that lie in the body fills the chord over the point \(p\) except for short pieces at the ends, because \(g\) and \(h\) change little on a small rectangle. Therefore the sum over the column is almost the inner integral along the chord times the area of the rectangle under it, and the iterated integral by which we defined the integral in section 4.2.8 is indeed the limit of sums over cells.

The answer to both questions follows at once from the theorem.

Corollary 4.34 The integral does not depend on the order or the cut (integral ni odvisen od vrstnega reda in razreza)

Let \(f\) be a function that is continuous on a set of points \(V\).

  1. If \(V\) is a body between graphs for two namings of the axes, the iterated integrals of the function \(f\) over \(V\) (definition 4.20) for the two namings are equal.
  2. If \(V\) is cut into the pieces \(V_1, \dots, V_{\mathrm{m}}\) (definition 4.21), \(V\) is a set with volume, and the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m} \int_{\mathrm{V}_\mathrm{k}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\) of definition 4.21 equals the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\) of definition 4.30. Hence it is the same for all cuts of the same body.

The same holds in the plane for a region that is the union of regions between graphs, of which no interior point of one lies in another.

Proof

We must show both items. We compare both numbers with the integral of definition 4.30, which knows neither an order nor a cut.

  1. By theorem 4.33 each of the iterated integrals equals the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\) of definition 4.30, so they are equal.
  2. By the same theorem every piece \(V_{\mathrm{k}}\) is a set with volume, and the iterated integral over it equals the integral over it of definition 4.30. By definition 4.21 no interior point of any piece lies in another. By lemma 4.32, item 4, \(V\) is therefore a set with volume, and \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\) is the sum of the integrals over the pieces, that is, the sum of definition 4.21.
  3. Two cuts of the same body give sums that by step 2 both equal the same number \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  4. In the plane the steps are the same, with the plane form of the theorem and of the lemma.

Source: KREYSZIG (PDF pp. 453 and 478) states that the limit of the sums over cells does not depend on the choice of the grids and the points. The corollary and its proof are not from the sources.

Let us test the first item on a prism cut out of the round bar. Its cross section is the triangle with the vertices \((0, 0)\), \((3, 0)\) and \((3, 4)\) in millimetres, in the plane of the axes \(y\) and \(z\) (figure 4.30). The vertex \((3, 4)\) lies on the circle, because \(3^2 + 4^2 = 25\). The prism is the set of points with \(0 \le x \le L\), \(0 \le y \le 3\) and \(0 \le z \le 4y/3\). It lies in the bar. Indeed, for each of its points \(0 \le z \le 4y/3\), so \(z^2 \le 16y^2/9\) by lemma 1.28, that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, and since \(0 \le y \le 3\), \(y^2 + z^2 \le y^2 + 16y^2/9 = 25y^2/9 \le 25\). The prism is a body between the graphs of the functions \(0\) and \(4y/3\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [0, 3]\) in the variables \(x\) and \(y\). But it is also a body between the graphs of the functions \(3z/4\) and \(3\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [0, 4]\) in the variables \(x\) and \(z\). Indeed, from \(0 \le z \le 4y/3\) and \(y \le 3\) it follows that \(z \le 4\) and \(y \ge 3z/4\), and conversely from \(3z/4 \le y \le 3\) and \(z \ge 0\) it follows that \(0 \le z \le 4y/3\). All four functions are linear and therefore continuously differentiable everywhere.

Let us integrate the function \(y^2 + z^2\), the square of the distance from the axis of the bar, which appears in the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\) of the hanging bar in the term \(-0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\). In the first description the inner integral is over \(z\), in the second over \(y\). SymPy gives

\[\int_0^3 \int_0^{4y/3} (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y = \int_0^3 \frac{172}{81}\,y^3\,\mathrm{d}y = 43\ \text{mm}^4 ,\]
\[\int_0^4 \int_{3\mathrm{z}/4}^{3} (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}z = \int_0^4 \Big( 9 + 3z^2 - \frac{57}{64}\,z^3 \Big)\,\mathrm{d}z = 43\ \text{mm}^4 .\]

The outer integral over \(x\) multiplies both numbers by \(L = 10\,000\) mm, and in both descriptions we get \(430\,000\ \text{mm}^5\). The inner integrals are different functions, the first depends on \(y\), the second on \(z\), but the final numbers are equal by corollary 4.34, item 1. For the function \(1\) both descriptions give the area of the triangle, \(6\) mm², half the product of the legs \(3\) and \(4\) mm.

Let us also test the second item on the round bar. In section 4.2.6 we cut it by the planes \(y = \pm 3\) mm. Now let us cut it by the planes \(y = \pm 4\) mm (figure 4.31). The middle piece consists of the points with \(-4 \le y \le 4\), between the graphs of the functions \(-q(y)\) and \(q(y)\), where \(q(t) = \sqrt{25 - t^2}\). The function \(q\) is continuously differentiable on \((-5, 5)\), which contains \([-4, 4]\), by lemma 4.16. The right piece consists of the points with \(y \ge 4\). For them \(z^2 \le 25 - 16 = 9\), so \(-3 \le z \le 3\), and the piece is a body between the graphs of the functions \(4\) and \(q(z)\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [-3, 3]\), like the piece \(D\) in section 4.2.6. The left piece is the same with \(-q(z)\) and \(-4\). SymPy gives the areas of the cross sections of the pieces

\[\int_{-4}^{4} 2\,q(y)\,\mathrm{d}y = 70{,}36\ \text{mm}^2 , \qquad \int_{-3}^{3} \big(q(z) - 4\big)\,\mathrm{d}z = 4{,}088\ \text{mm}^2 .\]

Together \(70{,}36 + 2 \cdot 4{,}088 = 78{,}54\) mm², as for the cut by the planes \(y = \pm 3\) mm, where we got \(56{,}18 + 2 \cdot 11{,}18 = 78{,}54\) mm². The pieces are different, and so are their areas, but the sum is the same, as item 2 of corollary 4.34 predicts. So the area of the cross section is a property of the cross section, \(A = 78{,}54\) mm², and it lies between the bounds that item 7 of lemma 4.32 gave. Likewise the volume of the bar \(L\,A = 785\,400\ \text{mm}^3\) and its weight are properties of the bar.

With this the questions from the end of section 4.2.8 are answered. The integral over a body between graphs and over a body cut into pieces is a number that belongs to the body, not to a chosen order or cut. We still compute it by iterated integrals, because we know how to evaluate them, and the sum over cells tells what they mean. The next section moves from the body to its surface.

4.2.11 Integral over a curved surface

The surface of a body between graphs has six pieces (figure 4.20). The four side pieces are flat, in the planes \(x = a\), \(x = b\), \(y = c\) and \(y = d\), with the outward normals \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). Each is a region between graphs in its own plane. The piece in the plane \(x = a\) consists of the points \((a, y, z)\) with \(c \le y \le d\) and \(g(a, y) \le z \le h(a, y)\), and we will write the integral over it as an iterated integral, with the inner integral over \(z\). The two lids are new, and they are curved. How do we compute the area of a small patch on a curved lid, and where does the normal to it point?

Take the top lid, the graph of the function \(h\), and on it the patch above a small rectangle of the shadow with sides \(\Delta x\) and \(\Delta y\) (figure 4.32). When we move from the point \((x, y)\) by \(\Delta x\) in the direction of the axis \(x\), the height of the lid changes by about \(\frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\,\Delta x\), by theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step, written for two variables. The side of the patch above the side \(\Delta x\) is therefore about the vector \(\vek a\), and the side above the side \(\Delta y\) about the vector \(\vek b\), where

\[\vek a = \Big(\Delta x,\ 0,\ \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\,\Delta x\Big) , \qquad \vek b = \Big(0,\ \Delta y,\ \frac{\partial h}{\partial y}\,\Delta y\Big) .\]

The patch is approximately the parallelogram spanned by \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\). By definition 2.30

\[\begin{aligned} \vek a\times\vek b &= \Big( 0 - \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\,\Delta x\,\Delta y,\ \ 0 - \Delta x\,\frac{\partial h}{\partial y}\,\Delta y,\ \ \Delta x\,\Delta y - 0 \Big) \\ &= \Big( -\frac{\partial h}{\partial x},\ -\frac{\partial h}{\partial y},\ 1 \Big)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y . \end{aligned}\]

By item 4 of lemma 2.31 this vector is perpendicular to both sides, hence to the patch, and its length is the area of the parallelogram (section 2.8). We write

\[\vek N_{\mathrm{h}} = \Big( -\frac{\partial h}{\partial x},\ -\frac{\partial h}{\partial y},\ 1 \Big) .\]

The area of the patch is about \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\), and the unit normal to it is \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}/|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|\) (definition 2.17). The component \(z\) of the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\) is \(1\), so the normal points up, out of the body, which lies below the top lid. For the bottom lid we take the opposite vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{g}} = (\partial g/\partial x,\ \partial g/\partial y,\ -1)\), which points down, out of the body.

The divergence theorem will add up the products \(\vek v\cdot\vek n\,\Delta A\) over the patches. In each of them the length of the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\), which has a root, cancels:

\[\vek v\cdot\frac{\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}}{|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|}\,|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|\,\Delta x\,\Delta y = \vek v\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\,\Delta x\,\Delta y = \Big( v_{\mathrm{z}} - \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} - \frac{\partial h}{\partial y}\,v_{\mathrm{y}} \Big)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y .\]

This is what the divergence theorem will need. For the integral of a function that is not of the form \(\vek v\cdot\vek n\), however, the root remains.

The integrand on the lid is the value of a function at the point \((x, y, h(x, y))\), which depends on the point \((x, y)\) of the shadow through the function \(h\). The following lemma says that it is continuous.

Lemma 4.35 Continuity of a composite function (zveznost sestavljene funkcije)

Let \(f\) be a function that is continuous on a set of points of space \(W\). Let \(p_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(p_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(p_{\mathrm{z}}\) be functions defined on a set \(M\), which is an interval or a set of points of the plane, such that the point \(p(Q) = \big(p_{\mathrm{x}}(Q), p_{\mathrm{y}}(Q), p_{\mathrm{z}}(Q)\big)\) lies in \(W\) for every \(Q \in M\). If \(p_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(p_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(p_{\mathrm{z}}\) are continuous at the point \(Q_0 \in M\), the function \(Q \mapsto f(p(Q))\) is continuous at \(Q_0\).

Proof

We must show that the values \(f(p(Q_{\mathrm{n}}))\) converge to \(f(p(Q_0))\) for every sequence \((Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) of \(M\) that converges to \(Q_0\). We use the lemma on continuity through sequences twice.

  1. Let the sequence \((Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) of \(M\) converge to \(Q_0\). The function \(p_{\mathrm{x}}\) is continuous at \(Q_0\), so by lemma 1.68 on continuity through sequences of points (on an interval by lemma 1.61) \(p_{\mathrm{x}}(Q_{\mathrm{n}}) \to p_{\mathrm{x}}(Q_0)\). Likewise \(p_{\mathrm{y}}(Q_{\mathrm{n}}) \to p_{\mathrm{y}}(Q_0)\) and \(p_{\mathrm{z}}(Q_{\mathrm{n}}) \to p_{\mathrm{z}}(Q_0)\).
  2. By lemma 1.66 on convergence coordinate by coordinate, the points \(p(Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) therefore converge to \(p(Q_0)\). They all lie in \(W\), and \(f\) is continuous at \(p(Q_0)\), so by lemma 1.68 \(f(p(Q_{\mathrm{n}})) \to f(p(Q_0))\).
  3. The sequence \((Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) was arbitrary, so by the same lemma, in the other direction, the function \(Q \mapsto f(p(Q))\) is continuous at \(Q_0\).

Source: LEBL1 Proposition 3.2.7 (PDF p. 125) for functions of one variable. The proof with sequences for points is not from the sources.

Now we can write down how we integrate over the surface of a body between graphs.

Definition 4.36 Flux and integral over the surface of a body between two graphs (pretok in integral po površini telesa med grafoma)

Let \(V\) be a body between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) (definition 4.15). Its surface (površina) \(S\) consists of six pieces:

  • the top lid \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\), the points \((x, y, h(x, y))\) with \((x, y) \in R\), with the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}} = \big(-\frac{\partial h}{\partial x},\ -\frac{\partial h}{\partial y},\ 1\big)\),
  • the bottom lid \(S_{\mathrm{g}}\), the points \((x, y, g(x, y))\) with \((x, y) \in R\), with the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{g}} = \big(\frac{\partial g}{\partial x},\ \frac{\partial g}{\partial y},\ -1\big)\),
  • the side pieces \(S_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\), the points \((a, y, z)\) and \((b, y, z)\) with \(c \le y \le d\) and \(z\) between \(g\) and \(h\) at the point \((a, y)\) or \((b, y)\), with the vectors \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\),
  • the side pieces \(S_{\mathrm{c}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\), the points \((x, c, z)\) and \((x, d, z)\) with \(a \le x \le b\) and \(z\) between \(g\) and \(h\) at the point \((x, c)\) or \((x, d)\), with the vectors \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\).

On every piece with the vector \(\vek N\) the outward unit normal (zunanja enotska normala) is \(\vek n = \vek N/|\vek N|\). The surface integral of a function \(f\) over the top lid is the number

\[\int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{h}} f\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d f\big(x, y, h(x, y)\big)\,\big|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}(x, y)\big|\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x , \tag{4.18}\]

and over the bottom lid likewise, with \(g\) and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{g}}\). Over the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{a}}\) it is the number \(\int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(a, y)} f(a, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y\), over \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\) the same with \(b\), over \(S_{\mathrm{c}}\) the number \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{c})}^{h(x, c)} f(x, c, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}x\), over \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\) the same with \(d\). The integral over the surface \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,\mathrm{d}A\) is the sum of these six numbers, when all the integrals exist. For a field \(\vek v\) the flux (pretok) of the field through the surface is the integral over the surface of the function \(\vek v\cdot\vek n\), \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\). For a body with exchanged roles of the coordinates we rename the coordinates in these formulas, so that the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\) has the component \(1\) in the direction of the coordinate that runs between the graphs.

Source: KREYSZIG §10.6, (2) and (3) (PDF p. 469): \(\vek N = \vek r_{\mathrm{u}}\times\vek r_{\mathrm{v}}\), \(\vek n = \vek N/|\vek N|\) and \(\mathrm{d}A = |\vek N|\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v\), and §10.5, Problem 13 (PDF p. 469), \(\vek N = (-f_{\mathrm{u}}, -f_{\mathrm{v}}, 1)\) for the surface \(z = f(x, y)\). The definition with the pieces of the surface of a body between graphs is not from the sources.

Lemma 4.37 Flux through the surface of a body between two graphs (pretok skozi površino telesa med grafoma)

Let \(V\) be a body between graphs with the surface \(S\) of definition 4.36.

  1. If the function \(f\) is continuous on \(S\), the integrals over all six pieces of the surface exist.
  2. If \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) are continuous on \(V\), then
    \[\begin{aligned} \int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A = {} & \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \Big[ v_{\mathrm{z}} - \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} - \frac{\partial h}{\partial y}\,v_{\mathrm{y}} \Big]_{\mathrm{h}} \mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x \\ & - \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \Big[ v_{\mathrm{z}} - \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} - \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\,v_{\mathrm{y}} \Big]_{\mathrm{g}} \mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x \\ & + \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(b, y)} v_{\mathrm{x}}(b, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y \\ & - \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(a, y)} v_{\mathrm{x}}(a, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y \\ & + \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{d})}^{h(x, d)} v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, d, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}x \\ & - \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{c})}^{h(x, c)} v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, c, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}x , \end{aligned} \tag{4.19}\]
    where the bracket with the index \(h\) means that \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) are taken at the point \((x, y, h(x, y))\) and the partial derivatives at the point \((x, y)\), and likewise with the index \(g\).
Proof

We must show that the integrands are continuous and that on the lids the root cancels.

1. Existence.

  1. The top lid. The function \((x, y) \mapsto f(x, y, h(x, y))\) is continuous on \(R\) by lemma 4.35, with the functions \(p_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y) = x\), \(p_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y) = y\) and \(p_{\mathrm{z}} = h\), which are continuous.
  2. The square of the length \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|^2 = 1 + (\partial h/\partial x)^2 + (\partial h/\partial y)^2\) is a sum of products of continuous functions, hence continuous by corollary 1.69, item 1. For numbers \(A, B \ge 1\) we have \(|A - B| = |A^2 - B^2|/(A + B) \le |A^2 - B^2|/2\), and \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}| \ge 1\). The difference of the lengths at two points is therefore at most half the difference of the squares, and \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|\) is continuous.
  3. The integrand in (4.18) is a product of continuous functions and is continuous on \(R\). Since \(R\) is closed and bounded, it is uniformly continuous by theorem 4.6, so it has the property of item 1 of lemma 4.7, and by its item 2 the iterated integral exists. For the bottom lid it is the same.
  4. The side piece \(S_{\mathrm{a}}\) is the intersection of the closed set \(V\) (lemma 4.17) with the plane \(x = a\), which is closed (lemma 1.75, item 1), so by item 2 of the same lemma it is closed, and it is bounded. The proof of lemma 4.18, in which the numbers \(y\) of the interval \([c, d]\) take the place of the points \((x, y)\) of the rectangle, shows that the function \(y \mapsto \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(a, y)} f(a, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\) is continuous on \([c, d]\), hence integrable. For the other three side pieces it is the same.

2. Flux.

  1. On the top lid \(\vek n = \vek N_{\mathrm{h}}/|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|\), so at every point \((\vek v\cdot\vek n)\,|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}| = \vek v\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{h}} = v_{\mathrm{z}} - \frac{\partial h}{\partial x}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} - \frac{\partial h}{\partial y}\,v_{\mathrm{y}}\). The integrand in (4.18) with \(f = \vek v\cdot\vek n\) is thus the first bracket in (4.19). It is continuous on \(R\) by lemma 4.35 and corollary 1.69, so the integral exists as in step 3 of the first part.
  2. On the bottom lid likewise \((\vek v\cdot\vek n)\,|\vek N_{\mathrm{g}}| = \vek v\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{g}} = -\big(v_{\mathrm{z}} - \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\,v_{\mathrm{x}} - \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\,v_{\mathrm{y}}\big)\), and by linearity (lemma 3.39, item 1), applied to both iterated integrals, we take the minus sign out.
  3. On \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\) we have \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek v\cdot\vek n = v_{\mathrm{x}}\), on \(S_{\mathrm{a}}\) \(\vek v\cdot\vek n = -v_{\mathrm{x}}\), and likewise on \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{c}}\) with \(\pm v_{\mathrm{y}}\). The integrals exist by lemma 4.18, because \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) are continuous on \(V\).
  4. The sum of the six integrals is the right side of (4.19).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.6, (3) and (3*) (PDF p. 469), \(\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A = \vek N\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}v\), and (5″) (PDF p. 470) for the lid \(z = h(x, y)\). The proof is not from the sources.

The definition describes every piece of the surface in a single way, with the two variables given by the description of the body. The same surface can be described in other ways too. The part of the plane \(y = 3\) between the pieces \(C\) and \(D\) of the round bar is, for the piece \(C\), a side piece \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\) above the edge \(y = 3\) of its shadow, and for the piece \(D\) the bottom lid. That two descriptions of the same surface give the same integral when a suitable map between their pairs of variables joins them, we will show in section 4.3.6, where we describe surfaces more generally. We do not need it for the divergence theorem of section 4.2.12, and for the bar we will check the agreement of the two descriptions directly.

Let us test the definition on the mantle of the round bar. The top lid of the piece \(C\) is the graph of the function \(h(x, y) = q(y)\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [-3, 3]\). By lemma 4.16 \(\partial h/\partial y = q'(y) = -y/q(y)\), and the partial derivative with respect to \(x\) is zero. Hence

\[\vek N_{\mathrm{h}} = \Big(0,\ \frac{y}{q(y)},\ 1\Big) , \qquad |\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|^2 = 1 + \frac{y^2}{q(y)^2} = \frac{q(y)^2 + y^2}{q(y)^2} = \frac{r^2}{q(y)^2} ,\]

and \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}| = r/q(y)\). The outward unit normal is \(\vek n = \vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\,q(y)/r = (0,\ y/r,\ q(y)/r)\). On the lid \(z = q(y)\), so \(\vek n = (0, y/r, z/r)\), the normal of the mantle that we wrote at the beginning of section 4.2.6 (figure 4.19, right). The area of the lid is the integral of the function \(1\):

\[\int_0^L \int_{-3}^{3} \frac{r}{q(y)}\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x = L \cdot 6{,}435\ \text{mm} ,\]

where \(\int_{-3}^{3} 5/q(y)\,\mathrm{d}y = 6{,}435\) mm was computed by SymPy, because it again needs the inverse sine. This is the length of the arc of the circle above the chord from \(y = -3\) to \(y = 3\). The bottom lid of the piece \(C\) has the same area. For the piece \(D\) the top lid is the graph of the function \(q(z)\) over \([0, L] \times [-4, 4]\), with \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}} = (0,\ 1,\ z/q(z))\) and \(|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}| = r/q(z)\), and its area is \(L \cdot 9{,}273\) mm. The same holds for the bottom lid of the piece \(E\). The mantle of the bar consists of these four lids, with the total area

\[L \cdot (2 \cdot 6{,}435 + 2 \cdot 9{,}273)\ \text{mm} = L \cdot 31{,}42\ \text{mm} ,\]

which is the length of the bar times the circumference of the circle \(2\pi r = 31{,}42\) mm, the area of the mantle of a cylinder from school geometry. The integral of a constant function over a flat side piece is its value times the area of the region between graphs in its plane. The top face of the bar, \(x = 0\), consists of the side pieces \(S_{\mathrm{a}}\) of all three pieces, with the total area \(A_{\mathrm{C}} + 2A_{\mathrm{D}} = A\).

4.2.12 Divergence theorem for curved bodies

Now we have all the parts. The proof will follow the proof for a box. The term with the derivative with respect to \(z\) is handled by the fundamental theorem of calculus along the chords from the bottom to the top lid. The terms with the derivatives with respect to \(y\) and to \(x\) are brought out of the inner integral over \(z\) by lemma 4.19, item 2, at the price of terms on the lids, and then the fundamental theorem of calculus does its work along \(y\) or \(x\). Before that we must settle one more technical question. The lemma on differentiating an integral needs the function on a rectangle around the chord, while we know the field \(\vek v\) only on an open set \(D\) containing the body. Near the edge of the body the rectangle reaches a little out of the body. The following lemma says that it stays in \(D\) if it is narrow enough.

Lemma 4.38 Neighbourhood of a closed bounded set (okolica zaprte omejene množice)

Let \(K\) be a closed and bounded set of points of space (definition 1.74) and \(D\) an open set of points that contains \(K\). Then there is a number \(\delta > 0\) such that every point that is less than \(\delta\) away from some point of the set \(K\) lies in \(D\).

Proof

We must show that a single radius suffices for all points of \(K\). We argue by contradiction, with the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, as in the proof of theorem 4.6.

  1. Suppose that no such \(\delta\) exists. Then for every natural number \(n\) there are a point \(P_{\mathrm{n}} \in K\) and a point \(Q_{\mathrm{n}}\) that does not lie in \(D\), with \(|P_{\mathrm{n}} Q_{\mathrm{n}}| < 1/n\).
  2. The set \(K\) is bounded, so by lemma 1.77 the sequence \((P_{\mathrm{n}})\) has a subsequence \((P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) that converges to some point \(C\). The set \(K\) is closed, so \(C\) lies in \(K\) and therefore in \(D\).
  3. The sequence \((Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) also converges to \(C\). The proof is the same as in steps 5 and 6 of the proof of theorem 4.6.
  4. The set \(D\) is open, so there is an \(r > 0\) such that all points less than \(r\) away from \(C\) lie in \(D\). Since \((Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) converges to \(C\), for large enough \(k\) the distance \(|C Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}|\) is smaller than \(r\) (definition 1.65), and \(Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}\) lies in \(D\). This contradicts step 1, so the assumption is false.

Source: LEBL1 Lemma 7.4.10 (the Lebesgue covering lemma, PDF p. 282), with open covers instead of a single open set. The proof with sequences is not from the sources.

Theorem 4.39 Divergence theorem for a body between two graphs (izrek o divergenci za telo med grafoma)

Let \(V\) be a body between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) (definition 4.15), with the surface \(S\) and the outward unit normal \(\vek n\) (definition 4.36). Let \(D\) be an open set of points that contains \(V\), and \(\vek v = (v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\) a field that is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 1.90). Then

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \Big( \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{4.20}\]

The same holds for a body with exchanged roles of the coordinates.

Proof

We must show that the integral of each of the three partial derivatives equals the part of the right side of (4.19) in which the same component of the field appears.

1. Preparation.

  1. The body \(V\) is closed and bounded (lemma 4.17). By lemma 4.38 there is a \(\delta_0 > 0\) such that every point that is less than \(\delta_0\) away from some point of \(V\) lies in \(D\).
  2. The partial derivatives of the components of the field are continuous on \(D\) by definition 1.90, and the components themselves by lemma 1.91, that a continuously differentiable function is continuous. All of them are therefore continuous on \(V\). The integrals of the partial derivatives over \(V\) therefore exist (definition 4.20), and by linearity (lemma 4.22) the left side of (4.20) is the sum \(I_{\mathrm{x}} + I_{\mathrm{y}} + I_{\mathrm{z}}\) of the integrals of the functions \(\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x\), \(\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y\) and \(\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z\) over \(V\).
  3. For a function \(w\) that is continuous on \(V\), the functions \((x, y) \mapsto w(x, y, h(x, y))\) and \((x, y) \mapsto w(x, y, g(x, y))\) are continuous on \(R\) by lemma 4.35, and so are their products with the partial derivatives of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) by corollary 1.69, item 1. Since \(R\) is closed and bounded, these functions are uniformly continuous by theorem 4.6, and by lemma 4.7 their iterated integrals over \(R\) in both orders exist.

2. The derivative with respect to \(z\).

  1. Let \((x, y) \in R\) and \(g(x, y) < h(x, y)\). The points \((x, y, z)\) with \(g(x, y) \le z \le h(x, y)\) lie in \(V\) and therefore in \(D\), where \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) has a continuous partial derivative with respect to \(z\). The function \(z \mapsto v_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, z)\) is therefore differentiable at every point of this interval, and its derivative is continuous. It is continuous on this interval, because \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) is continuous on \(D\) (lemma 1.91) and the distance between the points \((x, y, z)\) and \((x, y, z')\) is \(|z - z'|\). By the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.40, item 1,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})}^{h(x, y)} \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z = v_{\mathrm{z}}\big(x, y, h(x, y)\big) - v_{\mathrm{z}}\big(x, y, g(x, y)\big) .\]
    If \(g(x, y) = h(x, y)\), both sides are zero.
  2. Both functions on the right are continuous on \(R\) by step 3 of the preparation. We integrate the equality over \(y\) and over \(x\) and use linearity (lemma 3.39, item 1). The integral \(I_{\mathrm{z}}\) therefore equals the two terms with the component \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) in the first two lines of (4.19).

3. The derivative with respect to \(y\).

  1. Let \(x \in [a, b]\) be fixed. For \(y \in [c, d]\) let
    \[\begin{aligned} F(y) &= \int_{\mathrm{g}}^{h} v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z , \\ E(y) &= \int_{\mathrm{g}}^{h} \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z + v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, h)\,\frac{\partial h}{\partial y} - v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, g)\,\frac{\partial g}{\partial y} , \end{aligned}\]
    where \(g\), \(h\) and their derivatives are taken at the point \((x, y)\). By lemma 4.18 and step 3 of the preparation, \(F\) and \(E\) are continuous on \([c, d]\).
  2. Let \(y_0 \in (c, d)\). Let us show that \(F'(y_0) = E(y_0)\). Let \(\alpha = g(x, y_0) - \delta_0/2\) and \(\beta = h(x, y_0) + \delta_0/2\). The functions \(y \mapsto g(x, y)\) and \(y \mapsto h(x, y)\) are continuous at \(y_0\), so there is a \(\delta_1\) with \(0 < \delta_1 \le \delta_0/2\) such that the interval \([y_0 - \delta_1, y_0 + \delta_1]\) lies in \((c, d)\) and \(\alpha \le g(x, y) \le h(x, y) \le \beta\) for every \(y\) with \(|y - y_0| \le \delta_1\).
  3. Every point \((x, y, z)\) with \(|y - y_0| \le \delta_1\) and \(\alpha \le z \le \beta\) lies in \(D\). Let \(z^*\) be the number of the interval \([g(x, y_0), h(x, y_0)]\) closest to \(z\): \(z\) itself if it lies in the interval, otherwise the nearer end. Then \(|z - z^*| \le \delta_0/2\), the point \((x, y_0, z^*)\) lies in \(V\), and the distance between the two points is \(\sqrt{(y - y_0)^2 + (z - z^*)^2} \le \sqrt{\delta_0^2/4 + \delta_0^2/4} < \delta_0\). By step 1 of the preparation the point lies in \(D\).
  4. On the rectangle \([\alpha, \beta] \times [y_0 - \delta_1, y_0 + \delta_1]\) with the variables \(t = z\) and \(s = y\) let \(f(z, y) = v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, z)\). By step 3 the rectangle lies in \(D\), which is open, so \(f\) has the partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial y = \partial v_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y\) at every point of it. At \(y = y_0 \pm \delta_1\) this is a limit on both sides, so it is also the one-sided derivative of the function \(y \mapsto f(z, y)\) on \([y_0 - \delta_1, y_0 + \delta_1]\) that lemma 4.19 requires (section 1.3.3). Both functions are continuous on the rectangle, because the distance between the points \((x, y, z)\) and \((x, y', z')\) equals the distance between \((z, y)\) and \((z', y')\). The functions \(\varphi(y) = g(x, y)\) and \(\psi(y) = h(x, y)\) have values in \([\alpha, \beta]\) and are differentiable at \(y_0\), with the derivatives \(\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}(x, y_0)\) and \(\frac{\partial h}{\partial y}(x, y_0)\) (definition 1.25). By lemma 4.19, item 2, \(F'(y_0) = E(y_0)\).
  5. The function \(F\) is thus continuous on \([c, d]\) and differentiable at every point of \((c, d)\), and its derivative \(E\) is continuous on \([c, d]\). By the fundamental theorem of calculus, item 1, \(\int_{\mathrm{c}}^d E(y)\,\mathrm{d}y = F(d) - F(c)\). By the definition of the function \(E\) and by linearity, therefore,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_{\mathrm{g}}^{h} \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y = F(d) - F(c) - \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \Big( v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, h)\,\frac{\partial h}{\partial y} - v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, y, g)\,\frac{\partial g}{\partial y} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}y .\]
  6. All three terms on the right are continuous functions of \(x\). For \(F(d) = \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{d})}^{h(x, d)} v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, d, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\) and \(F(c)\) this is lemma 4.18, for the last integral lemma 4.7, item 2, with step 3 of the preparation. We integrate the equality over \(x\) and use linearity. The integral \(I_{\mathrm{y}}\) therefore equals the last two lines of (4.19), together with the two terms with the component \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) in the first two lines.

4. The derivative with respect to \(x\).

  1. For \((x, y) \in R\) let
    \[\begin{aligned} \tilde F(x, y) &= \int_{\mathrm{g}}^{h} v_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z , \\ \tilde E(x, y) &= \int_{\mathrm{g}}^{h} \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}(x, y, z)\,\mathrm{d}z + v_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, h)\,\frac{\partial h}{\partial x} - v_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, g)\,\frac{\partial g}{\partial x} . \end{aligned}\]
    As in steps 2 to 5 of the third part, only with the roles of \(x\) and \(y\) exchanged, for fixed \(y\) the function \(x \mapsto \tilde F(x, y)\) is continuous on \([a, b]\) and differentiable at every point of \((a, b)\) with the derivative \(\tilde E(x, y)\), and \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \tilde E(x, y)\,\mathrm{d}x = \tilde F(b, y) - \tilde F(a, y)\).
  2. The function \(\tilde E\) is continuous on the rectangle \(R\) by lemma 4.18 and step 3 of the preparation. By theorem 4.9 on the order of integration, for a rectangle,
    \[\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \tilde E\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \tilde E\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y = \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \big(\tilde F(b, y) - \tilde F(a, y)\big)\,\mathrm{d}y .\]
  3. By the definition of the function \(\tilde E\) and by linearity
    \[I_{\mathrm{x}} = \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \tilde E\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x - \int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \Big( v_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, h)\,\frac{\partial h}{\partial x} - v_{\mathrm{x}}(x, y, g)\,\frac{\partial g}{\partial x} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x .\]
    By step 2 this equals the third and the fourth line of (4.19), together with the two terms with the component \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\) in the first two lines.

5. The sum.

  1. We add \(I_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(I_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(I_{\mathrm{z}}\) from the fourth, third and second part. We obtain the right side of (4.19), which by lemma 4.37, item 2, is the flux \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7, Theorem 1, (2*) (PDF p. 479), with a proof for bodies that lie between graphs in the direction of all three axes (PDF pp. 480-482). It treats the term with the derivative with respect to \(z\) as we do. The proof of the terms with the derivatives with respect to \(x\) and \(y\) by lemma 4.19 is not from the sources.

The proof has shown where the terms on the lids with the derivatives of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) come from. When we bring the derivative with respect to \(y\) out of the integral over \(z\), the limits move, and the lemma on differentiating an integral adds the values of the field on the lids, multiplied by the slope of the lid in the direction \(y\). These are exactly the components \(-\partial h/\partial y\) and \(\partial g/\partial y\) of the vectors \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\) and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{g}}\). The normal to the lid, which we obtained geometrically in section 4.2.11, from the vector product of the sides of a patch, has thus also come out of the computation. The fundamental theorem of calculus appeared three times in the proof, once for each coordinate, as for the box. We needed the rectangle \(R\) only in step 2 of the fourth part, where we exchanged the order of integration in \(x\) and in \(y\).

Let us test the theorem on the right piece \(D\) of the round hanging bar, with the displacement field of the hanging bar (1.18),

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}} &= a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2) , \\ u_{\mathrm{y}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y , \\ u_{\mathrm{z}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,z , \end{aligned}\]

with \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\), the length \(L = 10\) m and the radius of the cross section \(r = 5\) mm. The bar hangs under its own weight and is held in the idealized way of section 1.7.1. The piece \(D\) consists of the points of the bar with \(y \ge 3\) mm, a body between the graphs of the constant function \(3\) mm and the function \(q(z)\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [-4, 4]\) in the variables \(x\) and \(z\) (section 4.2.6, figure 4.21, right). The components of the field are polynomials, so they are continuously differentiable in all of space, which we take as the open set of the theorem.

The left side. In section 4.2.5 we computed the divergence \(0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\). It does not depend on \(y\) and \(z\), so the inner and the middle integral give \(0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\,A_{\mathrm{D}}\), with the area of the cross section of the piece \(A_{\mathrm{D}} = 11{,}18\ \text{mm}^2\) from section 4.2.8, and the outer one

\[0{,}8\,a\,\frac{L^2}{2}\,A_{\mathrm{D}} = 0{,}4\,a L^2 A_{\mathrm{D}} = 0{,}4 \cdot 0{,}01952\ \text{mm} \cdot 11{,}18\ \text{mm}^2 = 0{,}08731\ \text{mm}^3 ,\]

where \(a L^2 = 19{,}52\) µm \(= 0{,}01952\) mm is the displacement of the lower end of the bar.

The right side. The flux through the six pieces of the surface of the piece \(D\), by lemma 4.37 with \(y\) as the coordinate that runs between the graphs:

  1. The side piece \(x = L\), part of the bottom face of the bar, with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The integral of the function \(u_{\mathrm{x}}(L, y, z) = aL^2 - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\) over the cross section of the piece is \(aL^2 A_{\mathrm{D}} - 0{,}3\,a\,\Theta_{\mathrm{D}} = 0{,}2183\ \text{mm}^3\), where \(\Theta_{\mathrm{D}} = \int_{-4}^{4}\int_3^{q(z)} (y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}z = 203{,}8\ \text{mm}^4\). The second term is very small, \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-8}\ \text{mm}^3\).
  2. The side piece \(x = 0\), part of the top face of the bar, with the normal \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). The integrand is \(-u_{\mathrm{x}}(0, y, z) = 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\), the flux \(0{,}3\,a\,\Theta_{\mathrm{D}} = 1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-8}\ \text{mm}^3\).
  3. The top lid \(y = q(z)\), part of the mantle, with \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}} = (0,\ 1,\ z/q(z))\). At a point of the lid \(\vek u\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{h}} = u_{\mathrm{y}} + u_{\mathrm{z}}\,z/q(z) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,\big(q(z) + z^2/q(z)\big) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,r^2/q(z)\). The integral over \(z\) is \(r\) times the arc length \(9{,}273\) mm from section 4.2.11, and the integral over \(x\) gives \(L^2/2\). The flux is \(-0{,}6\,a\,\tfrac{L^2}{2} \cdot 5\ \text{mm} \cdot 9{,}273\ \text{mm} = -0{,}2715\ \text{mm}^3\).
  4. The bottom lid \(y = 3\), the cut toward the piece \(C\), with \(\vek N_{\mathrm{g}} = (0, -1, 0)\). The integrand is \(-u_{\mathrm{y}}(x, 3, z) = 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) \cdot 3\ \text{mm}\). The integral over \(z\) from \(-4\) to \(4\) gives the factor \(8\) mm, the one over \(x\) the factor \(L^2/2\), together \(0{,}6\,a\,\tfrac{L^2}{2} \cdot 24\ \text{mm}^2 = 0{,}1405\ \text{mm}^3\).
  5. The side pieces \(z = \pm 4\). There \(q(\pm 4) = 3\), so \(y\) runs from \(3\) to \(3\), and the integrals are zero by the convention of definition 3.34. The pieces are segments on the mantle that have no area.

The sum is \(0{,}2183 + 0{,}0000 - 0{,}2715 + 0{,}1405 = 0{,}0873\ \text{mm}^3\), the same as the left side. We computed all the integrals with SymPy. What do they say? The lower end of the piece moves down and sweeps \(0{,}2183\ \text{mm}^3\) outward. The mantle moves toward the axis of the bar, because the bar gets thinner, and sweeps \(0{,}2715\ \text{mm}^3\) inward. The cut \(y = 3\) also moves toward the axis, in the direction \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), which for the piece \(D\) is the outward direction, so it contributes \(0{,}1405\ \text{mm}^3\). The piece \(D\) follows the thinning of the bar toward its axis.

The round bar itself is not one body between graphs but is cut into three pieces. We apply the theorem to each piece and add the equalities. On the left we get the integral over the bar (definition 4.21). On the right, however, we get the fluxes through all pieces of the surfaces of all three bodies, also through the cuts \(y = \pm 3\), which are not part of the surface of the bar. As with the cells of a body made of boxes, the contributions of each cut cancel, because the cut has the normal \(\vek n\) for the piece on one side and \(-\vek n\) for the piece on the other side (figure 4.33).

Corollary 4.40 Divergence theorem for a body cut into pieces (izrek o divergenci za telo, razrezano na kose)

Let \(V\) be cut into the pieces \(V_1, \dots, V_{\mathrm{m}}\), which are bodies between graphs (definition 4.21). Let the pieces of the surfaces of these bodies (definition 4.36) be divided into outer and inner ones, and the inner ones into pairs, so that each pair consists of pieces of the surfaces of two different bodies and the flux of every continuous field through one piece is the negative of the flux through the other. Let \(S\) be the union of the outer pieces, the surface of the body \(V\), and \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\) the sum of the fluxes through the outer pieces. Let \(D\) be an open set of points that contains \(V\), and \(\vek v\) a field that is continuously differentiable on \(D\). Then

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \Big( \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{4.21}\]
Proof

We must show that the fluxes through the inner pieces cancel.

  1. Every body \(V_{\mathrm{k}}\) lies in \(V\), hence in \(D\). By theorem 4.39 the integral of the divergence of the field \(\vek v\) over \(V_{\mathrm{k}}\) equals the flux through its surface, that is, the sum of the fluxes through its six pieces.
  2. We add the equalities over \(k\) from \(1\) to \(m\). The sum of the left sides is, by definition 4.21, the integral of the divergence over \(V\).
  3. The sum of the right sides is the sum of the fluxes through all pieces of the surfaces of all bodies \(V_{\mathrm{k}}\). The inner pieces come in pairs, and the two fluxes of each pair are opposite numbers that cancel. What remains is the sum of the fluxes through the outer pieces, which is \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7 (PDF p. 482): for a body that auxiliary surfaces cut into finitely many pieces, the integrals over the auxiliary surfaces cancel in pairs. The proof follows the source.

The condition on the pairs has to be checked for every cut. For two flat pieces in the same plane that both descriptions give by the same iterated integral and with opposite normals, it holds by itself. So it is for the bar. The cut \(y = 3\) is, for the piece \(C\), the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\) with the flux \(\int_0^L \int_{-\mathrm{q}(3)}^{q(3)} v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, 3, z)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}x\), and for the piece \(D\) the bottom lid with \(\vek N_{\mathrm{g}} = (0, -1, 0)\) and with the flux \(\int_0^L \int_{-4}^{4} \big(-v_{\mathrm{y}}(x, 3, z)\big)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}x\). Since \(q(3) = 4\), these are the same iterated integral with opposite signs, for every continuous field \(\vek v\). The same holds for the cut \(y = -3\) between the pieces \(C\) and \(E\). For pieces that the two descriptions give differently, we show the agreement in section 4.3.6.

Let us check the corollary on the whole bar, with the same displacement field. The fluxes through the pieces of the surfaces and the integrals of the divergence are in cubic millimetres, computed with SymPy:

\(C\) \(D\) \(E\) bar
bottom face \(x = L\) \(1{,}0965\) \(0{,}2183\) \(0{,}2183\) \(1{,}5331\)
top face \(x = 0\) \(3{,}4 \cdot 10^{-8}\) \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-8}\) \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-8}\) \(5{,}7 \cdot 10^{-8}\)
mantle \(-0{,}3768\) \(-0{,}2715\) \(-0{,}2715\) \(-0{,}9199\)
cut \(y = 3\) \(-0{,}1405\) \(0{,}1405\) \(0\)
cut \(y = -3\) \(-0{,}1405\) \(0{,}1405\) \(0\)
sum of the fluxes \(0{,}4386\) \(0{,}0873\) \(0{,}0873\) \(0{,}6132\)
integral of the divergence \(0{,}4386\) \(0{,}0873\) \(0{,}0873\) \(0{,}6132\)

For each piece the last two rows are equal, as theorem 4.39 says. In the column of the bar the cuts cancel, as the corollary says. What remains is the bottom face, which moves down by \(aL^2 = 19{,}52\) µm and sweeps \(aL^2 A = 1{,}5331\ \text{mm}^3\), the mantle, which moves toward the axis and sweeps \(0{,}6\,aL^2 A = 0{,}9199\ \text{mm}^3\) inward, and a very small contribution of the top face, which rises a little at the rim. The volume of the bar increases by \(0{,}4\,aL^2 A = 0{,}6132\ \text{mm}^3\). The relative change is \(0{,}6132/785\,400 = 7{,}808 \cdot 10^{-7}\), the same as for the box in section 4.2.5. Why the same? The divergence \(0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\) depends only on the depth.
