For every part of the bar that spans its whole length, the relative change of volume is therefore the mean of this linear function, which is its value at the middle, \(0{,}4\,aL\), whatever the shape of the cross section.

With this we have proved the divergence theorem for all bodies that can be cut into finitely many bodies between graphs so that the inner pieces of the surfaces pair up. Such are the box, the body made of boxes and the round bar, that is, all the bodies of our examples so far. Three more things remain. The first are the bodies that we cannot cut in this way, for instance a ball. We prove the theorem for them in section 4.3.7, for all bodies that we cut into bodies between graphs and into bodies that we get by bending a box continuously. This covers all the bodies of our examples, the ball, the thick spherical shell and the tube included. KREYSZIG states the theorem also for bodies with an arbitrary surface made of smooth pieces (§10.7, Theorem 1, PDF p. 479) and only mentions that they would need a further limit process (PDF p. 482). The second, the independence of the integral of the order of integration and of the cut, is already proved. By corollary 4.34 the sum of definition 4.21 is the integral over a set with volume, which knows nothing of the cut. The third, the independence of the surface integral of the description of the surface, we show in section 4.3.6 for descriptions joined by a suitable map between their variables.

4.2.13 Equilibrium of a part of a body

Now we can keep the promise of section 2.7.6. We derived the equilibrium equations (2.31) from the equilibrium of small cubes. Do they also imply the equilibrium of every finite part of the body? Two kinds of forces act on such a part. The rest of the body acts on it across its surface \(S\), with the traction vector \(\vek t(\vek n)\) per unit area, where \(\vek n\) is the outward normal of the part (definition 2.20). On all its material acts the body force \(\vek b\) per unit volume. The total force across the surface is the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek t\,\mathrm{d}A\), the total body force the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\,\mathrm{d}V\), both by components, as we agreed in section 4.2.3.

Corollary 4.41 Equilibrium of a part of a body (ravnovesje dela telesa)

Let a body be in equilibrium and let \(V\) be a part of it that is a body made of boxes with the surface \(S\) and the outward normal \(\vek n\), and let every point of \(V\) be an interior point of the body. Let the stress components be continuously differentiable on an open set \(D\) that contains \(V\) (definition 1.90), let the body force \(\vek b\) be continuous on \(V\), let the equilibrium equations (2.31) hold at every point of \(V\), and let the assumption of Cauchy's formula (theorem 2.24) hold at every point of \(V\), that the average force per unit area on a plane face approaches the traction vector at the point when we shrink the face towards this point. Then

\[\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek t(\vek n)\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\,\mathrm{d}V = \vek 0 , \tag{4.22}\]

where \(\vek t(\vek n)\) is the traction vector at a point of the surface \(S\) for the outward normal \(\vek n\) of the part \(V\).

Proof

We must show that each component of the left side is zero. We integrate the equilibrium equations over \(V\) and use the divergence theorem and Cauchy's formula.

  1. At every point of \(V\) the first equation (2.31) holds, \(\dfrac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \dfrac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} + b_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\). All four terms are continuous on \(V\).
  2. The integral of the zero function is zero (lemma 4.10, item 2, on each cell). By linearity (same lemma, item 1) therefore
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \Big( \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}}{\partial z} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{V}} b_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}V = 0 .\]
  3. By the divergence theorem 4.14, item 2, with the field \((v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}}) = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}})\), which is continuously differentiable on \(D\), the first integral equals
    \[\int_{\mathrm{S}} \big( \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yx}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} \big)\,\mathrm{d}A .\]
  4. Every point of the surface \(S\) is an interior point of the body at which the assumption of Cauchy's formula holds, so Cauchy's formula holds there (theorem 2.24). By (2.24) the integrand of step 3 is the component \(t_{\mathrm{x}}(\vek n)\) of the traction vector. From step 2 we get \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} t_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}A + \int_{\mathrm{V}} b_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\).
  5. For the component \(y\) we repeat steps 1 to 4 with the second equation (2.31) and the field \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zy}})\), for the component \(z\) with the third equation and the field \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}})\). By (2.24) the integrands on the surface are \(t_{\mathrm{y}}(\vek n)\) and \(t_{\mathrm{z}}(\vek n)\).

Source: SADD (3.7.1)-(3.7.3) (PDF pp. 77-78), where the argument runs the other way: the equilibrium equations follow from the equilibrium of every part.

The proof wrote out exactly the picture of a wall of bricks from section 2.7.6. In the proof of the divergence theorem for a body made of boxes the contributions of the inner faces cancelled, because the outward normal of a shared face is \(\vek n\) for one cell and \(-\vek n\) for the other. By lemma 2.21 the two forces across the shared face are therefore opposite too. What remains are the forces on the surface of the part and the body forces. For a body that moves with an acceleration, the right side of (4.22) would hold, instead of the zero vector, the integral of the density times the acceleration, as in the equations of motion of section 2.7.6. We did not use the symmetry of stress (theorem 2.36). We need it for the second condition of equilibrium of a part, that the sum of the moments of the forces across the surface and of the body forces is zero. That follows in the same way from the equilibrium equations, the divergence theorem and the symmetry of stress (SADD (3.7.6) onward, PDF pp. 78-79), which we do not write out here.

Let us test the corollary on the box \(K = [x_1, x_2] \times [-c, c] \times [-c, c]\) in the hanging bar, with \(x_1 = 3\) m, \(x_2 = 6\) m and \(c = 0{,}003\) m, as in section 4.2.3 (figure 4.34). The bar of length \(L = 10\) m hangs under its own weight, is held in the idealized way, and has the axis \(x\) pointing down. The only stress component that is not zero is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \rho g\,(L - x)\) (section 2.7.6), a polynomial that is continuously differentiable in the whole space. All points of the box are interior points of the bar. Each is at most 4,243 mm from the axis, so at least \(5 - 4{,}243 = 0{,}757\) mm from the mantle of the bar, at least 3 m from the top face and at least 4 m from the bottom face. By (2.24), \(\vek t(\vek n) = (\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}, 0, 0)\).

  1. On the top face \(x = x_1\) we have \(\vek n = -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek t = (-\rho g\,(L - x_1), 0, 0)\). The integrand is constant, so the integral over the face of area \(4c^2\) is \((-4c^2\rho g\,(L - x_1), 0, 0)\). The part of the bar above the box pulls it up with the force \(36 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2 \cdot 76\,518\ \text{N/m}^3 \cdot 7\ \text{m} = 19{,}28\) N.
  2. On the bottom face \(x = x_2\) we have \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek t = (\rho g\,(L - x_2), 0, 0)\). The part of the bar below the box pulls it down with the force \(4c^2\rho g\,(L - x_2) = 11{,}02\) N.
  3. On the four side faces \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), so \(\vek t = \vek 0\). The neighbouring material does not act on the side faces.
  4. The weight of the box is \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} \vek b\,\mathrm{d}V = (4c^2\rho g\,(x_2 - x_1), 0, 0)\), that is \(8{,}264\) N down, as we computed in section 4.2.3.

The component \(x\) of the left side of (4.22) is \(4c^2\rho g\,\big({-(L - x_1)} + (L - x_2) + (x_2 - x_1)\big) = 0\), with the numbers rounded to hundredths of a newton \(-19{,}28 + 11{,}02 + 8{,}26 = 0\). The weight of the box is thus exactly the difference between the forces on its top and bottom faces. This is the same reasoning as in section 2.1, where we got the axial force from the equilibrium of the part of the bar below a cross section, only the box does not reach the bottom.

What about the whole bar (figure 4.34, left)? It is a cylinder, not a body made of boxes, and its surface is not in the interior of the body. On the surface of a body the traction vector is the force of the surroundings per unit area. SADD requires on the surface that this force be related to the stresses at the points of the surface by Cauchy's formula (§5.2, PDF pp. 104-106). For the hanging bar this is so: the top face is pulled up by the force \(\rho g L\) per unit area, which is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(0)\), while the bottom face and the mantle are free, \(\vek t = \vek 0\), which agrees with \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(L) = 0\) and with \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) on the mantle. The integrands are constant on each face, so we compute the integrals with the cross-section area \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\) and the volume \(AL\), which we computed with the cut of the bar into three pieces in sections 4.2.8 and 4.2.11. The force on the surface is \((-\rho g L A, 0, 0)\), a force of \(60{,}10\) N up, and the body force is \((\rho g A L, 0, 0)\), the weight of \(60{,}10\) N down. The sum is the zero vector, as (4.22) requires. The divergence theorem for a body cut into pieces (corollary 4.40) tells us that the test is no accident. With it corollary 4.41 holds, with the same proof, also for a part of a body that is cut into pieces between graphs, if in step 2 we use the linearity of lemma 4.22, and in step 3 corollary 4.40 in place of theorem 4.14. So it holds for round parts of the bar in its interior, which are not made of boxes. It holds also for the whole bar, although the points of its surface are not interior points. At the points of the surface step 4 needs only Cauchy's formula, which holds on the surface of the bar by the requirement of SADD. The equilibrium equations, which step 1 needs, hold at all points of the bar for the polynomial stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \rho g\,(L - x)\).

SADD takes this road in the opposite direction. From the equilibrium of every part of the body it obtains, with the divergence theorem, that the integral of the left side of the equilibrium equations is zero over every part, and concludes from this that the integrand is zero at every point (SADD (3.7.3) and (3.7.4) with (1.8.12), PDF pp. 28-29 and 78). We will need a similar conclusion in the next sections: a continuous function is zero if every integral of it of a certain kind is zero.

With this we have, for a body in space, the integral over a body and over its surface and the theorem that connects them, for all bodies that we can cut into pieces between graphs. Before we write equilibrium in a new form, with the work of the forces, the next section shows how an integral changes when we describe the points of a body by other variables. With this we will extend the divergence theorem to bodies that we cannot cut into pieces between graphs, and say exactly how the volume of a small piece changes under loading.
